theory_units.summary: If a dominant player must be on the left, compensate by giving them preferential compositional treatment such as better lighting, favorable body angling, stronger contrast, or separation from the background.
theory_units.applies_when: When narrative or blocking necessitates placing the dominant subject on the left side of the frame.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures the left-positioned player still maintains dominance and visual importance despite being on the 'weaker' side.

theory_units.title: Leading Lines Diminishing Rightward
theory_units.summary: Arrange leading lines in the composition so they diminish toward the right side of the frame.
theory_units.applies_when: When using natural or constructed lines to guide viewer attention within a frame.
theory_units.expected_effect: Attracts the viewer's eye to the center of interest more effectively.

theory_units.title: Strategic Frame Positions for Dramatic Emphasis
theory_units.summary: Be aware of the merits of various frame positions to strategically place subjects for best dramatic emphasis.
theory_units.applies_when: When composing any shot where dramatic impact is desired.
theory_units.expected_effect: Optimizes visual storytelling by using frame positions to enhance emotional or narrative significance.

theory_units.title: Cheating Player Height for Dominance
theory_units.summary: In theatrical films, subtly cheat a leading player's height to make them appear taller and more dominant, especially in medium or close shots.
theory_units.applies_when: When a leading player needs to appear taller or more commanding than others, particularly in theatrical films.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a visual hierarchy, making the 'taller' player appear more powerful or significant.
theory_units.caution: Must be done subtly to avoid detection, especially in medium or close shots.

theory_units.title: Using Forced Perspective Sets
theory_units.summary: Design converging sets with built-in forced perspective where normal-sized players are in the foreground and under-sized or midget players are in the distance.
theory_units.applies_when: When needing to manipulate perceived size and distance within a theatrical film, creating illusions of scale.
theory_units.expected_effect: Deceives the eye regarding the apparent size of objects and figures, allowing for dramatic scale changes.

theory_units.title: True Size Representation (Non-Theatrical Films)
theory_units.summary: In non-theatrical films, avoid falsification and strive to show the true size of objects, often by including operators, objects of known size, or familiar backgrounds for scale.
theory_units.applies_when: In documentary, instructional, or scientific films where factual accuracy of scale is paramount.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains credibility and provides accurate information about the size of objects.
theory_units.caution: Falsification of size must usually be avoided; otherwise, the true size of objects must be shown.

theory_units.title: Perceived Size through Framing
theory_units.summary: Images that crowd the frame are perceived as larger than images with more space around them, regardless of actual physical size.
theory_units.applies_when: When manipulating the perceived size or dominance of a subject within the frame.
theory_units.expected_effect: Can make a tiny object appear huge by crowding the frame, or a large object appear small by providing ample space.

theory_units.title: Enhancing Loftiness through High Framing
theory_units.summary: Make an object appear loftier by positioning it high in the frame with little sky visible above it.
theory_units.applies_when: When emphasizing the height or grandeur of a tall object like a mountain.
theory_units.expected_effect: Conveys a sense of immense height and scale.

theory_units.title: Suggesting Larger Quantity through Overlapping/Framing
theory_units.summary: Make a relatively small number of subjects appear greater by crowding them to overlap the frame, suggesting more are outside the picture.
theory_units.applies_when: When needing to imply a larger crowd, organization, or quantity than is actually present or fully visible.
theory_units.expected_effect: Relays the impression that the entire picture is vast or complicated, suggesting a large scale beyond the frame.

theory_units.title: Conveying Vastness/Complexity through Partial View
theory_units.summary: Show less than the whole of a group or object (e.g., partial crowds, electronic circuits) to convey an impression of vastness or complexity.
theory_units.applies_when: When aiming to make a scene feel expansive, intricate, or overwhelming.
theory_units.expected_effect: Relays the impression that the entire picture is too vast or complicated to capture in its entirety.

theory_units.title: Enhancing Height with Upward Camera Angle
theory_units.summary: Make a figure or object appear taller by angling the camera upward, especially if the image contains converging vertical parallel lines.
theory_units.applies_when: When emphasizing the height, power, or dominance of a subject.
theory_units.expected_effect: Visually elongates the subject, making it appear taller and potentially more imposing.

theory_units.title: Enhancing Height with Low Angle & Wide-Angle Lens
theory_units.summary: Use a low angle and a wide-angle lens to make a tall building appear even taller.
theory_units.applies_when: Specifically for architectural subjects like tall buildings, to exaggerate their height.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a dramatic exaggeration of height and scale.

theory_units.title: Enhancing Subjective Height with Low Angle & Crowded Frame
theory_units.summary: For a subjective height effect (e.g., from a child's viewpoint), use a low-angle shot with the subject crowding the frame.
theory_units.applies_when: When attempting to convey a character's (e.g., child's) perception of height and scale from their perspective.
theory_units.expected_effect: Conveys a similar height effect, making the viewed subject appear larger and more imposing from the subjective viewpoint.

theory_units.title: Emotional Impact of Extreme Shots
theory_units.summary: Employ extreme long shots (especially high angle, looking down on tiny subjects) or extreme close-ups to provoke greater emotional response and audience involvement.
theory_units.applies_when: To portray hardships, vastness, isolation, or intense intimacy and evoke strong emotions in the audience.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provokes the audience into greater involvement in the story by arousing emotions, provides visual variety.

theory_units.title: Composing for Multiple Viewpoints
theory_units.summary: Compose shots with definite viewpoints in mind, recognizing that a composition perfect for one angle may be poor from another, especially in sequences with multiple angles.
theory_units.applies_when: When planning any scene that will be covered from several different camera angles.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures that all shots within a sequence are visually effective and cohesive, regardless of camera position.
theory_units.caution: A composition perfect for a particular camera angle may be very poor when viewed from an opposite angle.

theory_units.title: Integrated Composition and Camera Angles
theory_units.summary: Integrate composition and camera angles so that players and pictorial elements remain properly composed as the camera moves through a sequence.
theory_units.applies_when: Essential for any sequence involving camera or player movement and multiple setups.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains a consistently strong visual aesthetic throughout the sequence, avoiding jarring compositional shifts.

theory_units.title: Maintaining Composition from Long Shot to Close-up
theory_units.summary: A good long-shot composition will generally work well for closer shots if camera set-ups are not drastically altered, requiring careful lining up during rehearsal.
theory_units.applies_when: When shooting a sequence that moves from wide to closer shots of the same subject matter.
theory_units.expected_effect: Preserves the player/background relationship and overall composition across different shot sizes, creating smooth transitions.
theory_units.caution: Drastically altered camera set-ups can change the player/background relationship and undermine composition.

theory_units.title: Continuous Composition through Harmonious Movement
theory_units.summary: Plan player and/or camera movement to work in harmony, continuously composing the scene and revising player/background relationships as action progresses.
theory_units.applies_when: In dynamic scenes with significant movement, where maintaining strong composition throughout is crucial.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures the scene remains continuously well-composed, prevents awkward pictorial situations, and allows for smooth transitions into closer shots.
theory_units.caution: An excellent static composition may deteriorate into confusion if movements are unplanned or player/background relationships change drastically.

theory_units.title: Avoiding Distractions from Frame Edges in Closer Shots
theory_units.summary: When moving into side angles or over-the-shoulder close-ups, be vigilant for distracting objects (e.g., lamps, furniture) that may suddenly appear or merge with players' features.
theory_units.applies_when: When planning closer shots, especially those from new angles like side profiles or over-the-shoulder.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains focus on the main action and characters by preventing unintended visual interference.
theory_units.caution: Distracting objects can detract from the main action or create awkward visual mergers with players.

theory_units.title: Maintaining Continuous Composition Vigilance
theory_units.summary: Continuously maintain proper framing for players, pleasing player/background relationships, and well-composed pauses at key positions throughout moving shots.
theory_units.applies_when: Throughout any scene involving movement, to ensure consistent compositional quality.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures a polished and professional visual flow, keeping the audience engaged without distractions from compositional errors.
theory_units.caution: Requires constant vigilance to avoid compositional problems.

theory_units.title: Choreographing Movement for Continuous Composition
theory_units.summary: To best achieve continuous composition, first compose players carefully in each key position for optimal pictorial effect, then work out the movements between those key positions.
theory_units.applies_when: When planning complex scenes with significant player movement and multiple important stopping points.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures that both static and dynamic moments within a scene are optimally composed, creating a seamless and visually strong sequence.

theory_units.title: Linear Perspective for Depth and Solidity
theory_units.summary: Linear perspective creates the illusion of depth and solidity in a picture through the convergence of parallel lines and diminishing sizes of objects with distance.
theory_units.applies_when: A fundamental principle to enhance the three-dimensional quality of a two-dimensional image.
theory_units.expected_effect: Helps viewers judge distance, creating a realistic sense of depth and form.

theory_units.title: Increasing Solidity with Angle-Plus-Angle Shots
theory_units.summary: Choose camera angles that portray the greatest number of planes or facets of a subject, shooting 'angle-plus-angle' to record front, side, and top/bottom for maximum solidity.
theory_units.applies_when: When emphasizing the three-dimensional form and physical presence of an object.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a stronger sense of solidity and volume for the subject.

theory_units.title: Using Lens & Angle for Linear Convergence without Distortion
theory_units.summary: Select a short focal length lens (not necessarily wide-angle) and a suitable camera angle to record realistic linear perspective with converging lines that lead the eye into the scene, without distortion.
theory_units.applies_when: When aiming to enhance depth and guide viewer attention into the far reaches of a scene.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a realistic sense of depth and draws the viewer's eye into the background of the scene, without undesirable distortion.

theory_units.title: Extreme Wide-Angle Lenses for Special Convergence
theory_units.summary: Use extreme wide-angle lenses exclusively for special effects when a greater than normal degree of linear convergence is desired.
theory_units.applies_when: Only when specifically aiming for exaggerated perspective or a distorted visual effect.
theory_units.expected_effect: Produces strong, exaggerated linear convergence.
theory_units.caution: Extreme wide-angle lenses typically introduce distortion and should not be used for realistic perspective unless intended for special effects.

theory_units.title: Audience Involvement through Camera Proximity
theory_units.summary: Achieve the finest modeling of players and setting, and greatest audience involvement, by bringing the camera as close as possible to the subject.
theory_units.applies_when: When aiming for intimacy, detail, and strong emotional connection with the subject.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhances the tactile quality of the visuals and increases the audience's emotional engagement with the scene.

theory_units.title: Overlapping Objects for Spatial Depth
theory_units.summary: Position players, props, and objects to partially overlap, naturally conveying their spatial relationships and distance from the camera.
theory_units.applies_when: When needing to clearly establish spatial relationships between multiple objects or figures in a scene, especially when their known size is not obvious.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates an immediate and unambiguous sense of spatial depth, clarity on which objects are nearer, and a three-dimensional illusion on a two-dimensional screen.

theory_units.title: Motion Parallax for Dynamic Depth
theory_units.summary: Introduce motion parallax by moving players or the camera to partially cover and uncover other elements, or by moving the camera through foreground objects, to convey position and distance.
theory_units.applies_when: When players or the camera are in motion, and there's an opportunity to reveal or obscure parts of the scene to enhance depth perception.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhances the viewer's understanding of spatial relationships, creates a dynamic sense of depth, and adds visual interest to movement.

theory_units.title: Angled Movement for Enhanced Depth
theory_units.summary: Stage player or vehicle movement toward or away from the camera, or angle cross-screen movement slightly, to impart a change in image size and convey spatial depth.
theory_units.applies_when: Whenever players or vehicles are moving, to maximize the sense of three-dimensional space.
theory_units.expected_effect: A feeling of spatial depth and distance; a more dynamic and less flat portrayal of movement.
theory_units.caution: Avoid movements precisely at right angles to the lens, which flatten the image.

theory_units.title: Avoid Flat Lighting
theory_units.summary: Do not use overall shadowless illumination, as it flattens the field, removes modeling, and prevents separation of figures and objects.
theory_units.applies_when: In any filming situation, indoors or outdoors, where depth and three-dimensionality are desired.
theory_units.expected_effect: Prevents flatness of field, ensures figures and objects have texture and separation.
theory_units.caution: Over-all shadowless illumination produces a flatness of field, minus projections and modeling, lacking texture, and preventing separation of figures and objects.

theory_units.title: Utilize Side & Differential Lighting for 3D Modeling
theory_units.summary: Employ side lighting or contrasting planes of light and shade in interior scenes to create shadow areas and impart three-dimensional modeling and a front-to-back quality.
theory_units.applies_when: When lighting figures and settings, especially indoors, to enhance their three-dimensional appearance.
theory_units.expected_effect: Figures and setting appear well-modeled, with depth and a clear front-to-back quality, preventing flatness.

theory_units.title: Aerial Perspective through Background Lighting
theory_units.summary: Enhance aerial perspective outdoors by including lighter, distant backgrounds, or indoors by lighting the background slightly 'hotter' to draw the viewer's eye into the depth of the setting.
theory_units.applies_when: When filming outdoors with distant elements or indoors to create a sense of deep space.
theory_units.expected_effect: Adds additional aerial perspective, guiding the viewer's eye into the far reaches of the setting and enhancing depth.

theory_units.title: Backgrounds as Storytelling Aids
theory_units.summary: Integrate backgrounds into the story to contribute activity, authenticity, and realism, choosing camera angles and staging action against backgrounds that clearly convey the specific activity.
theory_units.applies_when: Whenever filming on location, especially for non-theatrical or documentary subjects, to enrich the narrative.
theory_units.expected_effect: Adds greater scope, pictorial interest, and a 'you-are-there' feeling, making the story more believable and informative.
theory_units.caution: Many cameramen ignore or misuse backgrounds, missing opportunities to enhance the story.

theory_units.title: Subtle Background Reinforcement
theory_units.summary: The background should constantly, yet subtly, remind the viewer of the story's location, adding realism without distracting from the main action.
theory_units.applies_when: Throughout a film, especially documentary or location-based narratives, to ground the story in its setting.
theory_units.expected_effect: Adds realism and context, ensuring the viewer consistently understands the environment the story unfolds in.

theory_units.title: Avoid Nondescript/Distracting Backgrounds
theory_units.summary: Carefully scout indoor locations to avoid backgrounds that are quiet, nondescript, or detract from the story, ensuring they contribute rather than hinder the narrative.
theory_units.applies_when: When choosing staging for interior scenes, or when tempted to use plain settings for convenience after establishing shots.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains story coherence and viewer engagement, preventing loss of location's true meaning.
theory_units.caution: Staging scenes against nondescript backgrounds deters from the story; filming only establishing long shots then retiring to plain settings loses the purpose of expensive travel to location.

theory_units.title: Isolate Players for Concentrated Focus
theory_units.summary: Isolate players against a simple, nondescript background (like the sky) when action or dialogue demands complete audience concentration without distracting elements.
theory_units.applies_when: When the camera moves closer to a small group or single player, and their action/dialogue is paramount.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures the audience's complete attention is on the players, preventing distractions.

theory_units.title: Background Does Not Distract
theory_units.summary: Ensure the background never steals the show by being more interesting than the main action or dialogue, or by distracting the audience with its make-up, movement, or color.
theory_units.applies_when: In all compositions, but especially as the camera moves closer to the subjects.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains audience focus on the primary subject and narrative, ensuring clear communication of the story.
theory_units.caution: A background that is too interesting will steal the show; it should not intrude on foreground players or action.

theory_units.title: Distinct Foreground-Background Separation
theory_units.summary: Position players and objects to ensure distinct separation from the background, utilizing lighting effects, contrasting tones, or distinct colors to prevent flattening of the picture.
theory_units.applies_when: Always, but particularly important in close-ups where the player's head should stand out from the background.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a three-dimensional appearance, ensures figures 'stand out', and avoids merging that flattens the image.
theory_units.caution: A figure or object similarly toned or colored, merging with the background, will flatten the picture. Annoying lines or shapes piercing a player's body/head, or disturbing background elements.

theory_units.title: Foreground Frames for Compositional Aid
theory_units.summary: Utilize foreground pictorial elements (e.g., arches, windows, branches) to partially or completely frame the main subject, containing the action and preventing viewer's eyes from wandering off-screen.
theory_units.applies_when: When a scene benefits from enhanced depth, contained action, or directed viewer focus.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides a pictorial foreground element, contains the action, prevents viewer's eyes from wandering off-screen, and adds depth.
theory_units.caution: Frames should not be composed evenly on all sides unless perfectly symmetrical.

theory_units.title: Lighting Foreground Frames for Depth and Separation
theory_units.summary: Employ back-cross or complete backlighting for frames to edge-light and outline them, separating them from the distant view, adding depth through shadows, and preventing merging caused by flat front light.
theory_units.applies_when: When using foreground frames to enhance their three-dimensional appearance and distinction from the background.
theory_units.expected_effect: Adds depth, solidity, edge-lights the frame, imparts a luminous/ethereal quality to translucent objects, and creates shadows for depth. Prevents a 'cardboard cut-out' appearance and frame-scene merging.
theory_units.caution: A frame should not be shot in a flat front light, or it will include the same tonal values as the main scene and merge with it.

theory_units.title: Appropriate and Non-Distracting Frames
theory_units.summary: Ensure frames are appropriate to the scene and do not detract from the main subject; avoid elaborate, artificial, or otherwise distracting frames.
theory_units.applies_when: When selecting or creating foreground frames for a shot.
theory_units.expected_effect: The frame serves as an aid without competing for attention, keeping the focus on the main subject.
theory_units.caution: Improper frames are often artificially contrived and can cause trouble if too elaborate or distracting. The subject is the picture; the frame is only a compositional aid.

theory_units.title: Effective Partial Frames with Solid Connection
theory_units.summary: When a full frame isn't present, use a partial frame (e.g., top and one side) to break up empty space, but ensure it shows solid connection and isn't so minimal it teases the audience.
theory_units.applies_when: When dealing with large expanses of empty foreground or bald skies, and a full frame is not feasible.
theory_units.expected_effect: Breaks up dull areas, adds compositional interest, and enhances depth without confusing the viewer.
theory_units.caution: A part of a tree branch, or other object, should not just 'hang in space'. Too little of a frame may tease the audience if they cannot deduce what it is.

theory_units.title: Sharp Frame Focus for Clarity
theory_units.summary: Keep foreground frames sharp to avoid distracting the viewer, using split focus or hyperfocal distance to ensure both frame and main object are equally sharp.
theory_units.applies_when: When using foreground frames, especially those occupying a major portion of the picture.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains clarity and prevents audience distraction from an out-of-focus foreground.
theory_units.caution: An out-of-focus foreground object, occupying a major portion of the picture, can prove very disturbing. A slightly soft-focus frame is only permissible if underexposed or in silhouette and sufficient depth-of-field is unavailable.

theory_units.title: Adjusting Camera/Lens for Subject-Frame Size Relationship
theory_units.summary: If the main subject appears too small in relation to the frame, move the camera back and employ a longer focal length lens to make the subject appear larger while still recording the full frame.
theory_units.applies_when: When composing a shot with a foreground frame where the main subject is too small and needs to be emphasized.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a clearer hierarchy, making the main subject more prominent within the framed composition.

theory_units.title: Controlled Frame Movement
theory_units.summary: Avoid wildly moving frames that distract from the main subject. Camera movement is permissible if the frame itself remains static, allowing for smooth pans or dollies into a framed composition.
theory_units.applies_when: When integrating camera or subject movement with a foreground frame.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains focus on the main subject while allowing for dynamic camera work and effective reveals.
theory_units.caution: Wildly moving frames (e.g., branches in wind) should be avoided because they may detract from the main subject. Panning across a frame with strong verticals close to the camera can cause an annoying 'shipping' effect.

theory_units.title: Dynamic Composition for Abrupt Effects
theory_units.summary: Employ dynamic composition to evoke sudden change in a static setup, introducing forceful pictorial elements (figures, objects, vehicles) abruptly into the frame to surprise or invigorate a scene.
theory_units.applies_when: When abrupt or surprising effects are desired, to bring quiet scenes to life, or to recapture audience attention after a calm passage.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a startling, vigorous, or dramatically active effect, drawing immediate attention and disrupting complacency.
theory_units.caution: Requires utmost discretion and should be limited to properly-motivated dramatic situations to avoid being jarring or arbitrary.

theory_units.title: Suspenseful Composition through Concealment or Prolongation
theory_units.summary: Utilize composition to hide significant action, create absence, or prolong a reveal, keeping the audience in doubt and building suspense.
theory_units.applies_when: When 'cliff-hanging' suspense is the keynote of a sequence, needing to prolong audience uncertainty.
theory_units.expected_effect: Builds tension and emotional engagement by keeping the audience eager for a reveal or resolution, making them feel the duration of a difficult moment.
theory_units.caution: Requires careful staging and camera work to effectively withhold information without frustrating the viewer.

theory_units.title: Dynamic and Aesthetic Catalog Composition
theory_units.summary: Compose catalog-style shots of objects not as static displays but using patterns, forms, and movement (pan, dolly, zoom) to create aesthetic or emotional impact, convey purpose, or group elements harmoniously.
theory_units.applies_when: When photographing groups of tools, machines, products, or similar items for industrial, military, or training films.
theory_units.expected_effect: Transforms potentially static shots into engaging compositions, conveying action, purposefulness, or a sense of unity, avoiding clutter.
theory_units.caution: Avoid showing static catalog shots that interrupt the film's flow; equipment should be shown in the course of work.

theory_units.title: Compositional Variety for Viewer Engagement
theory_units.summary: Maintain a unified style while presenting a variety of compositions, camera angles, and image sizes to prevent monotony and sustain viewer interest.
theory_units.applies_when: Throughout the entire film, but especially when dealing with similar settings or repeated actions.
theory_units.expected_effect: Keeps players and settings from being depicted in a monotonous pattern, adding interest and avoiding viewer disengagement.
theory_units.caution: Avoid similar compositional treatment, staging, player movement, or camera movement across different settings or sequences. Cameramen may slip into a rut on tight schedules.

theory_units.title: Comprehensive 'Compose in Depth' Strategy
theory_units.summary: Proactively create compositions in depth to build a three-dimensional illusion on screen, utilizing a combination of staging, camera angles, lighting, and foreground/background elements to immerse the viewer.
theory_units.applies_when: As a foundational approach to almost all cinematography, whenever striving for a rich, immersive visual experience.
theory_units.expected_effect: Viewers feel immersed in the setting, rather than observing from afar; creates a solid, three-dimensional appearance for players, setting, and objects.
theory_units.caution: Avoid restricting depth for ease of lighting or focus. Always think in depth. Avoid flat angles, flat lighting, cross-screen movement, and lined-up, straight-across staging.

theory_units.title: Simplicity as the Core of Good Composition
theory_units.summary: Strive for simplicity in composition, focusing on a single center of interest and economizing elements to ensure immediate viewer recognition and assimilation, preventing clutter and distraction.
theory_units.applies_when: In every compositional decision, from framing to object arrangement, ensuring clarity and impact.
theory_units.expected_effect: A composition that is immediately recognizable and readily assimilated by the audience, who does not have to search for the shot's meaning. Prevents irritation and loss of interest.
theory_units.caution: A complicated or cluttered composition, even if technically correct, will not be as effective. Any element not required for storytelling attracts unwarranted attention and may steal the scene.

theory_units.title: Balance in Composition
theory_units.summary: Understand the differences between formal and informal balance, and apply them strategically to elicit the desired audience response.
theory_units.applies_when: When composing any shot or sequence where the arrangement of elements influences audience perception and emotion.
theory_units.expected_effect: Guides audience emotions and understanding, ensuring the visual presentation aligns with the script's intent.

theory_units.title: Single Center of Interest
theory_units.summary: Limit each screen composition to a single, clear center of interest to maintain audience focus, unless a disturbed or scattered effect is deliberately intended.
theory_units.applies_when: Composing any shot where a clear focal point is desired, or when intentionally creating a sense of disturbance.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures the audience's attention is directed to the intended subject, preventing visual confusion.
theory_units.caution: Avoid multiple centers of interest unless intentionally aiming for a disturbed or scattered effect.

theory_units.title: Lead Room for Moving Subjects
theory_units.summary: Frame moving subjects (players or vehicles) with adequate space in the direction of their movement, known as 'lead room' or 'looking room'.
theory_units.applies_when: Framing any shot that includes a subject in motion or about to move.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides visual comfort for the viewer, anticipates the subject's movement, and enhances the sense of motion and natural flow.

theory_units.title: Pre-planning Camera Angles for Sequences
theory_units.summary: When composing a master scene, consider and plan for all subsequent camera angles required to cover the entire sequence, not just the initial long shot.
theory_units.applies_when: During the planning and blocking phase of any scene that will be covered with multiple shots, starting from a master scene.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures comprehensive and continuous coverage, facilitates efficient shooting, and maintains visual continuity across edits.
theory_units.caution: Do not solely plan for the master long shot, as this can lead to coverage gaps or continuity problems.

theory_units.title: Composition in Depth for 3D Appearance
theory_units.summary: Arrange elements within the frame to create a sense of depth, giving the screen a three-dimensional appearance.
theory_units.applies_when: Composing any shot, particularly to avoid a flat or two-dimensional image.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhances immersion, realism, and visual interest by creating the illusion of space and dimension on a flat screen.

theory_units.title: Using Foreground Frames
theory_units.summary: Employ appropriate foreground elements to frame the main subject, enhancing composition and guiding the viewer's eye.
theory_units.applies_when: Seeking to add depth, direct attention, or improve the aesthetic appeal of a composition.
theory_units.expected_effect: Adds layers of depth, directs focus to the main subject, and makes the composition more dynamic and aesthetically pleasing.
theory_units.caution: Ensure foreground frames are appropriate to the scene and do not distract from the main subject.

theory_units.title: Connecting Backgrounds to Action
theory_units.summary: Integrate backgrounds with the principal action to provide context and meaning, making them an active part of the narrative rather than mere scenery.
theory_units.applies_when: Composing any shot that includes a significant background, especially to enrich the narrative or character's environment.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enriches the narrative, adds depth to the scene, and creates a more cohesive and meaningful visual experience.

theory_units.title: Viewer Eye Scan Across Shots
theory_units.summary: Consider how the viewer's eye will naturally move and locate points of interest from one shot to the next when planning shot transitions.
theory_units.applies_when: Planning shot sequences and editing decisions to ensure smooth visual flow and audience comprehension.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a seamless and intuitive viewing experience, prevents disorientation, and maintains visual continuity.

theory_units.title: Visual Variety in Composition
theory_units.summary: Regularly change compositional effects within a sequence to maintain audience engagement and prevent visual monotony.
theory_units.applies_when: Directing a series of shots or planning the overall visual style of a scene or sequence.
theory_units.expected_effect: Keeps the audience interested, prevents visual fatigue, and adds dynamic energy to the storytelling.

theory_units.title: Simplicity in Composition
theory_units.summary: Prioritize clear and simple compositions, avoiding unnecessary frills, gimmicks, or overly complex arrangements.
theory_units.applies_when: Composing any shot, especially when tempted to add decorative or superfluous elements.
theory_units.expected_effect: Achieves greater clarity and impact, prevents audience distraction, and makes the main subject stand out.
theory_units.caution: Avoid unnecessary frills, gimmicks, and overly complex arrangements which can confuse or detract from the message.

theory_units.title: Environmental Object Juxtaposition for Impact
theory_units.summary: Utilize environmental objects in a shot to visually suggest quantities or the abstract impact of an event, particularly when juxtaposed with a character.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character's actions or situation has a broad, abstract impact (e.g., number of people affected) that can be symbolized by surrounding objects.
theory_units.expected_effect: Subtly communicates the scale or consequence of an action to the audience without explicit dialogue, fostering empathy or understanding.

theory_units.title: High Angle for Vulnerability
theory_units.summary: A high camera angle can visualize emotions like defeat, vulnerability, and distraughtness in characters by looking down on them.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character is experiencing emotional distress, weakness, or a sense of being overwhelmed.
theory_units.expected_effect: Makes the character appear smaller, more isolated, and less powerful, eliciting audience empathy for their emotional state.
theory_units.caution: Remember narrative context is key; a high angle can also convey dominance if context supports it (as mentioned on page 56).

theory_units.title: Rule of Thirds for Dynamic Composition
theory_units.summary: Placing subjects according to the Rule of Thirds creates dynamic compositions and provides 'looking room' or 'leading room' in the frame.
theory_units.applies_when: When a director wants to create visual interest and guide the audience's eye, rather than a static, centered image.
theory_units.expected_effect: Produces a more engaging and less static image, subtly directing the audience's attention and implying future movement or thought.

theory_units.title: Reduced Headroom for Unusual Drama
theory_units.summary: Departing from standard headroom in a shot can reinforce an unusual or awkward dramatic moment.
theory_units.applies_when: When the scene contains an uncomfortable, tense, or dramatically unusual moment that requires visual emphasis.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a sense of confinement, unease, or visual tension that mirrors the dramatic situation, making the audience feel the moment's intensity.
theory_units.caution: Use judiciously, as excessive or unintentional deviation from standard headroom can simply look amateurish.

theory_units.title: Framing for Environmental Pressure
theory_units.summary: Placing a comparatively small subject in a frame with surrounding objects can suggest they are being pressured, cornered, or retaliated against by their environment.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character is feeling overwhelmed, cornered, or experiencing the negative consequences (retaliation) of their actions, symbolized by their surroundings.
theory_units.expected_effect: Visually conveys the character's psychological state of being under duress or facing consequences, fostering audience empathy or understanding of their situation.
theory_units.caution: Centering the subject would negate this effect, conveying stability rather than pressure.

theory_units.title: Haphazard Arrangement for Turmoil
theory_units.summary: The haphazard arrangement of environmental objects can visualize the turmoil or chaos caused by or experienced by a character.
theory_units.applies_when: When portraying a character's internal emotional state, the impact of their actions, or a chaotic environment reflective of the narrative.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a visual metaphor for disorder or distress, communicating psychological turmoil or external disruption to the audience.

theory_units.title: Deep Depth of Field for Contextual Focus
theory_units.summary: Using a deep depth of field keeps both the subject and their environment in sharp focus, ensuring the audience considers everything in the frame.
theory_units.applies_when: When the environment and its objects are as narratively significant as the subject, and the audience needs to absorb all visual information.
theory_units.expected_effect: Guarantees audience attention is distributed across the entire frame, allowing for complex contextual meaning to be absorbed from the interaction of the subject and their surroundings.
theory_units.caution: Shallow depth of field would blur background/foreground, losing contextual detail.

theory_units.title: Close-up for Emotion
theory_units.summary: Close-ups are conventionally used to showcase strong emotions in characters.
theory_units.applies_when: When the primary narrative goal is to reveal or emphasize a character's emotional state, thoughts, or reaction.
theory_units.expected_effect: Draws the audience's attention intimately to the character's face or a specific detail, creating a strong emotional connection or understanding.

theory_units.title: Extreme Long Shot for Location
theory_units.summary: Extreme long shots are conventionally used to introduce locations and establish setting.
theory_units.applies_when: At the beginning of a scene or sequence to establish the geographical or environmental context of the upcoming action.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides a wide overview of the setting, orienting the audience and conveying the scale or atmosphere of the location.

theory_units.title: Rule Subversion for Impact
theory_units.summary: Rules of composition can and should be subverted when appropriate to create shots with fresh impact, surprising, or contradictory resonance.
theory_units.applies_when: When conventional approaches feel inadequate or when aiming for a unique, memorable, or thematically complex visual statement.
theory_units.expected_effect: Generates a unique and powerful visual impression, challenging audience expectations and creating deeper or unconventional meanings.
theory_units.caution: Requires a deep understanding of the rules first ('learn them so you know how to break them properly') to ensure subversion is intentional and effective, not merely accidental or amateurish.

theory_units.title: Intentional Framing (Relevance)
theory_units.summary: Identify exactly what each shot is supposed to communicate, ensuring only relevant visual information is included and extraneous details are excluded to avoid audience confusion.
theory_units.applies_when: When composing any shot, especially when the narrative depends on subtle details or clear communication of a specific point.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures the audience's attention is directed to the most important elements, leading to a clear understanding of the shot's narrative purpose and preventing misinterpretation.
theory_units.caution: Audiences assume everything in a frame is meaningful; including too much unnecessary visual information can distract from the core message and prevent key details from being noticed.

theory_units.title: Director's Subjective Commentary
theory_units.summary: The framing of every shot should reflect the director's understanding of the story, their perspective, idiosyncrasies, and overall vision, adding a subjective layer of meaning.
theory_units.applies_when: When moving beyond literal depiction to imbue a scene with deeper thematic meaning, personal interpretation, or authorial commentary.
theory_units.expected_effect: Elevates the shot beyond mere action depiction, allowing the director to 'comment' on the story, enriching the narrative with complex layers of meaning for the audience.

theory_units.title: Narrative Context Defines Meaning
theory_units.summary: A shot's composition communicates meaning not just through visual arrangement, but fundamentally through the narrative context in which it is presented.
theory_units.applies_when: Always; when selecting any shot composition, it must be considered within the broader story arc, character development, and preceding events.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures that compositional choices resonate authentically and profoundly with the audience, avoiding superficiality or misinterpretation.
theory_units.caution: Replicating a visually striking shot from another film without its original narrative context will render it meaningless or confusing for the audience.

theory_units.title: Thematic Guidance for Visuals
theory_units.summary: Identify the story's core themes and essence to serve as a compass, guiding all visual decisions (composition, lighting, camerawork, etc.) for a unified vision.
theory_units.applies_when: During pre-production and throughout the filmmaking process, as the foundational principle for developing a cohesive visual language.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a powerful, emotionally deep, and narratively coherent film where every visual choice reinforces the story's underlying message, achieving a master director's unified vision.
theory_units.caution: Without clear thematic guidance, visual choices can become disjointed and fail to support the story's true meaning.

theory_units.title: Angle Shift for Confidence Arc
theory_units.summary: Varying camera angles from high to low can subtly visualize a character's journey from lack of confidence and vulnerability to growing self-confidence and resolve.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character undergoes a transformation in their emotional state or self-perception throughout the narrative.
theory_units.expected_effect: Visually maps the character's internal journey, making their development tangible and emotionally resonant for the audience.

theory_units.title: Frame Balance for Character Resolve
theory_units.summary: Use off-center, unbalanced compositions to reflect a character's uncertainty or lack of motivation, and shift to balanced framings as they gain resolve and self-respect.
theory_units.applies_when: To visually represent a character's internal struggle and ultimate achievement of a goal or state of mind.
theory_units.expected_effect: Mirrors the character's internal stability or instability, making their psychological journey clear through visual equilibrium.

theory_units.title: Lens Shift for Character Perspective
theory_units.summary: Employ wide-angle lenses to distort a character's appearance when they are unconfident or struggling, and transition to normal lenses as they gain confidence and clarity.
theory_units.applies_when: To visually represent a character's internal state of mind or their distorted self-perception, evolving over a narrative arc.
theory_units.expected_effect: The shift in lens perspective visually communicates the character's internal transformation, from unease to self-assurance.

theory_units.title: Depth of Field for Isolation/Connection
theory_units.summary: Use shallow depth of field to isolate a character, visualizing their desire to block out the world; then use deep depth of field as they feel more accepted or connected.
theory_units.applies_when: To visually portray a character's emotional journey regarding their relationship with their environment or other characters, from detachment to integration.
theory_units.expected_effect: Visually reinforces the character's internal state of being disconnected or connected, fostering audience understanding of their emotional arc.

theory_units.title: Two-Shot to Close-up for Detail
theory_units.summary: Use a two-shot to establish interaction, then tilt down to a tight close-up at a key moment to reveal a significant, often subtle, detail.
theory_units.applies_when: When a subtle physical detail holds significant narrative meaning and needs to be highlighted after establishing a broader interaction.
theory_units.expected_effect: Draws the audience's attention to a critical detail, emphasizing its importance and revealing a character's internal state or a plot point.

theory_units.title: Partial Cropping for Nervousness
theory_units.summary: In an over-the-shoulder shot, partially cropping a character from the frame can visualize their nervousness or discomfort.
theory_units.applies_when: When aiming to subtly convey a character's internal state of anxiety or unease without explicit dialogue or performance.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a sense of visual discomfort or incompleteness that reflects the character's internal nervousness, making them appear more vulnerable or unsettled.
theory_units.caution: Ensure the cropping is intentional and serves a narrative purpose, not just poor framing.

theory_units.title: Contrasting Framing for Character States
theory_units.summary: Use contrasting compositional elements, like canted shots/excessive headroom versus even horizons/conventional framing, to visualize different emotional states between characters.
theory_units.applies_when: When comparing or highlighting the differing emotional or psychological states of two or more characters within the same scene.
theory_units.expected_effect: Visually accentuates the disparity in characters' internal experiences, making their individual states clear and creating subtle dramatic tension or commentary.

theory_units.title: Kuleshov Effect (Contiguous Shots)
theory_units.summary: The juxtaposition of contiguous shots can create a new meaning that is absent from each individual shot, guiding audience interpretation of emotion or narrative.
theory_units.applies_when: When editing a sequence of shots, particularly to convey emotion or build a new idea through the interaction of distinct images.
theory_units.expected_effect: Generates a powerful, cumulative meaning from the sequence, often leading the audience to infer emotions or connections that aren't explicitly shown in any single shot.
theory_units.caution: The perceived meaning is highly dependent on the audience's interpretation and cultural context.

theory_units.title: Recontextualized Recurring Image
theory_units.summary: A visually striking image revisited later in a film can attain an entirely new meaning, recontextualized by all the events that transpired since its first appearance.
theory_units.applies_when: When designing recurring visual motifs, character introductions, or location shots that are intended to evolve in meaning over the course of the film.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a deeper, more complex thematic resonance and emotional impact by demonstrating character or narrative change, engaging the audience's memory and comparative understanding.
theory_units.caution: Requires significant narrative development between repetitions for the recontextualization to be effective; superficial repetition will not yield the desired effect.

theory_units.title: Designed Image System for Storytelling
theory_units.summary: A film's image system, a unique interaction of all its images, should be intentionally designed to communicate themes, core ideas, motifs, character arcs, and tone cohesively.
theory_units.applies_when: Throughout the entire filmmaking process, from conceptualization to post-production, as the guiding principle for all visual choices.
theory_units.expected_effect: Results in a powerful and coherent visual narrative that seamlessly reinforces the story's underlying messages, characters, and emotional tone, creating a unique cinematic experience.
theory_units.caution: Unplanned image systems can still occur but may lack narrative precision or fail to fully support the story's intended meaning.

theory_units.title: Avoid Abstract or Abstruse Narration
theory_units.summary: Contemporary audiences tend to prefer clear representations of reality, whether external, internal, or imagined, over abstract or abstruse film narration that is heavily loaded with unintelligible symbols.
theory_units.applies_when: Crafting narrative style and selecting visual storytelling methods, especially when aiming for broad audience appeal.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains audience interest and comprehension, prevents viewer 'repugnance' or alienation due to ambiguity.
theory_units.caution: Overly abstract or obscure symbolism may alienate viewers and result in a negative audience reaction.

theory_units.title: Portray Abstract Ideas Through Behavior
theory_units.summary: Abstract thoughts and ideas cannot be clearly expressed directly on film. Instead, they must be shown as acting upon the observable behavior (actions and reactions) of characters, animals, or objects recorded by the camera.
theory_units.applies_when: Attempting to convey internal states, abstract concepts, or non-physical ideas to the audience through film.
theory_units.expected_effect: Makes abstract concepts tangible and understandable through visual means, leveraging film's strength in showing external results and their emotional impact.
theory_units.caution: Attempting to convey abstract ideas directly without behavioral manifestation will likely result in ambiguity, confusion, or lack of conviction for the audience.

theory_units.title: Technical Mastery as Second Nature
theory_units.summary: Filmmakers must acquire technical knowledge so thoroughly that it becomes second nature, allowing techniques to serve and enhance the story's vision rather than drawing attention to themselves or distorting the material.
theory_units.applies_when: Directing, editing, or making any technical choices during pre-production, production, or post-production.
theory_units.expected_effect: Technical choices seamlessly integrate with and clarify the story's vision, making the filmmaking invisible and the narrative paramount.
theory_units.caution: Over-focusing on mechanics or using technical possibilities merely for their own sake can lead to losing sight of the scene's purpose and distorting the material, thereby undermining the story.

theory_units.title: Parallel Film Editing (Alternating Centers of Interest)
theory_units.summary: Parallel editing involves alternating between two or more distinct centers of interest to present conflicting or related story lines or to show comparative behaviors, which audiences are conditioned to expect.
theory_units.applies_when: Presenting multiple concurrent or related story threads, characters, events, or comparative actions/reactions to the audience.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a clear understanding of conflicting or related narratives, enhances drama, builds suspense, reveals connections, and can highlight differences in behavior or situation.
theory_units.caution: Avoiding this technique when the narrative calls for it can irritate the viewer, even if they cannot articulate why.

theory_units.title: Parallel Editing: Same Space Interaction
theory_units.summary: A specific type of parallel editing where two or more lines of interaction occur close together within the same physical space, observed separately by the camera.
theory_units.applies_when: Showing simultaneous actions, reactions, or a dialogue between characters within a shared, unified location.
theory_units.expected_effect: Emphasizes the immediate relationship and interaction between the elements, allowing for comparative observation of behaviors within a unified setting.

theory_units.title: Parallel Editing: Different Space, Common Motivation
theory_units.summary: A specific type of parallel editing where two or more lines of interaction occur in different physical places, linked by a common motivation, goal, or thematic connection.
theory_units.applies_when: Relating events happening in separate, often distant, locations, building suspense, revealing information gradually, or establishing overarching thematic connections.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates mutual dependence between distant storylines, allows for delayed revelations (e.g., identity of a link), and can enhance audience understanding or mystery.
theory_units.caution: The common motivation or link between the disparate locations must eventually become clear to the audience to avoid confusion or a sense of arbitrariness.

theory_units.title: Action-Reaction Grouping for Clarity
theory_units.summary: To enhance audience comprehension, group the informative 'action' parts of shots together (e.g., aiming, flying), followed by the 'reaction' parts (e.g., firing, being hit), potentially alternating between subjects in a parallel editing pattern.
theory_units.applies_when: Editing a sequence that involves an action and its subsequent reaction, especially when involving multiple subjects or shots, to ensure maximum clarity and impact.
theory_units.expected_effect: Improves the audience's understanding of what is happening and the outcome of actions by presenting information in a logical, grouped sequence, making the narrative more comprehensible.
theory_units.caution: Presenting actions and reactions without grouping them strategically can reduce effectiveness and audience comprehension, making the sequence less impactful.

theory_units.title: Edit for Peak Moments
theory_units.summary: Only the most significant 'peak moments' of a story should be shown on screen; events or actions that delay the narrative or do not add new, significant material should be deleted.
theory_units.applies_when: Structuring a scene or sequence, selecting takes, and making editing decisions to maintain narrative drive and audience engagement.
theory_units.expected_effect: Compresses or expands time effectively, maintains audience engagement by focusing on crucial narrative points, and ensures efficient, impactful storytelling. Allows for the illusion of 'real time' despite manipulation.
theory_units.caution: Including non-essential material or dwelling on non-peak moments can slow pacing, dilute the impact of key events, and disengage the audience.

theory_units.title: Parallel Editing for Mutual Story Building
theory_units.summary: Utilize parallel editing when two or more story lines are designed to mutually support each other, with each alternate contribution progressively building up the overall narrative and shared data.
theory_units.applies_when: Building a story where distinct plot threads contribute cooperatively and cumulatively to the audience's understanding of the larger narrative.
theory_units.expected_effect: A comprehensive and layered narrative understanding for the audience as information from separate threads combines and reinforces each other.

theory_units.title: Parallel Editing for Varied Reaction
theory_units.summary: Employ parallel editing by maintaining a consistent movement or intention in one story line, while simultaneously showing varied reactions or responses to that steady repetition in another line.
theory_units.applies_when: Exploring the impact of a sustained action or intention on different characters or situations, or to highlight changing dynamics and evolving responses.
theory_units.expected_effect: Emphasizes the psychological or emotional responses to an ongoing situation, creates contrast, and reveals nuances in character or environmental impact.

theory_units.title: Parallel Editing for Dramatic Irony
theory_units.summary: Use parallel editing to present two narrative lines where the characters involved are unaware of what the other group is doing, but the audience is privy to all the facts.
theory_units.applies_when: Building suspense, tension, or emotional investment by informing the audience of dangers, surprises, or developments that characters on screen are oblivious to.
theory_units.expected_effect: Heightened audience engagement, anticipation, and emotional investment due to their privileged knowledge compared to the characters.
theory_units.caution: Overuse can make the narrative predictable or diminish character agency if characters constantly appear oblivious to obvious information, potentially frustrating the audience.

theory_units.title: Parallel Editing for Audience Mystery
theory_units.summary: Apply parallel editing where the information given in both narrative lines is incomplete for the audience, while the characters possess all the facts, purposely keeping the audience in the dark.
theory_units.applies_when: Creating a sense of intrigue, mystery, or puzzlement for the audience, compelling them to actively piece together information or anticipate revelations.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increased audience curiosity, speculation, and a strong desire to uncover the full story or the missing pieces of information.
theory_units.caution: The director must eventually provide enough information to satisfy the audience's curiosity; prolonged or unresolved ambiguity can lead to frustration or disengagement.

theory_units.title: Narration for Disconnected Shots
theory_units.summary: When covering unrepeatable acts or events results in a series of visually disconnected shots, a narrator can be used to provide unity, context, and coherence to the ensemble.
theory_units.applies_when: Editing raw footage of spontaneous, uncontrolled, or fragmented events where direct visual continuity is difficult to achieve.
theory_units.expected_effect: Brings coherence, contextual understanding, and a sense of narrative flow to otherwise chaotic or visually incomplete information, bridging gaps for the audience.

theory_units.title: Bridging Disconnected Shots with Spectator Reactions
theory_units.summary: To provide unity and an action-reaction relationship in newsreels or similar footage, bridge disconnected shots of an event by inserting shots of spectators reacting to it.
theory_units.applies_when: Editing raw footage of spontaneous or uncontrollable events to improve coherence, emotional connection, and audience acceptance, especially when direct event continuity is compromised.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a sense of action and reaction, drawing the audience into the event's emotional or social context, even if the main event itself remains visually incomplete. Facilitates audience identification.
theory_units.caution: The audience may still be conscious of seeing an incomplete occurrence, but their acceptance of the narrative is improved.

theory_units.title: Documentary Idea Progression through Behavioral Patterns
theory_units.summary: In documentaries, disrupt temporal continuity by fragmenting individual subjects' actions and regrouping them into sequences based on common stimuli or patterns of behavior, thereby achieving an idea progression rather than strict chronology.
theory_units.applies_when: Structuring documentary material to explore thematic ideas, patterns, or arguments rather than strict chronological events, especially when comparing responses to stimuli.
theory_units.expected_effect: Facilitates the development of abstract ideas or arguments by visually grouping related behaviors or responses, creating a powerful thematic statement.
theory_units.caution: This technique consciously disrupts real-world temporal continuity; it must be done with a clear intention to serve an explicit idea progression, not to mislead.

theory_units.title: Explanatory Visual Variants in Documentary
theory_units.summary: Interrupt the linear recording of an event in documentaries to introduce different forms of visual explanation, such as animated drawings, to clarify processes or concepts that cannot be effectively photographed using real elements.
theory_units.applies_when: Needing to explain complex, invisible, or abstract processes within a documentary narrative that are beyond the scope of direct live-action photography.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhances audience understanding of difficult-to-visualize concepts or procedures, making complex information accessible and engaging.

theory_units.title: Repeating Events for Exploratory Presentation
theory_units.summary: Present a series of events in different patterns or orders of presentation to explore diverse approaches, interpretations, or solutions to a problem or theme within a film.
theory_units.applies_when: Seeking to analyze an event or theme from multiple angles, demonstrate different outcomes based on varied sequencing, or encourage deeper audience reflection.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides a deeper, multi-faceted understanding of an event or problem, encouraging critical thinking and allowing for a richer exploration of cinematic possibilities.

theory_units.title: Controlling Emphasis with Camera Distance
theory_units.summary: Varying camera distance can control points of emphasis in a story, drawing audience attention closer or pulling it back.
theory_units.applies_when: When needing to emphasize or de-emphasize main subjects or key story moments.
theory_units.expected_effect: Directs audience attention, creates emphasis, and controls the perceived importance of subjects.

theory_units.title: Camera Position for Cross-Cutting
theory_units.summary: Changing camera position between takes is consciously used to provide the editor with diverse material for cross-cutting and intercutting.
theory_units.applies_when: When shooting a scene that will require cross-cutting between different perspectives or for editorial flexibility to intercut shots.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enables dynamic editing, variety in visual presentation, and the ability to intercut different angles or subjects.
theory_units.caution: If the primary issue is a poor performance, repeat shots from the same position are generally preferred over changing camera positions.

theory_units.title: Camera Movement Supporting Action
theory_units.summary: The camera should move in a way that actively supports and complements the action it is recording.
theory_units.applies_when: When recording an event with significant movement or action.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhances the audience's understanding and immersion in the action, maintains visual fluidity, and avoids jarring cuts.

theory_units.title: Pleasing Human Figure Cutting Heights
theory_units.summary: Specific 'cutting heights' on the human figure (e.g., under armpits, chest, waist, crotch, knees) create aesthetically pleasing compositions.
theory_units.applies_when: When framing human subjects in any shot size to achieve aesthetically pleasing and balanced compositions.
theory_units.expected_effect: Aesthetically pleasing and natural-looking compositions of human subjects, avoiding awkward cuts.

theory_units.title: Full Shot Feet Inclusion
theory_units.summary: In a full shot of a human figure, the subject's feet must be included to achieve a pleasant and complete composition.
theory_units.applies_when: When framing a full shot of a human figure.
theory_units.expected_effect: Pleasing and balanced full shot composition that clearly defines the entire human figure.
theory_units.caution: Cutting above the ankles will not give a pleasant composition.

theory_units.title: Intercutting for Scene Emphasis
theory_units.summary: Shorter takes (inserts) covering fragments from different distances or introducing new subjects can be intercut into a master shot to emphasize key passages or details.
theory_units.applies_when: When specific moments, details, reactions, or new subjects within a scene need to be highlighted for the audience.
theory_units.expected_effect: Directs audience attention to important details or reactions, adds dramatic weight, and breaks visual monotony.

theory_units.title: Smooth Optical Transitions
theory_units.summary: Optical transitions like fades (out/in), dissolves, or wipes can be employed to achieve a smooth visual transition between sequences.
theory_units.applies_when: When a smooth, gradual, or less abrupt visual transition between sequences, significant scene shifts, or passages of time is desired.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a graceful or symbolic shift in time/space, avoids abruptness, and can enhance emotional tone.
theory_units.caution: Straight cuts provide an abrupt visual transition and serve a different purpose.

theory_units.title: Match Performer Position Across Cuts
theory_units.summary: Maintain a performer's screen position (e.g., left side) consistently across cuts to avoid jarring jumps and ensure continuous audience orientation.
theory_units.applies_when: When cutting between shots of the same performer or scene, especially when maintaining the same visual axis.
theory_units.expected_effect: Avoids distracting visual jumps, maintains a comfortable eye scan for the audience, and allows them to concentrate on the story.
theory_units.caution: Disregarding this rule results in awkward visual jumps, annoying and distracting the audience by forcing them to re-locate the character.

theory_units.title: Screen Division for Position Matching
theory_units.summary: Divide the screen into two or three vertical parts to consistently place main performers, which aids in matching their positions across cuts.
theory_units.applies_when: When framing main performers to ensure consistent screen position and facilitate continuity in editing.
theory_units.expected_effect: Facilitates consistent placement of subjects across shots, improves matching accuracy, and maintains visual balance.

theory_units.title: Match Direction of Movement Across Cuts
theory_units.summary: Maintain the same direction of continuous movement for a performer across consecutive shots to avoid audience confusion.
theory_units.applies_when: When cutting between shots that depict continuous motion of a performer.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains clarity of movement, prevents audience confusion about the subject's supposed direction, and preserves spatial logic.
theory_units.caution: If the direction of movement is suddenly reversed in the second shot, there will be confusion as to where the subject is going.

theory_units.title: Opposed Glances for Two-Shot Dialogue
theory_units.summary: When two subjects exchange looks, their glances must be in opposed directions, especially if framed in separate shots, to clearly indicate they are looking at each other and maintain visual continuity.
theory_units.applies_when: When framing two individuals exchanging dialogue or looks, whether in the same shot or in separate close-ups.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clearly establishes that subjects are interacting with each other, maintains proper visual continuity, and prevents scenes from becoming weak or meaningless.
theory_units.caution: If players look in the same direction, it logically implies they are looking at a third person or object, not at each other, which will confuse the scene's meaning.

theory_units.title: Arbiter of Attention in a Trio
theory_units.summary: In a group of three, one player acts as an 'arbiter of attention,' shifting their gaze to guide the audience's focus as the center of interest changes between the other two.
theory_units.applies_when: When directing a scene with three characters where the focus of dialogue or attention shifts between them.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clearly guides audience attention to the current speaker or point of interest, preventing confusion and maintaining engagement.
theory_units.caution: Audience interest can be destroyed if players look at the wrong places or in multiple directions; the arbiter's head movement must be visible to effectively guide the audience.

theory_units.title: Guide Audience Gaze, Avoid Confusion
theory_units.summary: Directors must actively guide the audience's attention using player gazes, consistently leading their eye and avoiding conflicting or confusing eye lines.
theory_units.applies_when: Any scene involving multiple players or potential for conflicting gazes and points of interest.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains audience focus and clarity, prevents distraction and confusion, allowing full concentration on the story.
theory_units.caution: Interest in a scene can be destroyed by allowing players to look at the wrong places or in two or more directions, forcing the audience to choose and causing confusion.

theory_units.title: Large Group Unison Gaze for Focus
theory_units.summary: In large groups, all non-central players should focus their attention (look in unison) on the current central character, shifting their gazes together as the point of interest shifts.
theory_units.applies_when: When directing a large group of players and needing to clearly establish who the current center of attention is among them.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clearly identifies the center of interest, guiding audience focus without confusion, and reinforcing who is dominant.

theory_units.title: Introduce Third Center of Interest
theory_units.summary: Introduce a third center of interest in lengthy large-group scenes to prevent monotony from continually shifting attention between only two points.
theory_units.applies_when: In long scenes with large groups where audience attention is constantly shifting between only two main points of interest.
theory_units.expected_effect: Breaks monotony, maintains audience engagement by offering varied points of focus, and adds dynamic complexity.

theory_units.title: Dominant Group Near Camera
theory_units.summary: When multiple groups are present in a scene, the dominant or most interesting group should be placed near the camera.
theory_units.applies_when: When framing a scene containing several distinct groups of people and needing to establish a clear hierarchy of importance or focus.
theory_units.expected_effect: Directs immediate audience attention to the most important group, establishing them as predominant and requiring immediate attention.

theory_units.title: Background Group Gaze Shift for Foreground Emphasis
theory_units.summary: To dramatically emphasize a foreground situation, background groups can break their internal focus and turn to look at the forward group.
theory_units.applies_when: When needing to dramatically highlight or draw collective attention to the actions or presence of a foreground group.
theory_units.expected_effect: Strongly reinforces the importance of the foreground group by drawing collective attention to them from other groups, creating a moment of heightened drama.

theory_units.title: Inconspicuous Background Movement
theory_units.summary: Introduce subtle, inconspicuous movement in subordinate background groups (e.g., traffic, dancers) to add dynamism without distracting from static foreground action.
theory_units.applies_when: When foreground action is static but the scene needs more visual life, realism, or environmental context.
theory_units.expected_effect: Adds realism and visual interest to the scene without drawing focus away from the main action or characters in the foreground.
theory_units.caution: These movements must be inconspicuous; otherwise, they will interfere with and distract from the foreground action.

theory_units.title: Two-Player Linear Arrangements for Dialogue
theory_units.summary: For dialogued scenes with two central players, they can be deployed in either a straight-line composition or a right-angle relation.
theory_units.applies_when: When blocking and arranging two dominant characters who are engaged in dialogue.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides fundamental visual structures for two-player interactions, influencing their dynamic and the audience's perspective.

theory_units.title: Establishing a Line of Interest for Dialogue
theory_units.summary: Between two talking partners, a clear, straight 'line of interest' flows, which is fundamental for maintaining spatial continuity and orientation.
theory_units.applies_when: When setting up shots for a conversation between two characters to maintain their spatial orientation and avoid confusing jumps.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains consistent screen direction and spatial awareness for the audience, preventing disorientation and ensuring smooth viewing.
theory_units.caution: Violating this line by crossing it with the camera can disorient the audience.

theory_units.title: Maintaining the Line of Interest (180-degree Rule)
theory_units.summary: To prevent audience confusion and maintain consistent screen direction, select one side of the 'line of interest' between two central players for all camera positions and stick to it.
theory_units.applies_when: When covering a scene with two or more central players engaged in dialogue or interaction, especially for master shots and subsequent coverage.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains a steady emplacement of players on the same areas of the screen (e.g., Player A always on the left, Player B always on the right), ensuring spatial clarity and preventing audience disorientation.
theory_units.caution: Crossing the line (using camera positions from opposite triangular arrangements relative to the line of interest) will confuse the audience by shifting player positions on screen.

theory_units.title: Head-Centric Line of Interest Definition
theory_units.summary: The 'line of interest' between two interacting performers should always be established and flow between their heads, regardless of their body positions.
theory_units.applies_when: When defining or re-evaluating the line of interest, particularly in complex or non-standard body positions (e.g., lying down, back-to-back).
theory_units.expected_effect: Simplifies the establishment of spatial relationships and ensures the audience's focus remains on the primary points of interaction (faces, eyes) for dialogue and emotional exchange.

theory_units.title: External Reverse Angle Camera Coverage
theory_units.summary: Position cameras on the base of the triangular figure, behind the backs of the two central players, angled inwards towards the line of interest to cover both performers.
theory_units.applies_when: To cover a dialogue scene between two players, establishing depth and potentially emphasizing one player over the other through body position.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides depth in composition by placing actors on different planes, with one actor facing the camera (open body position) and the other with their back to it (closed position), drawing more attention to the 'open' actor.

theory_units.title: Internal Reverse Angle Camera Coverage
theory_units.summary: Place cameras between the two players, pivoted outwards from the triangular figure and close to the line of interest, to cover each player individually.
theory_units.applies_when: To show individual players during a dialogue, creating a direct, almost confrontational feel without being a subjective viewpoint.
theory_units.expected_effect: Emphasizes individual players and provides a sense of close proximity or direct engagement between them.
theory_units.caution: These shots are close to a head-on confrontation effect, but do not represent the actual subjective viewpoints of the performers.

theory_units.title: Subjective Camera Angle for Player POV
theory_units.summary: To represent a character's subjective viewpoint, position the camera back-to-back with another camera or player directly on the line of interest.
theory_units.applies_when: When the director wishes to immerse the audience directly into the visual perspective of a specific character, showing what they see.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a strong sense of audience immersion and identification with the character whose POV is being shown, excluding that character from the shot.

theory_units.title: Parallel Camera Positions for Profile Views
theory_units.summary: Place cameras on the base of the triangular figure, close to the line of interest, with their visual axes in parallel, covering each performer individually.
theory_units.applies_when: When desiring to capture individual players in profile during a dialogue, often for a more observational or neutral perspective.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides clear profile views of each player, which can convey a sense of observation, detachment, or a specific aesthetic without direct confrontation.

theory_units.title: Emphasis by Advancing Camera on Visual Axis
theory_units.summary: To emphasize a selected performer, advance the camera either optically (zoom in) or physically along its visual axis to achieve a closer shot of that performer.
theory_units.applies_when: When the director needs to highlight or draw immediate audience attention to one specific player in a multi-player scene.
theory_units.expected_effect: Visually singles out and emphasizes the selected performer, signaling their importance, reaction, or dialogue moment to the audience.

theory_units.title: Dominance Through Screen Space Distribution (2/3 - 1/3)
theory_units.summary: In an external reverse shot on standard screens, allocate two-thirds of the screen space to the performer facing the camera (the dominant one), and the remaining one-third to the performer with their back to the camera.
