theory_units.applies_when: When composing shots for dialogue, particularly external reverse angles, to visually establish and reinforce a dominant speaker or character.
theory_units.expected_effect: Accentuates the visual dominance of the performer facing the camera, drawing the audience's full attention to them and reinforcing their importance or role in the conversation.

theory_units.title: Strengthening Emphasis with Selective Focus
theory_units.summary: To further strengthen emphasis on a speaking performer, ensure they are in sharp focus while their interlocutor is rendered slightly out of focus.
theory_units.applies_when: When desiring to enhance the visual dominance and audience focus on a specific speaking character.
theory_units.expected_effect: Directs the audience's eye unequivocally to the in-focus character, enhancing their importance and visually separating them from other elements in the shot.

theory_units.title: Side View Shot for Pauses and Transitions
theory_units.summary: The camera position at the apex of the triangular arrangement, which views actors from the side with equal screen space, is weakest for emphasis and should be reserved for sequence opening/closing, introducing pauses, or preceding editorial pattern changes.
theory_units.applies_when: To signify the beginning or end of a conversation sequence, introduce a deliberate pause in the cutting rhythm, or precede a significant change in the editorial pattern.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides a neutral, less confrontational view of the actors, signaling a structural shift in the scene or dialogue pacing, rather than emphasizing a specific character.
theory_units.caution: This position is inherently weak for emphasizing individual performers.

theory_units.title: Wide Screen Central Composition for Reverse Shots
theory_units.summary: On wide screens, divide the frame into three equal parts compositionally, always placing the dominant player in each reverse shot into the central sector of the screen.
theory_units.applies_when: When composing reverse shots for dialogue on wide screens to mitigate jarring visual shifts and maintain audience attention.
theory_units.expected_effect: Focuses audience attention on the center of the screen, reduces the visual impact of shifting large volumes of screen image between takes, and maintains spatial continuity according to the triangle principle.
theory_units.caution: The remaining two-thirds of the screen (left and right sectors) may need to be balanced with background objects or detail to support the foreground composition.

theory_units.title: Wide Screen Foreground Silhouette Emphasis with Backlight
theory_units.summary: In wide screen reverse shots, compose by having a foreground player (back to camera) block half the screen, sparsely illuminated (in silhouette), while the background actor (facing camera) is brilliantly lit.
theory_units.applies_when: To create dramatic visual emphasis and compositional contrasts in wide screen dialogue scenes.
theory_units.expected_effect: Generates strong visual contrast and directs attention to the brilliantly lit background actor, while the foreground silhouette acts as a dynamic framing device. The shifting lighter areas between alternate reverse shots add visual interest.

theory_units.title: Wide Screen Extreme Foreground Dominance for Subtle Emphasis
theory_units.summary: Allocate most of the wide screen space to a minimally lit foreground player (back to audience), leaving only a small sector of the screen visible for the dominant actor positioned in the background.
theory_units.applies_when: When creating an extreme visual emphasis on a background actor by dramatically reducing their visible screen space, often for dramatic effect or to convey a sense of observation.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a distinct visual hierarchy where the small, visible background actor gains unique emphasis, often conveying a sense of being observed, framed, or subtly highlighted amidst a larger, less defined foreground.

theory_units.title: Foreground Blocking for Background Emphasis
theory_units.summary: Block a portion of the screen with a minimally lit foreground figure to emphasize a lighter figure or area in the background.
theory_units.applies_when: When you want to draw strong attention to a specific element or figure located in the background.
theory_units.expected_effect: Directs audience attention emphatically to the background, creating a visual hierarchy and sense of depth.

theory_units.title: Off-Centre Framing for Combined Reverse Shots
theory_units.summary: When combining internal and external reverse camera positions, place performers off-centre, close to one lateral side, and fill the remaining two-thirds of the screen with non-interfering elements.
theory_units.applies_when: When transitioning between internal and external reverse shots involving multiple performers, aiming for a distinct visual balance.
theory_units.expected_effect: Draws focused attention to the performer, creates an asymmetrical but balanced composition, and can enhance emphasis.

theory_units.title: Lateral Focus via Darkened Screen
theory_units.summary: Retain the center of interest on one lateral side of the picture in both master shots, darkening the rest of the screen to stress the key, well-lit area.
theory_units.applies_when: When a director wants to intensely emphasize a key figure or area, especially within master shots or internal reverse positions.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates strong, focused attention on the lit subject, imparting a sense of drama or isolation.

theory_units.title: Dominant Player Framing in Small Upper/Lower Screen Area
theory_units.summary: Frame the dominant or key player within a very small upper or lower area of the screen in reverse master shots.
theory_units.applies_when: When aiming to highlight a dominant player with an unconventional or emphatic composition in reverse master shots.
theory_units.expected_effect: Draws specific, unusual attention to the framed player; can convey scale, vulnerability, or power based on context.

theory_units.title: 2/3 Player Fill, 1/3 Breathing Space Composition
theory_units.summary: For internal reverse shots, compose the shot by filling two-thirds of the screen area with the player and leaving the remaining one-third in front of them free as 'breathing space' for a pleasing composition.
theory_units.applies_when: When composing internal reverse shots or framing a lone player, to achieve a visually balanced and un-cramped aesthetic.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates an aesthetically pleasing and balanced composition, providing a sense of space and naturalness.

theory_units.title: Opposed Side Framing for Alienated Mood
theory_units.summary: Frame players on opposed sides of the screen from shot to shot in external reverse angles (especially on wide screen) or internally with significant empty space behind the player's face, to create a shock effect or alienated mood.
theory_units.applies_when: When aiming to evoke a sense of alienation, shock, or unusual visual enhancement, particularly in intimate or emotionally intense scenes.
theory_units.expected_effect: A 'shock effect', an alienated mood, a 'strange imbalance', or 'special visual enhancement' depending on the specific application and scene context.
theory_units.caution: These compositions can quickly grasp attention and may distract from the scene's mood. They are best reserved for specific situations like intimate love scenes where the 'strange imbalance' can enhance the situation.

theory_units.title: Vertical Framing Variation in External Reverse Shots
theory_units.summary: In external reverse angles, vary the vertical placement of players by composing one player low in the frame and the other in the upper half, then interchanging their locations in the reverse shot. This technique often requires high camera angles directly behind the players on the line of interest.
theory_units.applies_when: When seeking to create dynamic vertical contrast and varied emphasis between two players in external reverse shots.
theory_units.expected_effect: Generates visual dynamism and contrasting emphasis, potentially implying shifts in power dynamics or relationships.
theory_units.caution: This specific alignment (cameras directly behind players on the line of interest with varied vertical framing) is typically only achievable with high camera angles.

theory_units.title: Triangular Camera Placement Principle (General)
theory_units.summary: The camera can be positioned along axis lines stemming from three points of a triangular figure established around central players, allowing for various shot distances (close-ups, close shots, medium shots, full shots).
theory_units.applies_when: When planning comprehensive camera coverage for scenes involving one, two, or more central players.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides a structured and versatile method for camera placement, ensuring consistent and adaptable coverage for editing.

theory_units.title: Line of Interest (Lone Player)
theory_units.summary: For a lone player, the direction of their gaze defines a 'line of interest,' which then dictates the application of the triangular camera placement principle, even if the object of their gaze is not visible.
theory_units.applies_when: When framing a lone player, particularly when their gaze is a significant element for narrative or emotional emphasis.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains visual continuity and guides audience focus in alignment with the player's internal or external attention.

theory_units.title: Camera Axis Alignment with Lone Player's Gaze
theory_units.summary: The camera's axis must be set parallel to the lone player's established line of interest (direction of gaze) to maintain a consistent sense of direction and prevent disorienting cuts in reverse shots.
theory_units.applies_when: When positioning the camera for a lone player, especially when planning for sequential reverse shots or cuts.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures visual continuity and prevents the audience from becoming disoriented regarding the player's spatial orientation.
theory_units.caution: If the player is looking straight ahead (north-south gaze), an east-west camera axis cannot be used for consecutive reverse shots, as it will break the sense of direction. Conversely, if the player is looking sideways (east-west gaze), a north-south camera axis will be ineffective.

theory_units.title: Camera Axis for Lone Player Head Turns
theory_units.summary: The camera axis for covering a lone player's head turn should be selected based on the degree of the turn: use an east-west axis for a turn of almost 180°, and a north-south axis for a 90° turn. The triangular camera coverage must be adjusted accordingly.
theory_units.applies_when: When covering a lone player performing significant head turns within a scene.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains seamless visual continuity and spatial understanding despite the actor's movement.

theory_units.title: External Reverse Angle Framing (Nose Rule)
theory_units.summary: In external reverse shots for face-to-face dialogue, when a performer is in the foreground with their back to the camera, ensure the camera is positioned so that the tip of their nose does not extend visually beyond the line of their cheek (i.e., their nose is not visible).
theory_units.applies_when: When shooting external reverse angles for face-to-face dialogue where a performer is in the foreground.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains a clean and undistracting profile of the foreground actor, ensuring focus on the background actor or the overall scene.

theory_units.title: 1/3-2/3 Screen Space for Face-to-Face Dialogue
theory_units.summary: Utilize a basic one-third/two-thirds screen space distribution for compositions in face-to-face dialogue.
theory_units.applies_when: When framing face-to-face dialogue, particularly when aiming for a classic and widely accepted compositional arrangement.
theory_units.expected_effect: Achieves a balanced and conventional pictorial composition that is readily understood and favored by audiences.
theory_units.caution: While a basic approach, variants based on the triangle principle can be used if desired for different creative effects.

theory_units.title: Static Dialogue Coverage (Two Parallel Positions)
theory_units.summary: For static dialogue between two players, use two strong camera positions placed parallel to the line of interest to create master shots. Cover the scene fully or partially from one position, then repeat from the other for parallel editing.
theory_units.applies_when: When covering static dialogue scenes involving two players, where comprehensive visual coverage for editing is desired.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides versatile visual coverage for editing, maintains consistent spatial relationships between players, and ensures a clear understanding of the scene's geography.

theory_units.title: Number Contrast with Reverse Shots
theory_units.summary: Combine external reverse shots (showing both players) with internal reverse shots (showing only one player) to vary the number of performers on screen.
theory_units.applies_when: When covering a conversation between two subjects where varying focus on individuals versus the pair is desired.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates visual variety, shifting emphasis between the individual and the pair, and can reflect psychological rapport or narrative focus.

theory_units.title: Simulated Vehicle Motion for Close-up Safety & Precision
theory_units.summary: For close-up shots of actors in moving vehicles, simulate vehicle motion and background in a controlled studio environment using static vehicles, back projection, or travelling matte.
theory_units.applies_when: When obtaining close shots of performers inside a moving vehicle at speed, where precision, controlled lighting, and actor safety are concerns.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures precise camera angles and actor safety while creating the illusion of movement, allowing for more controlled shot execution and consistent lighting.

theory_units.title: Emphasizing Players with Parallel Camera Axis Advance
theory_units.summary: In a parallel camera arrangement covering players aligned one behind the other, advancing the camera on a common visual axis can emphasize one player and create number contrast.
theory_units.applies_when: When covering two players positioned one behind the other in a dialogue scene, and you want to emphasize one player or create visual variation through number contrast.
theory_units.expected_effect: Emphasizes a specific player and creates visual variation (number contrast) when cutting between shots, drawing attention to the emphasized character.

theory_units.title: Maintaining Actor Eyelines in Individual Shots
theory_units.summary: Ensure actors maintain consistent eye-lines when filmed individually in a conversation to prevent continuity errors and ensure natural performance.
theory_units.applies_when: When filming individual shots (singles) of multiple players engaged in conversation, especially after camera repositioning, lens changes, or if actors are not simultaneously on set.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains visual continuity between shots, prevents actors from appearing to look in the wrong direction, and facilitates more natural acting by providing a consistent focal point.
theory_units.caution: Forgetting the previous looking direction can ruin the sequence. An actor looking in the wrong direction (e.g., right instead of left) will break continuity and audience immersion.

theory_units.title: Avoiding Direct Camera Gaze (Fiction Standard)
theory_units.summary: In most fiction films, performers should generally avoid looking directly into the camera lens, as it violates the line of interest and breaks the audience's immersion by making them feel directly addressed.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming actors in a narrative fiction film where audience immersion and the illusion of an observed reality are paramount, and no deliberate breaking of the fourth wall is intended.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains the illusion that the audience is observing a story unfolding, not being directly addressed, thus preserving immersion and the suspension of disbelief.
theory_units.caution: Violates the direction of the line of interest and makes the audience feel the player is looking directly at them, potentially breaking the narrative spell and making the scene feel unnatural.

theory_units.title: Breaking the Fourth Wall for Monologue
theory_units.summary: Allow a performer to look directly into the camera lens for a special purpose, such as delivering a monologue directly to the audience.
theory_units.applies_when: When a director intends for the performer to directly address the audience, offering personal insight or deliberately breaking the narrative flow (e.g., like Laurence Olivier in Richard III).
theory_units.expected_effect: The audience suddenly becomes a participant rather than a spectator, which can shock their feeling of security and draw them intimately into the narrative. It stresses important lines.
theory_units.caution: This convention can destroy the flow of a staged event. It must be used sparingly and with strong dramatic motivation. The player need not continually look into the camera, using it selectively for emphasis.

theory_units.title: Breaking the Fourth Wall as Announcer
theory_units.summary: Allow a performer to look directly into the camera lens to address the audience in the manner of a radio or TV announcer, simulating interaction with an off-screen person.
theory_units.applies_when: When the narrative context justifies the performer addressing the audience as if they were an announcer, or to simulate interaction with another character who may be off-screen.
theory_units.expected_effect: The audience accepts this direct gaze as more natural, as it aligns with their understanding of announcers relating to an unseen audience or other people. It can be used to stress important lines.
theory_units.caution: Must be used sparingly and with strong dramatic motivation. The player need not continually look into the camera, using it selectively for emphasis.

theory_units.title: Varying Camera Distance for Dialogue Emphasis and Dynamism
theory_units.summary: Utilize different camera-to-subject distances between shots in a dialogue scene to visually emphasize dialogue, concentrate attention, and create a more dynamic presentation.
theory_units.applies_when: When covering conversations between two players, particularly when one player or their dialogue is narratively more important, or when seeking to enhance visual interest and pacing.
theory_units.expected_effect: Visually stresses specific dialogue or players, focuses audience attention on the most important elements, and provides a livelier, more engaging scene presentation.
theory_units.caution: No more than four different distances (two pairs) are typically needed to obtain good results for a single dialogue scene to avoid excessive complexity.

theory_units.title: Standard Eye-Level Camera Height for Dialogue
theory_units.summary: During conversations, the camera lens is typically positioned at the same height as the actors, whether they are sitting or standing.
theory_units.applies_when: As a default or naturalistic approach when filming conversations between actors, aiming for a relatable and unobtrusive perspective.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides a neutral, natural, and relatable perspective for the audience, making them feel as if they are interacting with or observing the characters at eye level.

theory_units.title: Adaptive Camera Height for Reverse Shots (Standing/Sitting)
theory_units.summary: Adjust camera height for reverse shots to accommodate actors of differing heights, especially when one is standing and the other sitting, to maintain a naturalistic perspective. For internal reverse shots in this situation, alternate high and low camera positions to simulate each player's viewpoint.
theory_units.applies_when: When covering a scene with actors at different vertical heights (e.g., one standing, one sitting).
theory_units.expected_effect: Naturalistic perspective, matching eyelines, maintaining scene geography, and enhancing audience immersion through simulated viewpoints.

theory_units.title: Extreme Camera Angles for Shock or Emphasis
theory_units.summary: Reserve acutely tilted or extreme high/low camera angles for specific dramatic moments to create an unreal or shocking effect.
theory_units.applies_when: When an important story point or special event requires strong visual emphasis or a jarring effect.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates an unreal or shocking impression, drawing strong attention to the specific moment or subject.
theory_units.caution: Avoid for normal viewing, as it can appear unreal if overused or misplaced, disrupting audience engagement.

theory_units.title: Low Camera Positions for Height Contrast (Standing Actors)
theory_units.summary: When both actors are standing, place the camera low in both external reverse master shots to create an interplay of perceived heights between them.
theory_units.applies_when: When covering two standing actors in external reverse master shots, and a visual contrast in their perceived heights is desired.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a dynamic interplay of perceived heights between the actors, adding visual interest and highlighting their spatial relationship.

theory_units.title: Emphasizing a Player with Different Camera Height
theory_units.summary: Visually stress one player over another in an external reverse shot by employing a distinct camera height for their coverage.
theory_units.applies_when: When a director wishes to visually emphasize one of two standing players in an external reverse shot.
theory_units.expected_effect: Draws audience attention and subtly (or overtly) implies importance or dominance for the player filmed with the distinct camera height.

theory_units.title: Right Angle Camera Placement for Lying Subjects
theory_units.summary: When covering two players lying on the ground (face to face or on their backs), use a right-angle camera placement to alternately feature each actor distinctly on the screen.
theory_units.applies_when: When filming two actors lying on the ground in close proximity, and clear alternating coverage of each is desired.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides clear, alternating coverage of each actor, maintaining spatial relationship and avoiding ambiguity in screen direction.

theory_units.title: Flexible Camera Heights for Lying Subjects
theory_units.summary: When filming players lying on the ground, the camera can be positioned level with them for intimacy, or framed from above at a slanted or vertical angle for a more observational perspective.
theory_units.applies_when: When shooting actors lying on the ground.
theory_units.expected_effect: Varies the audience's perspective from intimate and grounded (level) to observational or dominant (above), influencing emotional connection.
theory_units.caution: Physical setup (e.g., platform, dug-out hole) may be required to comfortably achieve very low angles below the performer's level.

theory_units.title: Consistent Head Placement for Lying Subjects
theory_units.summary: In alternating shots of two lying subjects, consistently keep their heads within the same respective sectors of the screen to maintain visual continuity.
theory_units.applies_when: When cutting between shots of two players lying side-by-side to maintain visual continuity and prevent disorientation.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains screen geography and prevents disorienting the audience as they perceive the spatial relationship between the characters.

theory_units.title: Dominant Player in Higher Screen Position (Lying Subjects)
theory_units.summary: For lying subjects, subtly emphasize the dominant player by positioning their head in the higher screen position within the frame.
theory_units.applies_when: When filming two lying subjects and wishing to subtly or overtly emphasize one as dominant or more significant.
theory_units.expected_effect: Visually signifies dominance or importance of one character over the other, influencing audience perception without explicit dialogue.

theory_units.title: Opposed Glances for Normal Telephone Conversations
theory_units.summary: To create the feeling of a normal two-way telephone conversation, direct actors to look in opposite directions, particularly important for split-screen sequences.
theory_units.applies_when: When filming two actors having a telephone conversation, especially using single takes or split-screen to be combined in editing.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates the illusion of a natural two-way conversation, as if they are looking towards each other across the implied space of the screen.

theory_units.title: Interplay of Opposed Diagonals for Intimacy or Ease
theory_units.summary: Compose close shots with actors' heads subtly tilted to create an interplay of opposed diagonals, effectively conveying a mood of ease or intimacy.
theory_units.applies_when: When the scene calls for conveying a mood of comfort, rapport, ease, or intimacy between characters in close-up shots.
theory_units.expected_effect: Conveys a sense of comfort, rapport, or intimacy between characters through dynamic, yet subtle, visual lines.

theory_units.title: Camera Placement for Aligned Players with Diagonal Composition
theory_units.summary: When players are perfectly aligned, reverse camera positions must be placed close to the axis line of interest to achieve a dynamic diagonal composition of bodies on screen.
theory_units.applies_when: When covering two perfectly aligned players in reverse shots, where a clear, dynamic view is desired.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a dynamic diagonal composition of bodies, avoiding a muddled view of the dominant player and enhancing visual clarity.
theory_units.caution: Avoid placing cameras parallel to the line of interest, as it can muddle the view, especially of the dominant player.

theory_units.title: Nose Within Profile in Reverse Shots
theory_units.summary: In reverse shots, particularly over-the-shoulder compositions, ensure the tip of the nearby (foreground) actor's nose remains within their profile.
theory_units.applies_when: When framing a reverse shot, especially an over-the-shoulder shot with a foreground actor partially in frame.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains aesthetic balance, prevents distracting elements that might protrude awkwardly from the foreground actor's profile, and keeps the frame clean.

theory_units.title: External Reverse Angles for Small Lateral Gap
theory_units.summary: When a small lateral gap exists between two players, use specific external reverse camera positions, typically involving one with diagonal composition and another shooting over the shoulder.
theory_units.applies_when: When two players are standing with a small lateral gap between them, requiring clear reverse shot coverage.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides clear and natural-looking reverse shot coverage, maintaining spatial relationship and engagement despite the minor spatial separation.

theory_units.title: Right Angle Camera for Wide Lateral Gap
theory_units.summary: If a wide lateral gap exists between players (e.g., with an object between them), external reverse camera positions should assume a right-angle relationship to the line of interest.
theory_units.applies_when: When two players are separated by a wide lateral gap, possibly due to an intervening object or furniture.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains clear spatial relationships and avoids breaking the 180-degree rule, providing coherent coverage despite the wider separation.

theory_units.title: Line of Interest Dominance over Body Direction
theory_units.summary: The 'line of interest' principle for camera placement is always dominant; maintain the camera on one side of this line even if internal and external reverse shots make body directions appear violated.
theory_units.applies_when: When choosing camera positions for reverse shots, particularly when dealing with potential conflicts between maintaining the line of interest and apparent body direction.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures visual continuity and clear spatial relationships for the audience by prioritizing the central focus of interaction between characters.
theory_units.caution: An apparent violation of body direction (e.g., legs pointing opposed) is acceptable as long as the line of interest is consistently maintained across cuts.

theory_units.title: Translucent Density Masks for Sombre Compositions (Okamoto Technique)
theory_units.summary: Employ translucent density masks, placed obliquely and photographed out of focus, to enhance sombre compositions, create isolation, and add a stylized mood, especially in scenes like gunfights.
theory_units.applies_when: Enhancing sombre compositions, creating visual isolation of subjects, or adding a specific stylized mood, particularly effective in dark or tense scenes such as gunfights.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhanced sombre mood, visual isolation of the subject, darkness creeping around the main subject, creating an 'unreal' or highly stylized aesthetic.
theory_units.caution: Not suitable for bright or broad daylight scenes. Requires careful placement of the mask relative to the lens and subject, ensuring it is out of focus for the desired blur effect.

theory_units.title: Mirror Framing for Two-Player Scenes
theory_units.summary: Use a single mirror to reflect one player while another is in the foreground, creating a specific visual dynamic often used with two parallel master shots.
theory_units.applies_when: When depicting two players and desiring a unique visual effect, to imply presence without direct camera placement, or to add visual complexity.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a dynamic visual, implies a character's presence without showing them directly, adds depth to the scene, or creates a sense of detachment/observation.
theory_units.caution: Ensure the reflection is clear and serves the narrative purpose without being distracting.

theory_units.title: Straight Line Three-Player Staging
theory_units.summary: Arrange three players in a straight line, covering them with external reverse camera positions, ensuring each player maintains their screen area across shots.
theory_units.applies_when: When covering three-player dialogue where clear separation, consistent screen presence, and a formal visual order for each player is desired.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides clear visual order, predictable player positions for the audience, and maintains consistent screen geography.
theory_units.caution: Can appear too formal or static if variations in height, seating, or spacing are not introduced.

theory_units.title: Variations for Straight Line Staging
theory_units.summary: To prevent a straight line arrangement from appearing too formal, vary player positions by having some seated or at different heights, and adjust spacing between figures.
theory_units.applies_when: When using a straight line arrangement for multiple players and seeking to add visual interest or reduce perceived formality.
theory_units.expected_effect: Disguises overly formal pictorial compositions, adds visual depth and dynamism, and makes the scene feel more natural.
theory_units.caution: None specified, but ensure variations remain motivated by character or narrative.

theory_units.title: L-Shaped Three-Player Staging
theory_units.summary: Arrange three players in an 'L' shape, covering them with right-angle camera positions to maintain the regular order of players in master shots.
theory_units.applies_when: When covering three-player dialogue where a slightly less formal but still ordered arrangement is desired, maintaining consistent player order and screen geography.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains clear screen geography and player order, offers a visual alternative to a straight line, and can create a sense of direct engagement between two players.
theory_units.caution: None specified, but similar to straight-line, variations in height/seating could add further interest.

theory_units.title: Dynamic Attention Shift in Triangular Dialogues
theory_units.summary: In a triangular three-player arrangement, a subordinate player can shift the center of audience attention and on-screen group focus by turning their head between the other two players or around the entire group.
theory_units.applies_when: When directing a three-player dialogue in a triangular setup and needing to dynamically shift the audience's focus, imply a character's influence, or highlight power dynamics.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates dramatic tension, highlights which character is currently 'important' or holding the floor, and implies shifts in influence or agreement/disagreement.
theory_units.caution: Requires careful actor direction to ensure head turns are clearly motivated and effectively communicate the shift in attention without confusion.

theory_units.title: Formula A: Central Dominance in Triangular Dialogue
theory_units.summary: For closely knit triangular groups, use external reverse shots where the central dominant player remains in position across shots, while the side players exchange positions, providing alternating rear and frontal views.
theory_units.applies_when: Directing closely knit groups where the intimacy or directness of the situation requires detailed scrutiny of action and reaction, dividing players into two alternately featured sections.
theory_units.expected_effect: Highlights intimacy and individual reactions within the group, maintains focus on the central dominant figure, and creates a sense of close observation.
theory_units.caution: This geometric arrangement of players does not give each player a steady screen area, which may require careful management of audience orientation.

theory_units.title: Formula B: Off-Center Arbiter in Triangular Dialogue
theory_units.summary: Position the arbiting player (silent spectator) at one side of the screen, who then appears on the opposite side in the next shot, while the two conversing players maintain their relative positions along a diagonal line of interest.
theory_units.applies_when: When one player is primarily observing or arbiting the conversation of two others, and their shifting presence needs to be acknowledged while keeping the main dialogue central.
theory_units.expected_effect: Shifts the arbiting player's visual presence from side to side, maintains the visual flow of the conversation between the other two, and implies their watchful, influential role.
theory_units.caution: This arrangement does not give each player a steady screen area, which can make screen geography slightly less intuitive if not carefully managed.

theory_units.title: Formula C: Horizontal Dominance in Triangular Dialogue
theory_units.summary: Place the dominant player on one side of the screen, where they remain in both shots, while the other two performers exchange positions, with the arbiting actor positioned beyond the foreground's horizontal line of attention.
theory_units.applies_when: When a strong horizontal line of attention between two foreground players is desired, with a third arbiting actor positioned as an observer from further away, emphasizing the direct foreground interaction.
theory_units.expected_effect: Emphasizes the direct, horizontal interaction between the two foreground players, uses the arbiter as a background or observational element, and maintains a consistent dominant presence.
theory_units.caution: This arrangement does not give each player a steady screen area, potentially leading to varied screen geography across shots.

theory_units.title: Number Contrast for Variety in Three-Player Coverage
theory_units.summary: Combine external reverse shots (covering the whole group) with internal reverse shots (framing only a segment) to create 'number contrast' (e.g., 3 to 1, 3 to 2), adding visual variety to the presentation.
theory_units.applies_when: Desiring visual variety in covering a three-player scene, or to shift emphasis fluidly between the group as a whole and individual segments or reactions within it.
theory_units.expected_effect: Adds significant visual interest, can draw attention to specific individuals or relationships, and effectively breaks up static or repetitive compositions.
theory_units.caution: Ensure transitions between different 'number contrasts' are smooth and narratively motivated to avoid jarring the audience.

theory_units.title: Internal Reverse Shots for Trio Coverage
theory_units.summary: Use internal reverse shots to achieve a 2 to 1 number contrast or to cover each of three players individually, especially in a triangular form, complementing an external establishing shot.
theory_units.applies_when: Focusing on individual reactions within a trio, breaking down a group scene into individual contributions, or reminding the audience of the group's overall dynamic after focusing on individuals.
theory_units.expected_effect: Emphasizes individual expressions and reactions, allows for close scrutiny of characters, and helps the audience track individual contributions and emotional states within a group.
theory_units.caution: It is important to retain the correct interplay of directions of interest between the actors, especially when one holds the attention of the other two.

theory_units.title: Establishing Shot Use for Group Context
theory_units.summary: Employ an external camera position as an establishing shot to frame the whole group, re-inserting it from time to time to remind the audience of the group as an ensemble.
theory_units.applies_when: When covering a scene with multiple players, especially after focusing on individuals, to re-establish the group's context and spatial relationships.
theory_units.expected_effect: Orients the audience to the overall group and its setting, reinforces the ensemble dynamic, and prevents disorientation during closer coverage.
theory_units.caution: Traditionally used at the beginning, middle, or end of a scene, but its re-insertion should feel motivated, not arbitrary.

theory_units.title: Parallel Camera Positions for Profile & Dominance
theory_units.summary: Utilize parallel camera positions to show groups of three divided into two units (players presenting profiles to the camera, with two facing a dominant third) or three units (extremes in profile, with the center player facing the camera if acting as arbiter), achieving number contrast.
theory_units.applies_when: When desiring to emphasize profiles, clearly delineate dominant/subordinate roles within a three-player group, or create specific visual number contrasts with a strong sense of division.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates strong visual divisions within the group, provides clear focus on specific interactions, and offers a unique compositional style that can highlight power structures or observer roles.
theory_units.caution: None specified, but ensure the profile presentation serves the narrative and character relationships.

theory_units.title: Common Visual Axis for Shifting Group Focus
theory_units.summary: Use cameras on a common visual axis to initially show the whole group from a wider position, then transition to a closer view focusing solely on the dominant actor, whether they are at the center or side of the group.
theory_units.applies_when: When needing to shift audience focus from the overall group dynamic to a single, dominant individual within it, while maintaining visual consistency along a shared axis.
theory_units.expected_effect: Directs audience attention precisely to the dominant character, emphasizes their importance, reaction, or contribution, and visually narrows the scope of attention.
theory_units.caution: None specified, but ensure the transition is smooth and the dominant actor's importance is well-established.

theory_units.title: Varied Staging for Compositional Diversity
theory_units.summary: Place actors at different levels (e.g., seated, standing) and varying distances apart to create new and diverse screen compositions.
theory_units.applies_when: Whenever a scene involves multiple actors and there's a need to avoid static, flat, or overly formal compositions, adding visual interest and depth.
theory_units.expected_effect: Adds visual interest, creates a sense of depth and dynamism, prevents scenes from looking too formal or static, and can subtly highlight character relationships or status.
theory_units.caution: Ensure that variations in levels and distances are motivated by the narrative, character blocking, or emotional context, rather than being purely decorative.

theory_units.title: Pivoting Point Two-Shot for Trio Coverage
theory_units.summary: Cover a three-player scene by including only two players in each master shot, with one player acting as a 'pivoting point' by appearing in both shots, either maintaining their screen position or shifting from one side of the frame to the other.
theory_units.applies_when: When covering a three-player scene but focusing on pairs of interactions, using one character as a constant visual anchor around which the other two rotate, or to simplify complex three-shots.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains screen continuity around the pivoting character, highlights specific two-person dynamics within the trio, reduces visual complexity, and can create a sense of direct engagement.
theory_units.caution: Careful attention is needed to screen direction and continuity of the pivoting character, especially if they shift sides, to prevent audience disorientation.

theory_units.title: Pivoting Actor: Triangular Composition
theory_units.summary: When covering a triangular group of three actors, use a central actor as a pivot point for two master shots, placing the dominant camera sites at right angles to each other and keeping the pivot actor on the same side of the screen in both takes.
theory_units.applies_when: When filming a group of three actors in an approximately triangular arrangement and needing to establish two master shots that relate to each other.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a visually coherent relationship between master shots, maintaining spatial awareness for the audience despite camera position changes.

theory_units.title: Pivoting Actor: Distance Shift Continuity
theory_units.summary: When using a pivoting actor strategy, cuts between master shots with varying distances to the pivot actor (e.g., foreground to background) will be smooth if the pivoting performer remains on the same side of the screen in both takes.
theory_units.applies_when: When a pivoting actor changes their apparent distance from the camera between two master shots, for example, from foreground to background or vice-versa.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures visual continuity and a smooth cut, preventing audience disorientation despite a significant change in apparent distance.
theory_units.caution: Failure to keep the pivoting actor on the same side of the screen may lead to jarring cuts or a sense of discontinuity.

theory_units.title: Pivoting Actor: Directing Focus
theory_units.summary: To direct audience attention and vary the center of interest between other players in reverse shots, the actor used as a pivot should move their head.
theory_units.applies_when: When a pivoting actor is present in reverse shots and the director needs to subtly shift audience focus to other characters.
theory_units.expected_effect: Guides the audience's eye, clarifies the current point of interest in the dialogue or action, and enhances the naturalism of the actor's performance.
theory_units.caution: Over-exaggerated head movements might distract rather than guide.

theory_units.title: Pivoting Actor: Side Player External Reverse
theory_units.summary: Utilize a side player as a pivot point for a set of external reverse camera positions to cover a group of three, allowing the camera to 'pivot' around this specific actor.
theory_units.applies_when: When filming a group of three players and it's desirable to use one of the side players as the central reference point for establishing external reverse angles.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides clear coverage of the group while visually anchoring the shots around a specific character, even if they are not centrally positioned.

theory_units.title: Pivoting Actor: Straight Line Arrangement
theory_units.summary: When covering a straight line arrangement of three actors where two face the third, the central pivoting player can be included in both master shots even if they shift from one side of the screen to the other, to emphasize the irregular coverage.
theory_units.applies_when: When filming three actors in a straight line where one is a central pivot and the director desires a specific irregular coverage pattern with the pivot shifting screen sides.
theory_units.expected_effect: Can create a dynamic, if irregular, visual flow, emphasizing the interaction between the two facing actors across the pivot.
theory_units.caution: This can potentially disrupt screen direction continuity if not carefully managed or intended to create a specific effect.

theory_units.title: Pivoting Actor: Stressing Passivity
theory_units.summary: To emphasize a pivoting actor's passive role, position them in profile with downcast eyes, and minimize their screen area (e.g., to one-third of the frame).
theory_units.applies_when: When a central pivoting actor is intentionally passive and the director wants to visually reinforce their reduced involvement in the scene's action or dialogue.
theory_units.expected_effect: Visually communicates the actor's passivity and minimizes their dramatic weight, effectively transferring emphasis to other dominant characters.
theory_units.caution: This strategy should only be used when passivity is the desired character trait; otherwise, it may disengage the audience from the character.

theory_units.title: Pivoting Camera: Close-up Transition
theory_units.summary: Employ a close-up of a dominant performer, positioned as an advance on the visual axis of one of the main external reverse camera sites, as a 'pivoting camera' shot to mask screen position changes of other actors during cuts.
theory_units.applies_when: When transitioning between two external reverse shots of a group, and needing to smoothly mask the apparent shift in screen position of other characters.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a smooth, less jarring cut by providing a brief, focused moment on a key character, which optically hides the repositioning of background elements or other characters.
theory_units.caution: The close-up subject must be a clear 'center of interest' for the shot to be effective as a pivot.

theory_units.title: Partial Emphasis: Reducing Actor Involvement
theory_units.summary: To partially emphasize two dominant actors and reduce the involvement of a third, show all three players in the first master shot, then transition to a second master shot featuring only the two dominant performers.
theory_units.applies_when: When a scene with three actors develops to stress two characters and diminish the involvement of the third, regardless of their initial arrangement (straight line, L-shape, or triangle).
theory_units.expected_effect: Directs audience focus to the more active characters, visually reinforcing the shifting dynamics and narrative importance within the scene.

theory_units.title: Total Emphasis: 3 to 2 Player Transition
theory_units.summary: To achieve total emphasis on two players from a three-player group, use two pairs of master shots (one featuring three, one featuring two). When cutting from three-person to two-person coverage, the cut is more effective if the two-player shot is a reverse of the three-player shot's position, rather than an advance on the same visual axis. The same rule applies when returning from two-person to three-person coverage.
theory_units.applies_when: When a scene with three actors needs a strong, 'total' shift of emphasis to only two of them, and for smooth transitions back and forth.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a visually effective and clear shift in focus, reinforcing the dramatic change in character dynamics or importance, while maintaining spatial continuity.
theory_units.caution: Cutting with an advance on the same visual axis when shifting from three to two (or vice-versa) is less effective and can be jarring.

theory_units.title: Shifting Line of Interest: Crosswise Emphasis
theory_units.summary: To change the line of interest from one pair of actors to another (e.g., 'north-south' to 'east-west'), deploy camera positions that allow for a smooth passage between these lines. This is achieved using two sets of external-internal reverse shots, or for elementary coverage, four master external reverse camera positions (two for each line of interest).
theory_units.applies_when: When the dramatic focus in a three-person scene needs to shift from one pair of interacting characters to a different pair, conceptually changing the 'axis' of interaction.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clearly guides the audience's attention to the newly emphasized characters, reinforcing changes in narrative focus or dramatic tension through visual means.
theory_units.caution: Requires careful planning of camera positions to ensure smooth transitions and maintain spatial clarity.

theory_units.title: Shifting Line of Interest with External Reverse Shots
theory_units.summary: To shift the dominant line of interest in a three-person dialogue using four external reverse camera positions, specific camera sites are designated to witness or effect the change, for instance, position 2 can re-establish a north-south line.
theory_units.applies_when: When changing the dominant conversational focus between different pairs in a three-person static dialogue, particularly when re-establishing a specific line of interest (e.g., N-S) where the whole group is seen.
theory_units.expected_effect: Guides audience attention to the current speakers and their spatial relationship, allowing a clear shift in conversational focus.
theory_units.caution: The underlying formula is described as complicated to understand initially, but simple in practice.

theory_units.title: Assigning Shot Roles in 4-Site Internal/External Coverage
theory_units.summary: When covering a three-person dialogue using four camera sites, including at least one internal reverse shot, specific roles are assigned: an establishing shot, two main masters, and a reaction shot.
theory_units.applies_when: When covering a three-person dialogue with four camera sites, aiming for structured and versatile coverage.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides a clear and dynamic coverage strategy, allowing for varied emphasis and audience perspective on individual roles within the conversation.

theory_units.title: Achieving Number Contrast in Dialogue Coverage
theory_units.summary: Number contrast, where the number of visible performers changes from shot to shot, is obtained by alternating an establishing shot (full group) with a reaction shot (single player) or by cutting between three-person and two-person shots.
theory_units.applies_when: When covering a dialogue, especially involving a main speaker and a reacting player, and desiring a dynamic visual rhythm or emphasis on individual reactions.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates visual variety, can emphasize the isolated reaction of a single character, and draws attention to individual perspectives against the group context.

theory_units.title: Shifting Line of Interest with Internal/External Coverage
theory_units.summary: To shift the dominant line of interest from one conversational pair to another, the change is visually shown from an establishing shot, then moving to external reverse coverage of the newly emphasized pair, often intercutting a subordinate player's reaction.
theory_units.applies_when: When transitioning the focus of a three-person dialogue from one pair to another, particularly when one player becomes a silent onlooker.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clearly communicates the shift in conversational dynamics and audience attention, making the subordinate player's reaction visible while maintaining focus on the emphasized pair.

theory_units.title: Re-establishing the Whole Group Mid-Sequence
theory_units.summary: After shifting focus to a dominant line of interest between two players, an establishing shot of the entire group can be introduced mid-way through the sequence to re-establish the spatial context and the group's presence.
theory_units.applies_when: Mid-sequence or at key narrative points when the dialogue has focused on a subset of characters, and the director wishes to remind the audience of the broader group dynamic or prepare for a shift in focus back to the group.
theory_units.expected_effect: Grounds the audience in the scene's overall spatial arrangement and can signal a potential shift back to a wider group interaction or a re-assertion of the main line of interest.

theory_units.title: Using a Pivoting Player to Bridge Camera Positions
theory_units.summary: A specific player, often in an internal reverse position, can be used as a visual pivot to bridge distinct camera positions (e.g., reverse angles and those on a common visual axis), smoothly effecting shifts in the line of interest.
theory_units.applies_when: When making complex transitions between different lines of interest or camera setups, particularly when actors exchange screen positions or when needing to connect disparate camera angles fluidly.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a smooth, continuous transition for the audience, maintaining geographical clarity and flow despite significant shifts in camera perspective.

theory_units.title: Geometric Blocking for Emphasis with Cross/T-Figure Coverage
theory_units.summary: When covering a three-person dialogue, the two emphasized players form the 'arms' of a cross or 'T' figure, while the player whose attention is momentarily released is positioned at the 'bottom', guiding camera placement and audience focus.
theory_units.applies_when: When staging a three-person dialogue with varying emphasis on players, particularly when planning camera coverage (e.g., 4-8 positions) that aligns with a cross or T-figure pattern.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clearly communicates which players are dominant in a conversation and streamlines camera setup around this dynamic, making the shift in attention visually clear.

theory_units.title: Efficient Camera Position Deployment
theory_units.summary: When covering dialogue, only those camera positions specifically needed to achieve the desired effect or capture a particular interaction should be utilized, even if a larger set of theoretical positions exists.
theory_units.applies_when: Always, to optimize production efficiency and focus the narrative through selective camera work.
theory_units.expected_effect: Streamlined production, efficient use of resources, and a more focused narrative that avoids unnecessary shots.
theory_units.caution: Ensure all necessary angles and transitions for narrative clarity are still covered.

theory_units.title: Using Subordinate Masters in 3-Site Dialogue Coverage
theory_units.summary: In a simple three-camera setup for three-person dialogue, one acts as the main master covering all three performers, while the other two subordinate masters cover different pairs of actors and are edited in parallel with the main one.
theory_units.applies_when: When covering a three-person dialogue with a limited camera setup (three sites) where a central actor facilitates the shifts in attention.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides flexible coverage for shifting lines of interest while maintaining a clear understanding of the overall group and individual interactions with a minimal setup.
theory_units.caution: The two subordinate masters (e.g., Shots 2 and 3 if covering different pairs from the main master) cannot be edited together in parallel.

theory_units.title: Using a Close Shot as a Pivoting Point for Attention Shifts
theory_units.summary: A close shot of the central performer can act as a pivotal master shot, replacing an establishing shot, to clearly document when that performer shifts their attention from one player to another, dictating the line of interest.
theory_units.applies_when: When a single central performer is key to directing the flow of conversation and the shifts in attention between other characters, easing transitions between subordinate masters.
theory_units.expected_effect: Emphasizes the central performer's agency in the dialogue, clearly signaling shifts in focus to the audience, and creating smooth transitions between different conversational pairs.
theory_units.caution: The subordinate masters (e.g., Shots 2 and 3) that accompany the pivot shot cannot be edited together in parallel.

theory_units.title: Deliberately Omitting a Player for Visual Illusion
theory_units.summary: One or more players can be deliberately omitted from reverse shots, creating the illusion of breaking established coverage rules and allowing for unique compositions, often facilitated by set decoration or tight framing.
theory_units.applies_when: When desiring a stylistic or psychologically impactful composition that deviates from conventional full coverage, to create a sense of intimacy, exclusion, or dynamic visual shifts.
theory_units.expected_effect: Generates visual interest, can enhance intimacy with remaining players, highlight exclusion, or create a specific dramatic effect by selectively revealing information.

theory_units.title: Utilizing Set Decoration for Player Omission
theory_units.summary: Set decoration, such as obstructions like columns, can be strategically used to deliberately hide a player from a shot, enabling their omission and facilitating altered on-screen compositions.
theory_units.applies_when: When planning to omit a player from a shot for dramatic or compositional reasons, especially when the player is centrally located or in the background of a triangular arrangement.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a dynamic visual effect, allowing for selective focus and the impression of a different group composition than is physically present on set.

theory_units.title: Varying Camera Levels for Visual Variety
theory_units.summary: Employing different camera levels (e.g., high, eye-level, low) throughout a sequence adds visual interest and dynamism.
theory_units.applies_when: Routinely throughout a sequence to prevent visual monotony and enhance the aesthetic appeal or psychological impact of the coverage.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increased visual engagement, subtle shifts in perspective, and a more dynamic overall look and feel to the scene.

theory_units.title: Applying Visual Emphasis with External Reverse Shots
theory_units.summary: Visual emphasis on a single line of interest in a dialogue can be achieved through the exclusive use of external reverse shots, which can provide either partial or total emphasis.
theory_units.applies_when: When desiring to strictly control and direct audience attention to a specific two-person interaction within a larger group, maintaining an observational, external perspective.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clearly highlights the primary conversational axis and can create a sense of observation from an outside perspective, focusing attention without internalizing the viewpoint.

theory_units.title: Creating Depth Illusion with Player Proximity
theory_units.summary: Positioning some actors significantly closer to the camera than others within a group shot enhances the illusion of depth in the frame.
theory_units.applies_when: When composing group shots and desiring to add a sense of three-dimensionality and visual interest to the image.
theory_units.expected_effect: A more dynamic and realistic spatial representation of the group, increasing visual engagement and separating planes within the frame.

theory_units.title: Using Occult Balance for Group Emphasis
theory_units.summary: Occult balance, a technique from theatre, puts emphasis on a person within a group by balancing their posture (e.g., a standing figure balancing a group of sitting people, or vice-versa) to subtly draw attention.
theory_units.applies_when: When composing group shots and needing to subtly emphasize a particular individual or subgroup without resorting to overt camera movement or close-ups.
theory_units.expected_effect: Draws the eye to the emphasized figure by creating a visual contrast in posture or positioning within the group, establishing a soft visual hierarchy.

theory_units.title: Lighting for Main Characters and Subordinates in Groups
theory_units.summary: Conventionally, main characters receive stronger illumination, while other group members receive subdued lighting to keep them visible but subordinate in visual hierarchy.
theory_units.applies_when: When lighting group scenes where there is a clear distinction between main and supporting characters, or to guide audience attention to specific individuals.
theory_units.expected_effect: Directs audience attention to the most important characters, establishing a visual hierarchy and reinforcing their narrative or emotional focus.

theory_units.title: Basic Group Coverage with Master Shots
theory_units.summary: To effectively cover both the whole group and the center of interest in a dialogue, at least two basic master shots are needed: one framing the group full view, and the other a close shot of the main actor(s).
theory_units.applies_when: As a foundational strategy for covering any group dialogue, ensuring both wide contextual understanding and character-specific focus.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides comprehensive coverage, allowing the audience to understand the spatial dynamics of the group while also connecting with individual character reactions and dialogue.

theory_units.title: Geometric Blocking for Visual Pleasantness in Larger Groups
theory_units.summary: For larger dialogue groups (four or more persons), it is visually pleasing if some characters stand and some sit, arranged in geometric patterns like triangles, squares, or circles.
theory_units.applies_when: When staging a dialogue involving four or more persons, particularly to enhance visual appeal, naturalness, and dynamic composition.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a more dynamic and aesthetically balanced group composition, preventing a static or crowded look, and can subtly delineate subgroups.

theory_units.title: Common Visual Axis Intercutting
theory_units.summary: Alternately intercut two shots on the same visual axis to cover a conversation in depth.
theory_units.applies_when: Covering a conversation between multiple players, aiming for depth and continuity.
theory_units.expected_effect: Covers conversation in depth, maintains visual continuity and audience orientation.

theory_units.title: Visual Balance with Varying Heights
theory_units.summary: Achieve visual balance in group compositions by arranging standing and seated performers.
theory_units.applies_when: Composing shots with groups of actors at different body levels (standing, seated).
theory_units.expected_effect: A visually balanced and harmonious screen composition.

theory_units.title: Directing Audience Attention via Actor Facing
theory_units.summary: Actors facing away from the camera direct audience attention to others; actors facing towards the camera draw attention to themselves.
theory_units.applies_when: Composing group shots where audience focus needs to be controlled or shifted to specific actors.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience attention is effectively guided to desired characters or away from non-essential ones.

theory_units.title: Emphasizing Center of Interest (Common Visual Axis)
theory_units.summary: Use a second master shot on the same visual axis to visually emphasize the center of interest within a group.
theory_units.applies_when: Needing to draw focus to a specific part of a group while maintaining the context of a wider master shot.
theory_units.expected_effect: Visually emphasizes key players or areas of interest without fully isolating them.

theory_units.title: Reestablishing Shot for Context and Reaction
theory_units.summary: Periodically intercut an establishing shot into a closer master shot to show reactions of non-active participants or expand the visual context of the dialogue.
theory_units.applies_when: Actors are serving as witnesses whose reactions are important, or when needing to add 'colour' to dialogue by showing the wider group.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains awareness of the entire group's presence and reactions, enriching the dialogue sequence.
theory_units.caution: Overuse may slow down the pace of the central dialogue.

theory_units.title: Closer Shot at Right Angle to Master
theory_units.summary: Position a closer second shot at a right angle to the initial master shot for varied emphasis in group coverage.
theory_units.applies_when: Covering dialogue involving the whole group and central figures, or a discussion watched by others, seeking a different perspective for emphasis.
theory_units.expected_effect: Offers a distinct visual perspective on the center of interest, covering the whole group and its focus effectively.

theory_units.title: Triangular Camera Placement for Table Groups
theory_units.summary: Employ a triangular arrangement for camera placement when covering groups seated around a table to present them clearly and solve tricky script situations.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming groups of people seated around a table, especially in complex dialogue or interaction scenes.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clear presentation of the group to the audience, effective and flexible coverage for complex table scenes.

theory_units.title: Dialogue Coverage: Individual Emphasis within Group
theory_units.summary: Intercut a master group shot with individual close-ups of two central actors to emphasize their focused dialogue while maintaining awareness of the larger group context.
theory_units.applies_when: Two central actors are having a focused conversation within a larger group, and their individual contributions need emphasis alongside occasional group reactions.
theory_units.expected_effect: Highlights specific dialogue exchanges while reminding the audience of the broader group's presence and reactions.
theory_units.caution: Frequent cutting between individual shots and the master shot may feel repetitive if not motivated by clear narrative shifts.

theory_units.title: Right Angle Setup: Extreme Actor Shift (Case B)
theory_units.summary: Using a right-angle camera setup with consistent distance, an actor at one extreme of the frame in Shot 1 shifts to the opposite extreme in Shot 2, while others maintain their relative order.
theory_units.applies_when: Covering groups of 3-5 persons with a right-angle setup, aiming for a dynamic visual shift of a peripheral actor across the frame.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a subtle yet dynamic visual shift for a specific actor, adding visual interest while preserving the order of central figures.
theory_units.caution: Ensure the shift is motivated and not disorienting to the audience.

theory_units.title: External Reverse Angles: Diagonal Interest Line (Case C)
theory_units.summary: When covering a group of five with external reverse angles around a dominant diagonal line of interest, actors *not* on that line shift positions and sides of the screen between shots.
theory_units.applies_when: Covering a group of five where a specific diagonal line of interest (e.g., between C and E) is dominant, and peripheral actors need dynamic re-positioning.
theory_units.expected_effect: Dynamically emphasizes the central diagonal line of interest by repositioning non-dominant actors, enhancing visual flow and focus.

theory_units.title: External Reverse Angles: Central Player Dominance (Case D)
theory_units.summary: For a group at a table with central dominant players, external reverse angles are concentrated on one side of their line of interest, causing extreme actors to exchange screen sites while central players remain in their sectors.
theory_units.applies_when: The important conversation is between two central actors within a larger group at a table, and their central position needs to be maintained while peripheral actors provide dynamic background.
theory_units.expected_effect: Emphasizes the central dialogue, creates dynamic visual interest with shifting peripheral actors without disrupting the primary focus.

theory_units.title: Internal Reverse Sites: Group Subdivision
theory_units.summary: Utilize internal reverse camera sites to visually divide a group, opposing its parts, and creating visual interplay through number contrast.
theory_units.applies_when: Needing to create visual tension, highlight opposition, or add variety by breaking a larger group into smaller, distinct units.
theory_units.expected_effect: Divides the group visually, emphasizes opposition between parts, adds dynamic variety through contrasting numbers of subjects per frame.
theory_units.caution: Requires an establishing shot to set the initial context before subdivision.

theory_units.title: Group Subdivision: One Actor vs. Group
theory_units.summary: Employ two internal reverse camera positions within the group to frame one player in opposition to the rest, highlighting an individual against the collective.
theory_units.applies_when: A single actor is in direct opposition or dialogue with the rest of the group, and this dynamic needs strong visual emphasis.
theory_units.expected_effect: Strongly emphasizes the individual's isolation or opposition against the collective, creating visual tension and focus.
theory_units.caution: Requires an establishing shot to introduce the full group context.

theory_units.title: Group Subdivision: Unequal Portions
theory_units.summary: Divide a group into two smaller, unequal units using internal reverse camera positions for enhanced visual interest.
theory_units.applies_when: Subdividing a group for visual dynamics, especially preferring unequal portions to create more engaging compositions than equally sized segments.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates more dynamic and interesting visual compositions compared to symmetric subdivisions, preventing monotony.
theory_units.caution: Requires an establishing shot to introduce the full group context.

theory_units.title: Combined Internal/External Reverse Angles (Straight Line)
theory_units.summary: Cover five players in a straight line by using opposed diagonals with external reverse angles, and stress a specific sector of the line with an internal reverse angle.
theory_units.applies_when: Covering a straight-line arrangement of five players, aiming for dynamic diagonal shifts between external shots and focused emphasis on a specific sector with an internal shot.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides dynamic and varied coverage for straight-line groups, allowing for both broad movement and focused emphasis.

theory_units.title: Achieving Composition in Depth
theory_units.summary: Create composition in depth by strategically arranging players' floor plan distribution (determining viewing plane) and varying their heights/positions (lying, seated, standing).
theory_units.applies_when: Composing any shot with multiple actors, particularly group shots, to avoid a flat visual arrangement.
theory_units.expected_effect: A more dynamic, three-dimensional, and balanced screen composition, enhancing visual interest and realism.

theory_units.title: Triangular Composition: Apex and Base Emphasis
theory_units.summary: For a triangular group, use a first camera site viewing the whole group and emphasizing the apex, then a second site framing only the two players at the base for dialogue coverage.
theory_units.applies_when: Covering dialogue within a group arranged in a dominant triangular formation, needing to emphasize different parts of the triangle at different times.
theory_units.expected_effect: Effectively covers dialogue by shifting emphasis between the apex and base of a triangular group, aiding clarity and narrative flow.

theory_units.title: Dialogue Coverage: Multiple Opposed Sectors
theory_units.summary: Cover dialogue in groups distributed in three or more sectors using establishing and internal reverse shots, where closer angles may frame more than one person, similar to triangular formation coverage.
theory_units.applies_when: Covering dialogue within large, complex groups structured into multiple distinct sectors (three or more).
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides comprehensive and dynamic dialogue coverage for complex group arrangements, maintaining awareness of multiple participants even in closer frames.

theory_units.title: Circular Progression of Attention in Group Scenes
theory_units.summary: Guide audience attention through a group by having performers progressively shift their gaze and focus in a circular pattern, often utilizing off-screen space to imply continuation.
theory_units.applies_when: Handling group interactions where the line of interest needs to move dynamically between multiple participants to maintain engagement.
theory_units.expected_effect: Keeps audience engaged, clarifies who is interacting with whom, and provides a sense of a complete interaction cycle.

theory_units.title: Triangular Group Composition in Depth
theory_units.summary: Arrange larger groups in triangular formations, both horizontally and in depth, often placing dominant players in the foreground.
theory_units.applies_when: Composing large groups, especially when needing to differentiate between dominant and subsidiary characters or add visual interest.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates visual interest, guides the eye to key figures, emphasizes certain characters, and adds depth to the scene.

theory_units.title: Dynamic Group Subdivision for Coverage
theory_units.summary: Establish a whole group, then progressively break it into smaller sub-groups for closer coverage using varied camera setups, altering these subdivisions upon subsequent returns to the establishing shot.
theory_units.applies_when: Covering large groups over an extended period to maintain visual variety and progressively focus on different sub-interactions.
theory_units.expected_effect: Prevents visual monotony, allows for closer emotional focus on sub-groups, and provides varied visual arrangements over time.

theory_units.title: Central Pivot for Scattered Group Dialogue
theory_units.summary: In scenes with scattered groups, center the action on a single person or central group who acts as both speaker and listener, pivoting audience attention between distant groups.
theory_units.applies_when: Covering dialogue among widely dispersed groups or individuals in a complex setting.
theory_units.expected_effect: Simplifies complex interactions for the audience, provides a clear focal point, and maintains continuity and clarity of who is speaking to whom.

theory_units.title: Simplifying Complex Line of Interest Shifts
theory_units.summary: In scenes with frequently changing lines of interest, use a single player as a pivot in master or re-establishing shots to clearly indicate shifts in interaction direction.
theory_units.applies_when: Managing complex dialogues with shifting focus among many participants to avoid audience confusion.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains clear spatial relationships, prevents disorienting jumps, and simplifies audience understanding of group interactions.

theory_units.title: Static Camera for Complex Group Dialogue
theory_units.summary: Employ static camera setups and minimal, story-driven player movement to handle complex, multi-character dialogue scenes effectively.
theory_units.applies_when: Directors aim to maintain an observational feel, allowing the audience to discover the dynamics within a large, interacting group without overt camera direction.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a naturalistic or observational feel, places emphasis on character interaction and performance, and can enhance tension.
theory_units.caution: Requires careful blocking and character positioning to ensure clarity without camera movement.

theory_units.title: Impersonal Crowd Treatment
theory_units.summary: Treat a crowd as a single, undifferentiated, passive entity, with the central protagonist's fixed gaze establishing the main line of interest to the mass.
theory_units.applies_when: The crowd's individual reactions are not narratively important, and the focus is solely on the speaker's address to a generalized audience.
theory_units.expected_effect: Emphasizes the speaker's authority or address to a generalized mass, creating a formal or detached tone.

theory_units.title: Interactive Crowd Treatment
theory_units.summary: Subdivide an interactive crowd into identifiable sectors or small groups that radiate towards the protagonist, who then shifts their gaze between these sub-groups to engage them.
theory_units.applies_when: The protagonist actively engages with specific individuals or sub-groups within the crowd, or when individual crowd reactions are important to the narrative.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a more dynamic and engaging interaction, highlights individual reactions or questions, and makes the crowd feel more present and responsive.

theory_units.title: Protagonist Placement and Crowd Interaction
theory_units.summary: The protagonist's position, either on the rim or in the center of an interactive crowd, dictates camera placement options and influences their perceived integration or separation from the group.
theory_units.applies_when: Designing scenes where a protagonist interacts with various parts of a crowd, influencing the desired visual relationship.
theory_units.expected_effect: Influences the sense of the protagonist's integration or separation from the crowd and affects the available camera angles for coverage.

theory_units.title: Triangular Formation for Audience Internal Dialogue
theory_units.summary: When audience members engage in conversation among themselves, momentarily excluding the main performer, frame them in a triangular formation to highlight their internal dialogue.
theory_units.applies_when: Shifting narrative focus from the main performer to specific internal audience reactions or side conversations.
theory_units.expected_effect: Highlights specific audience reactions, adds depth to the scene by showing sub-plots or opinions within the crowd, and diversifies attention.

theory_units.title: Supporting Crowd Gaze as Chorus
theory_units.summary: Utilize secondary, anonymous crowd members to reinforce the importance of main characters and stress shifts in interest by having them directly look at the main characters.
theory_units.applies_when: Needing to visually emphasize the focus of attention within a crowd, or to make main characters feel more central and observed.
theory_units.expected_effect: Guides audience attention, visually validates the importance of main characters, and creates a sense of collective group reaction or focus.

theory_units.title: Screen Direction for Off-Screen Relationships
