theory_units.summary: In close shots, if two characters look to the same side of the screen, they are perceived as looking at a third party off-screen, not at each other, which dictates screen direction for clarity.
theory_units.applies_when: Cutting between individual close-ups in a multi-party conversation, especially when indicating off-screen focus or avoiding false eyelines.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains clear spatial relationships, prevents false eyelines or confusion about who characters are interacting with.
theory_units.caution: Violation leads to confusion about who characters are interacting with or where they are looking.

theory_units.title: Crosswise Line of Interest Shift
theory_units.summary: Shift the dominant line of interest between 'north-south' (e.g., stage to audience) and 'east-west' (e.g., characters talking among themselves) to emphasize different groups or interactions.
theory_units.applies_when: Directing scenes where the focus needs to alternate between different planes of action, such as performers on stage and audience members, or multiple interacting groups.
theory_units.expected_effect: Dynamically shifts audience focus between different areas of interest, clarifies who is interacting with whom, and adds visual variety to the scene.

theory_units.title: Central Player as Pivot in a Crowd
theory_units.summary: When a main player stands in the center of a crowd, they act as a central pivot around whom the camera can be placed to relate them to the surrounding crowd and define the scene's line of interest.
theory_units.applies_when: A protagonist is surrounded by a crowd and needs to interact with various parts of it, or when illustrating their central importance.
theory_units.expected_effect: Emphasizes the protagonist's central role, allows for comprehensive coverage of interactions with the surrounding crowd, and establishes a clear spatial relationship.

theory_units.title: Pivoting Player for General Group Coverage
theory_units.summary: Use a key player as a 'pivot' to organize and simplify camera coverage (master shots) of a group interaction, allowing for consistent spatial relationships by maintaining or shifting their screen position.
theory_units.applies_when: Covering interactions within groups of three or more players to ensure clear spatial orientation and facilitate editing.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains spatial continuity, simplifies complex blocking, and aids in assembling master shots effectively.

theory_units.title: Pivoting Actor for Subdivided Group Meaning
theory_units.summary: Employ a central pivoting actor to visually subdivide a group into distinct units (e.g., 'friends' behind, 'opponents' facing), using screen-side shifts for dynamism and to define relationships.
theory_units.applies_when: Desiring to visually represent distinct sub-groups within a larger crowd, especially in relation to a central figure, and to add visual dynamism or define alliances.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clearly defines alliances or opposing forces, emphasizes the central actor's importance, and creates visual interest through screen-side shifts.

theory_units.title: Dual Dominant Pivots for Group Coverage
theory_units.summary: Use two central, dominant players as visual pivots to frame the entire group around them, focusing on the interaction between the pivots while others serve as a backdrop.
theory_units.applies_when: Two characters are the primary focus of an interaction within a larger group, and the group's reactions are secondary or provide context.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clearly defines the central conflict or dialogue, uses the group as an effective backdrop, and simplifies coverage of the core interaction.

theory_units.title: Dominant Pivots on Group Rim
theory_units.summary: When two dominant pivoting players are positioned on the edge of a group, selectively include or omit the group from reverse shots to maintain focus on the central performers.
theory_units.applies_when: The main interaction occurs between two characters at the periphery of a group, and the group's constant presence is not essential for both reverse shots.
theory_units.expected_effect: Directs audience attention to the core interaction, uses the group selectively for contextual or establishing purposes, and simplifies framing.

theory_units.title: Passive Foreground Pivots for Sector-Divided Groups
theory_units.summary: Employ two passive players in the foreground as pivots, who remain on the sides of the screen, while the dominant central players change between shots, using right-angle camera positions for parallel editing.
theory_units.applies_when: Needing to divide a group into sectors and focus on changing central players, especially in a static setup like a table, or for logistical shooting challenges.
theory_units.expected_effect: Guides audience attention to the shifting central figures, creates a consistent framing reference, and facilitates flexible shooting methods.

theory_units.title: Asynchronous Group Filming with Foreground Pivots
theory_units.summary: Seamlessly relate two groups of players filmed at different times by using two passive foreground pivoting players who are present for both takes, maintaining continuity across the central changing figures.
theory_units.applies_when: Logistical constraints prevent all players from being present simultaneously in a group scene requiring interaction between different sub-groups.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows for efficient production scheduling, maintains visual continuity despite staggered filming, and creates the illusion of simultaneous interaction.
theory_units.caution: Requires careful matching of lighting between the different takes.

theory_units.title: Varied Cutting for Static Dialogue
theory_units.summary: In static dialogue scenes without actor or camera movement, variety and comprehensive coverage must rely on diverse cutting patterns to prevent visual stagnation.
theory_units.applies_when: Directing static dialogue scenes where actors don't move and the camera is fixed.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains audience interest, prevents visual monotony, and ensures comprehensive scene coverage.

theory_units.title: Dynamic Master Shot Self-Sufficiency
theory_units.summary: A master shot can be self-sufficient, requiring no additional cutaways or closer shots, if actors move dynamically within its frame.
theory_units.applies_when: Using a single master shot to cover a complete sequence or dialogue where actors perform significant movement within the frame.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains visual interest, can enhance realism by avoiding cuts.
theory_units.caution: Requires 'certain rules' to be respected (unspecified here) for shot sufficiency.

theory_units.title: Enhancing Static Dialogue Master Shots
theory_units.summary: For most static dialogue scenes, a single master shot is insufficient to maintain visual interest and should be enhanced by stressing certain passages with closer shots or cutaways.
theory_units.applies_when: Directing static dialogue scenes that lack inherent dramatic force to sustain interest with a single master shot.
theory_units.expected_effect: Prevents scene from becoming visually uninteresting; maintains audience engagement by highlighting key moments.
theory_units.caution: Exception: if the situation and dialogue are so full of meaning and dramatic force that visual variation would disturb the mood.

theory_units.title: Gradual Proximity for Building Dialogue Interest
theory_units.summary: As dialogue builds in interest, progressively move closer to performers to capture every nuance of movement and fleeting reactions in their faces, increasing audience engagement.
theory_units.applies_when: Directing dialogue scenes where interest or dramatic tension needs to increase over time.
theory_units.expected_effect: Intensifies audience focus, reveals subtle emotional cues, and builds dramatic tension.

theory_units.title: Approaching and Receding Editing Pattern
theory_units.summary: Utilize an editing pattern that visually 'approaches' performers (close shots/close-ups) during dramatic peak moments of lengthy dialogue and 'recedes' to medium shots during periods of emotional repose.
theory_units.applies_when: Directing lengthy dialogue scenes with identifiable peaks of interest and periods of emotional rest for the audience.
theory_units.expected_effect: Guides audience attention, allows emotional repose, heightens the impact of really important passages, and prevents concentration fatigue.
theory_units.caution: This method must not appear too obvious.

theory_units.title: Masking Approaching and Receding Transitions
theory_units.summary: To prevent the 'approaching and receding' editing method from appearing too obvious, use different editing patterns in each section of dialogue covered from peak to peak.
theory_units.applies_when: Implementing the 'approaching and receding' editing method in dialogue scenes.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains audience immersion by making the visual guidance less perceptible, creating a more seamless viewing experience.

theory_units.title: Natural Progression for Dialogue Openings
theory_units.summary: Begin dialogue sequences with a natural progression (e.g., performers meet, then talk, then part) allowing the audience to meet characters visually before engaging in closer dialogue.
theory_units.applies_when: Initiating a dialogue sequence, especially when characters are not already in their final conversation positions.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhances realism, introduces characters organically, and eases the audience into the scene.

theory_units.title: Dialogue Opening Variant: Players Enter and Approach
theory_units.summary: Open a dialogue sequence by having both players enter camera range, walk towards the camera, and then stop to talk.
theory_units.applies_when: Starting a dialogue where characters arrive at a location to converse, and a direct approach is desired.
theory_units.expected_effect: Naturalistically introduces characters, establishes their presence, and defines their starting point for dialogue.

theory_units.title: Dialogue Opening Variant: One Player Present, Other Enters
theory_units.summary: Open a dialogue sequence with one performer already in the frame, and the other entering to join them before they start talking.
theory_units.applies_when: Starting a dialogue where one character is waiting or already situated, and another joins them.
theory_units.expected_effect: Establishes a scene with an existing character, introduces dynamic interaction with the newcomer, and sets a clear meeting point.

theory_units.title: Camera Movement for Dialogue Entry
theory_units.summary: Instead of a fixed camera, use a pan or track to follow one or both actors as they move to their stopping places before a static dialogue begins.
theory_units.applies_when: Opening a dialogue sequence where actors move to their conversation spot, and visual dynamism is desired.
theory_units.expected_effect: Guides audience attention smoothly, adds visual dynamism to character entry, and can establish the location or journey.

theory_units.title: Opening with a Transient Third Character
theory_units.summary: Start a sequence using panning or tracking by having a third, transient character approach the main couple/group, interact briefly, and depart, while the camera remains on the main performers as they begin to speak.
theory_units.applies_when: Desiring a dynamic opening that transitions into static dialogue, providing an organic reason for the main characters to converse.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates initial intrigue, provides a natural trigger for the main dialogue, and adds narrative depth to the scene's setup.

theory_units.title: Panning/Tracking Reveal with Pre-heard Dialogue
theory_units.summary: Begin a scene with a pan or track across an empty part of the set, revealing the main players already speaking off-screen, as the camera frames them.
theory_units.applies_when: Wanting to build anticipation or establish environment before focusing on characters, or to create a sense of eavesdropping.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates suspense, establishes setting, and draws the audience into the scene through sound before sight.

theory_units.title: Multi-Shot Introduction to Static Dialogue
theory_units.summary: Cover the initial movements leading up to a static dialogue using several distinct shots, rather than a single continuous take.
theory_units.applies_when: Introducing a static dialogue with more visual dynamism, varied perspectives, or detailed information than a single shot allows.
theory_units.expected_effect: Adds visual interest, can convey more information or establish mood more effectively during character entry.

theory_units.title: Reversed Movement for Sequence Exits
theory_units.summary: Conclude a dialogue sequence by reversing the movements described for openings, such as characters moving away from the camera or the camera receding.
theory_units.applies_when: Ending a dialogue sequence where characters depart or the scene resolves, and a sense of completion or symmetry is desired.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides a clear sense of closure or continuation, can create visual symmetry with the opening, and allows for natural character departure.

theory_units.title: Re-establishing Shot for Spatial Awareness
theory_units.summary: Periodically insert re-establishing shots, at least once halfway through a sequence, to remind the audience of the locale and spatial relationships between performers.
theory_units.applies_when: Directing any sequence, especially those heavily reliant on closer shots, to prevent audience disorientation.
theory_units.expected_effect: Re-establishes place and spatial relationships, provides a visual pause, can end sequences or mask editing pattern changes, and reminds of excluded characters' presence.

theory_units.title: Delayed Establishing Shot
theory_units.summary: A scene can begin with close shots, delaying the establishing shot until later in the sequence. However, a scene should rarely, if ever, completely omit an establishing shot.
theory_units.applies_when: Desiring to create immediate intimacy or mystery at the start of a scene before providing full contextual information.
theory_units.expected_effect: Builds intrigue, allows immediate focus on character emotion, then provides necessary context.
theory_units.caution: Do not dispose completely of the establishing shot.

theory_units.title: Emphasizing Silent Reactions in Dialogue
theory_units.summary: Cut to a listening performer's silent reaction, often mid-speech, while the speaker's voice continues, to emphasize the reaction and potentially enhance expressiveness.
theory_units.applies_when: A listening performer's reaction is dramatically significant or more expressive than the speaker's immediate action.
theory_units.expected_effect: Highlights emotional subtext, adds depth to character interaction, and maintains audience engagement through non-verbal cues.
theory_units.caution: Refinements in cutting and timing must be dictated by the context of the scene and its meaning in the story as a whole.

theory_units.title: Sustaining Interest with Group Reaction Shots
theory_units.summary: When an actor delivers a long speech to a group, occasionally insert various silent reaction shots of the listening group, while the speaker's voice continues, to sustain audience interest.
theory_units.applies_when: A single character delivers a lengthy speech to a group of listeners, and visual interest needs to be maintained beyond the speaker.
theory_units.expected_effect: Prevents visual monotony of a single speaker, highlights the group's collective and individual responses, and maintains audience engagement.

theory_units.title: Insert Shot for Detail Emphasis
theory_units.summary: An insert shot is spliced into a master shot to show a specific part of the scene in greater detail, thereby emphasizing it.
theory_units.applies_when: Needing to highlight a specific detail within a master shot that requires closer audience attention.
theory_units.expected_effect: Draws audience attention to a particular element, provides visual clarity, and can stress importance.

theory_units.title: Cutaway Shot for Off-Master Coverage
theory_units.summary: A cutaway shot is inserted into a master shot to show something or somebody not covered by the master camera position, expanding the scene's visual information.
theory_units.applies_when: Needing to show an element (person, object, environment) that is relevant to the scene but outside the current master shot's frame.
theory_units.expected_effect: Expands the scene's visual context, can show reactions or related objects, and provides visual variety.

theory_units.title: Insert for Dialogue Clarification
theory_units.summary: Use a close insert shot, often on the same visual axis as the master, to visually clarify a point made in dialogue (e.g., pointing to a map).
theory_units.applies_when: A character refers to or points at something visually important that needs emphasis and clear understanding during dialogue.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhances audience understanding, stresses the importance of the visual detail, and makes the story clearer.

theory_units.title: Reverse Angle Insert for Procedural Clarity
theory_units.summary: Use a close insert shot from a reverse camera position to provide a clearer or more effective view of a specific action or exchange within a scene.
theory_units.applies_when: An action (e.g., handing an object, a specific gesture) is critical but not clearly visible or impactful from the master shot's perspective.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhances visual clarity and impact of a specific moment or procedure, guiding audience attention.

theory_units.title: Insert for Detailed Emotional Reaction
theory_units.summary: Use an insert shot to show, in detail, an emotional reaction as portrayed on the face of a performer.
theory_units.applies_when: A character's emotional reaction is key to the scene's meaning and requires close-up emphasis.
theory_units.expected_effect: Amplifies emotional impact, reveals subtle nuances of performance, and deepens character understanding.

theory_units.title: Multiple Inserts for Repeated Reactions
theory_units.summary: Utilize multiple close-up inserts of the same performer, replacing their reactions seen in a master shot, to highlight specific silent responses at different points in a dialogue.
theory_units.applies_when: A single performer has multiple significant, silent reactions during a dialogue covered by a master shot.
theory_units.expected_effect: Emphasizes key moments of reaction, breaks up the master shot, and adds emotional depth to the scene.

theory_units.title: Alternating Performer Inserts
theory_units.summary: When using multiple inserts within a master shot for reactions, alternate between different performers to highlight their individual responses to dialogue.
theory_units.applies_when: Multiple performers have significant reactions during a dialogue and individual emphasis on each is desired.
theory_units.expected_effect: Distributes audience focus, emphasizes the interplay and reactions between characters, and maintains visual interest.

theory_units.title: Sequence-Capping Insert
theory_units.summary: Use an insert shot at the end of a master shot or sequence to provide a specific detail or emotional reaction as a concluding note.
theory_units.applies_when: A particular detail or reaction offers a strong, poignant, or informative concluding statement for a sequence.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides a powerful final image, reinforces a theme or character emotion, and offers a sense of closure.

theory_units.title: Insert as Bridge Between Master Shots
theory_units.summary: Use an insert shot as a 'hinge' to smoothly transition between two different master shots, especially when changing camera angle or framing significantly.
theory_units.applies_when: Needing to change the master shot setup or camera position within a scene without a jarring cut.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides a smooth transition between different spatial or compositional perspectives, masks significant camera setup changes, and can emphasize a detail before the transition.

theory_units.title: Standard Static Dialogue Coverage (Historical Method)
theory_units.summary: A comprehensive shooting method for static dialogue involves first a full master shot, then groups repeating the scene, and finally close-ups of every player, all covering the entire event, to maximize editing flexibility.
theory_units.applies_when: Aiming for maximum editing flexibility to select camera angles, facilitate dialogue deletions, and bridge gaps with numerous cover shots.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides extensive footage for post-production, high flexibility for editing choices, and robustness against script changes or technical errors.
theory_units.caution: This method is 'perhaps not the most economical'.

theory_units.title: Prioritizing Performance in Psychological Dialogue
theory_units.summary: In psychological scenes heavily reliant on dialogue, the truthfulness and quality of performance and staging must take precedence over elaborate shot arrangements.
theory_units.applies_when: Directing scenes where the emotional and psychological depth of character interaction is paramount.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures authentic character portrayal and emotional impact, avoids distracting shot choices, and focuses audience on the core drama.

theory_units.title: Covering Specific Visual Details with Inserts (Pre-emptive)
theory_units.summary: A wise director preemptively shoots specific, visually important 'bits of business' (e.g., facial reactions, hand movements, detailed mechanisms) as inserts to ensure adequate coverage for the editor, even if not all are used in the final edit.
theory_units.applies_when: Any scene containing small, visually significant actions or details that might need emphasis later in editing.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides the editor with robust options to emphasize key visual information, allows for later directorial decision-making, and mitigates the risk of missed opportunities.
theory_units.caution: It is not necessary for the film editor to use all or even any of these inserts in the final version.

theory_units.title: Insert for Technical Error Correction
theory_units.summary: Insert shots can be used to repair technical errors (e.g., fogged film, light obstructions) unwittingly committed in a main shot, potentially saving costly or impossible reshoots.
theory_units.applies_when: A technical flaw is discovered in a master shot or key take during post-production that is too costly or impossible to reshoot.
theory_units.expected_effect: Rectifies visual errors, saves production costs and time, and maintains visual continuity.

theory_units.title: Cutaway to Off-Screen Reference
theory_units.summary: When characters in dialogue refer to something important off-screen (e.g., a building, person, or vehicle), insert a cutaway shot of that subject.
theory_units.applies_when: Dialogue references a significant object, person, or location that is relevant but not currently visible within the master shot.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides visual context for the dialogue, immerses the audience in the scene's world, and clarifies narrative points.
theory_units.caution: Use only 'if the subject involved is really important'.

theory_units.title: Multiple Thematic Cutaways
theory_units.summary: Insert multiple distinct cutaway shots into a master shot to visually represent different points of interest that characters refer to or discuss during their dialogue.
theory_units.applies_when: Dialogue covers multiple distinct off-screen subjects that all require visual representation for clarity or emphasis.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enriches the visual storytelling, provides context for different dialogue points, and breaks visual monotony of the master shot.

theory_units.title: Progressive Cutaways for Same Subject Detail
theory_units.summary: When characters repeatedly refer to the same off-screen subject, use multiple cutaways of that subject, progressing from wider to closer shots on the same visual axis, to progressively emphasize detail.
theory_units.applies_when: A single off-screen subject is referenced multiple times, and its detail, significance, or impact needs to be progressively emphasized.
theory_units.expected_effect: Builds visual focus and intensity on a single subject, guiding audience attention and enhancing its significance.

theory_units.title: Multi-Stage Progressive Zoom (Inserts/Cutaways)
theory_units.summary: Within a master shot, use a sequence of inserts or cutaways of the same subject, progressively zooming in from full shot to medium, close, and then close-up, to build visual intensity and focus.
theory_units.applies_when: A director wants to build visual intensity, suspense, or focus on a single subject (on- or off-screen) within a static scene, often towards a climax.
theory_units.expected_effect: Intensifies audience focus, creates a sense of approaching revelation or climax, and heightens emotional or dramatic impact.

theory_units.title: Progressive Intercutting for Building Tension (Threat & Reaction)
theory_units.summary: Build tension by intercutting a master shot of an unfolding threat (e.g., birds gathering) with progressively closer insert shots of a character's (often unaware) reaction, leading to a climax.
theory_units.applies_when: Directing a scene where an external threat is slowly escalating, and a character's impending realization or mounting terror needs to be emphasized.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates palpable suspense, guides the audience's emotional journey, and highlights the character's eventual realization or heightened state.
theory_units.caution: Ensure the progressive shots of the character maintain the same visual axis for consistency.

theory_units.title: Dynamic Cutaways for Group Reaction to Speech
theory_units.summary: For long speeches to a group, intersperse both static (full shots of the group) and dynamic (panning across faces) cutaways of the listening audience within the master shot of the speaker.
theory_units.applies_when: A single character delivers a lengthy speech to a group, and varied visual emphasis on the group's reactions and composition is desired.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains audience engagement by breaking monotony, highlights individual and collective reactions within the group, and adds visual dynamism.

theory_units.title: Cutaway as Flashback/Recollection (Narrative Trigger)
theory_units.summary: Use a cutaway shot to evoke a past event or memory, often triggered by the current scene's dialogue or subject, allowing two different times to coexist briefly on screen.
theory_units.applies_when: A character's past experiences or a piece of backstory is directly relevant to the current dialogue/scene and needs visual representation.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides context, deepens characterization, adds layers to the narrative, and allows for non-linear storytelling.
theory_units.caution: Audience acceptance depends on the cutaway being motivated by the performer’s train of thought or explicit dialogue.

theory_units.title: Sudden, Brief Flashback Intrusions (Psychological)
theory_units.summary: Employ quick, unexpected cutaways to past events that momentarily and jarringly intrude upon the present, often without an explicit verbal trigger.
theory_units.applies_when: Depicting a character's subconscious memories, psychological states, or the jarring, intrusive impact of the past on the present.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a sense of psychological depth, disorientation, or sudden emotional resonance, adding abstract layers to the narrative.

theory_units.title: Delayed Revelation through Shock Insert
theory_units.summary: Introduce a brief, unexpected close-up image without immediate explanation to create a sense of shock and mystery, which is resolved later in the narrative.
theory_units.applies_when: To create an immediate jarring effect and introduce an unexplained element that will gain meaning later.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience shock, confusion, and curiosity, leading to a deeper understanding when the context is eventually revealed.
theory_units.caution: May initially confuse the audience; its effectiveness relies on later contextualization.

theory_units.title: Insert/Cutaway Duration for Emphasized Motion
theory_units.summary: When an insert or cutaway frames an emphasized motion, its duration should match the beginning and end of that specific movement.
theory_units.applies_when: Framing a specific, emphasized movement within an insert or cutaway.
theory_units.expected_effect: A natural and precise rhythm, clearly highlighting the movement without feeling rushed or prolonged.

theory_units.title: Insert/Cutaway Duration for Static Subjects
theory_units.summary: For static objects or neutral expressions in an insert or cutaway, a very brief duration (around two seconds) is usually sufficient.
theory_units.applies_when: Framing a static object or a person with a neutral expression in an insert or cutaway.
theory_units.expected_effect: Prevents the shot from feeling over-long or stagnant, maintaining scene momentum.
theory_units.caution: Holding too long can make the shot seem tedious or draw unwanted attention.

theory_units.title: Insert/Cutaway Duration for Passive Listening/Reaction
theory_units.summary: When a silent character is passively listening to dialogue or music in a close shot, the image can be held for up to ten seconds without seeming over-long.
theory_units.applies_when: Showing a character's passive reaction or listening intently to sound (dialogue, music) in a close-up.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows the audience to register the character's internal state and emotional response to the sound, enhancing empathy or understanding.

theory_units.title: Dynamic Dialogue Pacing via Number Contrast
theory_units.summary: Varying the number of actors visible on screen from shot to shot masks the visual repetition of dialogue scenes, adding visual interest and building dramatic peaks.
theory_units.applies_when: Covering long dialogues to prevent visual monotony and create dynamic pacing, especially when building to a peak moment.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increased visual engagement, breaking the monotony of static dialogue, and reinforcing dramatic arcs within the conversation.

theory_units.title: Dramatic Introduction/Conclusion with Varying Subject Ranges
theory_units.summary: Using extreme differences in subject distance (e.g., full shot for establishing, close shots for reverse angles) provides a dramatic introduction and conclusion to a sequence.
theory_units.applies_when: Beginning or ending a sequence, particularly those using the triangle principle for reverse shots, to create a strong visual impact.
theory_units.expected_effect: Heightened dramatic tension and visual dynamism at key points in a scene.

theory_units.title: Parallel Editing for Flexible Scene Coverage
theory_units.summary: This technique covers a scene by dividing it into segments, each receiving a different visual treatment through pairs of camera positions edited in parallel, offering an alternative to a single master take.
theory_units.applies_when: When a scene requires varied visual emphasis across its parts, or when multiple perspectives on dialogue are desired. It emphasizes director's pre-planning.
theory_units.expected_effect: A dynamic and visually rich scene coverage that can highlight specific elements or shifts in interaction.
theory_units.caution: Requires careful pre-planning of camera positions and editing patterns by the director, limiting the editor's creative role to screen time control.

theory_units.title: Strategic Use of Inserts/Cutaways for Emphasis
theory_units.summary: Employ inserts and cutaways sparingly, only for specific effect, to stress an object, a spoken line, or a facial expression within the existing editing patterns of a sequence.
theory_units.applies_when: To draw specific attention to a crucial detail, reaction, or dialogue point within a larger editing scheme.
theory_units.expected_effect: Pinpointed focus on important elements, adding layers of meaning or intensifying a moment.
theory_units.caution: Overuse can dilute their impact or disrupt the flow of the main action.

theory_units.title: Dynamic Dialogue Presentation with Contrasting Shot Distances
theory_units.summary: To give a brisk dialogue a 'flashy presentation,' edit reverse shots by contrasting distances, potentially reversing the pattern halfway through the sequence (e.g., alternating close shots and close-ups).
theory_units.applies_when: For brisk, energetic dialogues that require a dynamic and engaging visual rhythm.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a lively and visually engaging presentation that matches the tempo of the dialogue.

theory_units.title: Emphasizing a Player in Long Static Dialogue by Moving Closer
theory_units.summary: For long two-player static dialogues, begin with medium shots, then halfway through, move to a closer position on the visual axis of one of the master takes to emphasize that player.
theory_units.applies_when: When covering a long, static two-person dialogue and a director wishes to bring focus or emphasis to one of the participants during the latter half.
theory_units.expected_effect: Draws audience attention to the emphasized player, suggesting a shift in importance or increasing intensity of their contribution.

theory_units.title: Crossing the Line of Interest via a Diversion
theory_units.summary: To break monotony in a long dialogue, temporarily shift the line of interest by introducing an off-screen diversion, allowing the main characters to naturally reposition on the other side of the original line.
theory_units.applies_when: When a long dialogue risks becoming monotonous due to static camera positions on one side of the line, and a fresh visual perspective is desired without jarring the audience.
theory_units.expected_effect: Refreshes the visual presentation of a dialogue, allowing for a new range of camera angles while the 'line crossing' goes unnoticed by the audience due to the diversion.
theory_units.caution: The diversion must be motivated and integrated smoothly to avoid feeling arbitrary or confusing.

theory_units.title: Visual Pauses for Dialogue Pacing
theory_units.summary: Replace bridging phrases in long dialogues with relevant visual pauses to isolate and emphasize only the peak moments of the conversation, preventing wordiness and maintaining visual interest.
theory_units.applies_when: When a dialogue is lengthy and contains 'unimportant' bridging information that would dilute the impact of key points, or to prevent visual monotony.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a clearer, sharper development of the story by presenting only essential dialogue, allowing peak moments to 'sink home' without distraction. Maintains visual engagement.
theory_units.caution: Visual pauses must be relevant to the scene and either pre-established or verbally announced to avoid being distracting digressions.

theory_units.title: Cinematic Time Compression for Dialogue
theory_units.summary: Compress the time span of dialogued sequences, especially the central part, by selecting and editing together only key fragments that convey complete ideas, using simple cuts.
theory_units.applies_when: When lengthy dialogue is necessary but risks slowing down the film's rhythm or becoming too wordy, and conciseness with impact is desired.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increases conciseness and impact, eliminates hesitations and repetitions, and maintains audience attention by focusing solely on important sectors of the scene.
theory_units.caution: Should avoid changing background or location within the compressed segment to maintain continuity; focus is solely on time compression.

theory_units.title: Time Compression with Changing Body Positions
theory_units.summary: Achieve time compression by presenting players in different body positions and parts of the location across edited fragments, while maintaining the same background.
theory_units.applies_when: As a variation of time compression, to add visual dynamism to the compressed sequence and implicitly suggest passage of time or changing states of mind.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhances the dynamism of the compressed scene, making it feel less static despite potentially omitting other characters' reactions or dialogues.
theory_units.caution: Ensure the changes in body position feel natural within the context of the compressed action.

theory_units.title: Staccato Rhythm with Time Compressed Dialogue
theory_units.summary: Apply time compression to create a staccato rhythm by using very brief shots (e.g., two phrases: question-answer) that change actors' sites, body positions, and framing, joined by direct cuts.
theory_units.applies_when: When a very brisk, impactful, and almost aggressive dialogue pace is desired, emphasizing the exchange of information.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a rapid, punchy, and attention-grabbing rhythm, making the dialogue feel urgent and direct.
theory_units.caution: Can become monotonous if a pause is not occasionally introduced to break the staccato rhythm.

theory_units.title: Time Compression with Alternating Speakers/Sources
theory_units.summary: Compress time by periodically replacing one player with another (e.g., alternating between two suspects during an interrogation) to provide non-repetitive information or showcase multiple perspectives.
theory_units.applies_when: When presenting similar information from multiple sources, or to combine distinct but thematically linked sequences (like multiple interrogations or performances) for conciseness and clarity.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhances clarity and impact by delivering only new, differing information, avoiding redundancy. Creates a dynamic, fragmented presentation of a continuous theme.

theory_units.title: Time Compression with Successive Close-ups and Wipes
theory_units.summary: Achieve time compression and deliver social commentary by presenting a series of swift wipes across the screen, transitioning between close-up shots of different individuals who speak directly to the camera, omitting reactions.
theory_units.applies_when: To efficiently convey a repetitive sequence of actions or responses from multiple characters, especially for a pointed social comment, while skipping intermediary reactions.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a blunt and impactful statement, quickly conveying a common experience or systemic issue by showing a rapid succession of similar interactions.
theory_units.caution: The direct address to camera and lack of reaction shots are very specific choices that should align with the desired commentary.

theory_units.title: Time Compression with Narrator Voiceover
theory_units.summary: Use a narrator's voice to verbally express the mood and bridge the visual gaps of a scene, contracting its visual parts to only peak moments, while characters gesticulate silently, occasionally interjecting with dialogue.
theory_units.applies_when: To condense a lengthy meeting or interaction into its essential emotional and informational peaks, relying on a narrator to convey the underlying mood and details.
theory_units.expected_effect: Efficiently conveys the essence of a prolonged event, allowing the narrator to provide context or internal thoughts, while showing only the most impactful visual fragments.
theory_units.caution: Requires careful balance between narration and character dialogue to maintain engagement.

theory_units.title: Speeding Dialogue Tempo for Large Screen Projection
theory_units.summary: To counteract the perceived slowdown of dialogue on a large screen, speed up the tempo of informative dialogue scenes by approximately one-third of the normal pace.
theory_units.applies_when: For static, informative dialogue scenes that will be projected on a large screen, where maintaining a brisk pace is crucial.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains a natural and engaging dialogue pace for a large audience, preventing the scene from feeling slow or dragged.
theory_units.caution: This method should NOT be used when the goal is to convey a specific mood or emotion; it is only suitable for informative dialogue. Actors should be instructed to speak quietly to sound natural.

theory_units.title: Segmented Coverage for Continuous Movement
theory_units.summary: Record a continuous movement using segments of the action shot from different angles, all from the same side of the subject's path, to create a more lively and interesting visual.
theory_units.applies_when: Covering a continuous movement or action sequence to add visual dynamism and maintain audience engagement.
theory_units.expected_effect: A more dynamic and engaging portrayal of movement than a single continuous take, while maintaining spatial continuity.
theory_units.caution: Crucially, all cameras must remain on the same side of the subject's line of movement to avoid jarring shifts in screen direction.

theory_units.title: Creating Implied Movement for Static Subjects
theory_units.summary: A sensation of movement can be achieved cinematically even with a static subject by using a projected moving background, or by cutting from a close shot of a character looking off-screen to a view from a moving vehicle.
theory_units.applies_when: When filming a static subject (e.g., inside a car/train) but needing to convey that they are in motion, or to create a transition that implies movement for a static character.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a convincing illusion of movement for the audience, enhancing immersion or facilitating scene transitions.
theory_units.caution: The illusion is reinforced if the actor subtly moves their head or body appropriately.

theory_units.title: Maintaining Screen Direction for Movement (180-Degree Rule)
theory_units.summary: To ensure continuous movement across cuts, all camera positions must remain on one side of the subject's line of movement; crossing this line will reverse screen direction and confuse the audience.
theory_units.applies_when: When filming any continuous movement, particularly across multiple cuts, to maintain clear spatial orientation for the audience.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures smooth intercutting of shots and consistent perceived direction of movement, preventing audience confusion.
theory_units.caution: Placing a camera on the opposite side of the line of movement will cause the subject to appear to move in the opposite direction, creating a disorienting jump.

theory_units.title: Framing Segmented Movement
theory_units.summary: When breaking down continuous movement into segments, frame the subject either by keeping them in the same sector of the screen, or by having them enter and leave the view, often covering half-screen areas.
theory_units.applies_when: When designing shots for a segmented continuous movement, to decide how the subject will appear within each frame.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides options for visual dynamism and continuity within segmented action, guiding audience attention and maintaining spatial awareness.

theory_units.title: Audience Orientation for Directional Changes
theory_units.summary: To prevent audience confusion, any change in a performer's screen direction must be explicitly shown through carefully constructed shot sequences.
theory_units.applies_when: Whenever a performer's movement changes direction, especially across the screen, to maintain clear spatial orientation for the audience.
theory_units.expected_effect: Prevents audience disorientation and confusion regarding character movement and spatial relationships.
theory_units.caution: Failing to show changes in direction leads to unnatural or confusing jumps in perceived movement.

theory_units.title: Crossing the Line of Motion
theory_units.summary: Breaking the 180-degree rule (crossing the line of motion) is possible and often desirable for dynamic compositions, achievable through specific techniques like cut-aways, neutral directions, performer indication, or contrasting motions.
theory_units.applies_when: When a director wishes to place the camera on the opposite side of a moving subject's line of motion to achieve a more dynamic composition or better view.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enables greater compositional flexibility without disorienting the audience, maintaining a sense of continuous action or space.
theory_units.caution: Simply cutting across the line of motion without a masking technique will confuse the audience about spatial relationships.

theory_units.title: Crossing Line with Cut-aways
theory_units.summary: Inserting cut-aways (shots of unrelated but relevant elements) between shots of a moving subject can make the audience 'forget' the previous screen direction, allowing for a new direction without seeming unnatural.
theory_units.applies_when: When needing to cross the line of motion for a moving subject, especially in sequences where the specific direction of the subject isn't crucial for a brief moment.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience accepts a change in screen direction for the main subject without conscious awareness of the camera crossing the line, due to diverted attention.
theory_units.caution: The audience's visual memory is short (1-2 shots), making this effective for brief directional 'resets'.

theory_units.title: Crossing Line with Neutral Direction Shots
theory_units.summary: Interposing shots where movement is directly towards or away from the camera (neutral direction) effectively 'resets' the audience's sense of lateral screen direction, allowing for a subsequent change.
theory_units.applies_when: When needing to cross the line of motion for a moving subject and transition smoothly to a new lateral screen direction.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience maintains a continuous sense of the subject's forward/backward movement, even when the lateral screen direction changes after the neutral shot.

theory_units.title: Crossing Line via Performer Indication
theory_units.summary: A performer's turn of head or body can motivate and link contradictory screen movements from different camera positions, preserving the audience's sense of continuous direction for a moving subject (e.g., a boat moving forward).
theory_units.applies_when: When showing a moving subject from opposing camera angles (e.g., tracking shots from opposite sides) and needing to maintain a clear sense of its continuous movement.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience perceives continuous motion and direction for the subject despite contradictory screen movements, as motivated by the performer's focus.
theory_units.caution: Careful blocking of the performer's background can allow studio shots to simulate moving vehicle contexts.

theory_units.title: Crossing Line by Player Exit/Entry Mask
theory_units.summary: A player exiting one side of the frame in the foreground of the first shot and entering from the opposite side in the next shot can unobtrusively mask a camera crossing the line of motion.
theory_units.applies_when: When needing to cross the line of motion without the audience consciously noticing, using foreground action as a mask.
theory_units.expected_effect: A smooth, unnoticed transition across the line of motion; audience accepts the new screen direction.

theory_units.title: Crossing Line by Player Walk & Camera Pan Mask
theory_units.summary: A player's contrasting walk combined with an accompanying camera pan can divert audience attention, allowing the main subject in the background to be shown moving in a reversed screen direction after crossing the line.
theory_units.applies_when: When needing to cross the line of motion for a main subject in the background, using a foreground player's movement and camera pan as a masking distraction.
theory_units.expected_effect: A smooth, unconscious transition across the line of motion; audience accepts the new screen direction for the background subject.

theory_units.title: Crossing Line by Player's Vertical Motion Mask
theory_units.summary: A foreground player's vertical movement (e.g., kneeling, rising) can effectively mask a cut across the line of motion, allowing subjects to reverse screen positions unobtrusively.
theory_units.applies_when: When needing to cross the line of motion and show subjects in reversed screen positions without a jarring cut.
theory_units.expected_effect: A smooth, unconscious transition across the line of motion; the camera 'flips' without audience awareness.

theory_units.title: Parallel Contrasting Movements for Conflict
theory_units.summary: Alternating external reverse shots of two subjects (or groups) moving in opposed screen directions (e.g., one left-to-right, one right-to-left) can depict conflict or convergence without confusing the audience.
theory_units.applies_when: When depicting two opposing forces or individuals moving towards each other, or in parallel but opposed directions.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a strong sense of impending confrontation or meeting; maintains individual screen direction clarity for each subject.
theory_units.caution: The screen position of both performers should remain consistent across cuts (e.g., character A always on the left, character B always on the right).

theory_units.title: Crossing Line via Static Onlooker POV
theory_units.summary: A static onlooker's head turn, or their implied subjective viewpoint, can naturally motivate a change in the main subject's screen direction, allowing the camera to cross the line of action.
theory_units.applies_when: When a moving subject needs to change its screen direction and a stationary character can serve as a natural point of transition/motivation.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience accepts the change in the moving subject's screen direction as a natural shift in viewpoint or focus, maintaining clarity.
theory_units.caution: Can be one person or a group, as long as their attention (head/eye turn) is consistent.

theory_units.title: Maintaining Direction with Static Anchor & Contrasting Motion (Same Half-Screen)
theory_units.summary: A static foreground element (person or object) positioned in one half of the screen can anchor the audience's orientation, allowing a moving subject to change its screen direction within the other half of the screen without losing a sense of continuous movement.
theory_units.applies_when: When needing to show a subject moving in contrasting directions across cuts (e.g., right-to-center then center-to-right) while preserving a continuous sense of direction for the audience, often with a change in camera angle.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience maintains a continuous sense of the moving subject's direction despite opposing screen movements, due to the consistent static anchor.
theory_units.caution: The static and moving subjects must be positioned in the same screen area across both takes.

theory_units.title: Maintaining Direction with Static Anchor & Contrasting Motion (Pause)
theory_units.summary: When a continuous movement includes a pause, contrasting screen directions in the same half-screen, anchored by a static element, can be used around the pause to maintain a clear sense of the subject's overall direction.
theory_units.applies_when: For movements that include a pause, where maintaining a continuous sense of direction is crucial, even with opposing screen movements.
theory_units.expected_effect: The audience perceives the movement as continuous relative to the static anchor, despite the pause and opposing screen directions.
theory_units.caution: The principle relies on the moving subject's consistent relationship to the static anchor in the same screen sector.

theory_units.title: Maintaining Direction with Static Anchor & Contrasting Motion (Moving Camera)
theory_units.summary: The principle of maintaining audience orientation with contrasting movements in the same screen sector (via a static anchor) can be effectively applied even when one of the camera placements involves a moving camera (e.g., a tracking shot).
theory_units.applies_when: When incorporating tracking shots into a sequence where opposing movements occur, but a continuous sense of direction must be maintained for the subject.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience perceives continuous motion and direction for the subject, even with a moving camera and opposed screen movements in the same screen half.
theory_units.caution: The opposed movements must occur on the same side of the screen in both shots, relative to the anchor.

theory_units.title: Cut Continuity Elements
theory_units.summary: To ensure a smooth visual flow and prevent audience confusion, cuts between shots must match key elements like position, movement, and eyeline.
theory_units.applies_when: Anytime two strips of film recording segments of the same continuous movement are joined.
theory_units.expected_effect: Seamless and unconfused presentation of material, maintaining audience immersion and understanding of spatial and temporal relationships.

theory_units.title: Cutting on Movement for Smooth Transitions
theory_units.summary: Cutting during or immediately after a subject's movement (even subtle ones) distracts the audience from the visual 'jar' or change in volume that occurs when transitioning between shots, making the cut seamless.
theory_units.applies_when: Almost every cut between two shots, especially when there is a change in camera distance or placement relative to the subject.
theory_units.expected_effect: Eliminates visual jumps, making cuts unnoticed by the audience and maintaining narrative flow and immersion.
theory_units.caution: Cutting between two static shots where no movement occurs will result in a jerky, noticeable transition.

theory_units.title: Cutting After the Movement (Continuity)
theory_units.summary: An editing technique where the cut to a closer shot occurs a few frames *after* a subject's or camera's movement in the preceding shot has fully completed, often on the same visual axis.
theory_units.applies_when: When approaching on the same visual axis; when a player performs vertical or neutral (towards/away) motion; when the camera travels or pans and stops; when an unemphatic visual approach is desired; to fulfill the audience's unconscious desire for a closer look at a subject.
theory_units.expected_effect: Smooth transition, advances the view, draws audience attention to the subject, provides a closer look, unemphatic visual approach, avoids unpleasant jumps if image size change is great and subjects don't move substantially.
theory_units.caution: Movements across the screen are generally less ideal for this type of cut; seldom used for cutting back from close to full shot (primarily for forward cuts); more dynamic approaches are typically used for receding movements or movements across the screen.

theory_units.title: Cutting on the Movement (General Principle)
theory_units.summary: A technique for continuity cuts that involves joining fragments of a continuous action from separate shots to create vitality and smoothly change viewpoint.
theory_units.applies_when: When changing viewpoint smoothly around one or a group of characters; to create vitality peculiar to the film medium; when performing continuity cuts of a single action across multiple shots.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhanced vitality, smooth change of viewpoint, seamless transition between shots of a continuous action.
theory_units.caution: The 1/3-2/3 rule is a good starting point, not a strict rule; all rules can be broken if understood. Ensure matched speed of movement between shots during shooting. If movement speeds are ill-matched, it is generally more satisfactory for the movement to appear faster in the second fragment.

theory_units.title: Covering Turning Movement
theory_units.summary: Strategies for photographing and editing a character's turning motion to maintain continuity and provide appropriate coverage.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character performs a turning motion on the spot (e.g., 90°, 180°, or full circle).
theory_units.expected_effect: Smooth capture of the turning motion, maintaining consistent character screen positions (if desired), and providing appropriate visual information to the audience.
theory_units.caution: Internal reverse angles and parallel camera positions are unsuitable for shooting continuous turning motion due to divergent coverage. Full circle turns are generally the least interesting of the three options for an action cut.

theory_units.title: Dividing Turning Movement into Two Shots
theory_units.summary: Divide a single turning movement into two shots using reverse angle camera coverage, ensuring players maintain their relative screen areas.
theory_units.applies_when: When covering a single player's turning movement, aiming for a matched action cut while emphasizing the turn and maintaining spatial coherence.
theory_units.expected_effect: A smooth and continuous transition across a turning action, making the movement clear to the audience despite the cut.

theory_units.title: Maintaining Visual Axis and Screen Sector for Turns
theory_units.summary: When cutting between two shots of a turning movement, maintain the same visual axis and position the player in the same sector of the screen (center or one of the three side areas).
theory_units.applies_when: Editing together multiple shots of a character's turning motion to ensure spatial continuity and clarity.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhanced spatial continuity and audience orientation, making the turn feel seamless and understandable.
theory_units.caution: Failing to maintain consistency can lead to confusing or disorienting cuts.

theory_units.title: Expanding/Contracting Group with Matched Turn
theory_units.summary: Widen or narrow the group of players introduced in the second shot, using a dominant player's turning motion as a natural trigger to introduce or exclude other characters.
theory_units.applies_when: Introducing or removing characters from focus within a scene by linking their appearance/disappearance to a character's turning movement.
theory_units.expected_effect: Subtly directs audience attention to the dominant player while dynamically altering the group composition, emphasizing or de-emphasizing supporting characters.

theory_units.title: Right Angle Turn for Group Introduction/Exclusion
theory_units.summary: When a dominant player turns 90 degrees, cut to a right-angle camera site. Position the dominant player (center or side) to dictate how newly introduced performers occupy the remaining screen area.
theory_units.applies_when: Introducing new characters or shifting focus within a group during a character's 90-degree turn, often as part of a group widening/narrowing strategy.
theory_units.expected_effect: Subtly integrates new characters into the scene's composition, using the turning motion as a natural transition point, and controlling their prominence.

theory_units.title: Group Widening/Narrowing with Common Visual Axis Turn
theory_units.summary: Employ an advance on a common visual axis to widen or narrow a group during a dominant player's turning motion, using the turn as justification to introduce or exclude other players.
theory_units.applies_when: When using a turning motion to naturally expand or contract the visible group of characters for compositional or narrative reasons, maintaining a smooth visual flow.
theory_units.expected_effect: Seamlessly adjusts group size on screen, directing focus based on the turning character's action, while preserving spatial continuity.

theory_units.title: Using Reverse Angles for Group Composition Changes
theory_units.summary: Combine external and internal reverse angles around a turning player to widen or reduce the group presented on screen, thereby shifting visual emphasis to the central performer.
theory_units.applies_when: Adjusting the number of visible characters in a scene, particularly when a central performer is turning, to emphasize them or alter group dynamics.
theory_units.expected_effect: Changes the perceived size of a group, drawing focus to or away from the central turning character, making them visually dominant.

theory_units.title: Prioritizing Foreground Motion Match
theory_units.summary: In shots involving both foreground and background movement, the foreground motion is dominant and must be precisely matched across cuts to ensure continuity.
theory_units.applies_when: Editing shots with complex movements, especially when characters are on moving vehicles or against dynamic backgrounds.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures smooth and believable continuity for the primary action, preventing jarring cuts that distract from the main subject.
theory_units.caution: Failure to precisely match foreground motion can lead to confusing or jarring edits that break immersion.

theory_units.title: Opposed Direction Turn with External Reverse Angles
theory_units.summary: Cover a lone performer's 180-degree turn using a pair of external reverse angles at the extreme points of the arc, resulting in opposed senses of screen direction for the movement.
theory_units.applies_when: Emphasizing a full 180-degree turn of a lone performer, especially for sudden turns, while maintaining dynamic visual interest.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a dynamic visual effect of opposed motion that, despite the direction change, remains clear to the audience because the performer's action is understood (e.g., starts and concludes facing us).
theory_units.caution: While effective for clear turns, unclear framing or an ambiguous turn might confuse the audience.

theory_units.title: Two-Person Turn with External Reverse Angles
theory_units.summary: When two players turn simultaneously, using external reverse angle camera sites will cause them to switch screen positions between shots, applying the same principle as for a lone performer's opposed direction turn.
theory_units.applies_when: Covering a simultaneous turn of two characters, maintaining dynamism while clearly showing their individual turns and interactions.
theory_units.expected_effect: Dynamic screen movement as characters switch positions, maintaining clarity of their combined action despite opposed screen directions.

theory_units.title: Emphasizing Arc-Shaped Turns While Walking
theory_units.summary: To stress a change of direction when an actor turns as he walks (an arc-shaped movement), use a pair of reverse external sites or a right angle camera position.
theory_units.applies_when: Highlighting a significant or dramatic change in direction during a character's walking turn.
theory_units.expected_effect: Amplifies the visual impact of the turn, making the change of direction more pronounced and noticeable to the audience.

theory_units.title: Editing Opposed Direction 180-degree Turn
theory_units.summary: When covering a 180-degree turn with external reverse angles, use the first half of the turn from the first shot and the complementary second half from the second shot. In the first, the player moves from center to one side; in the second, from the opposite side to the center.
theory_units.applies_when: Executing a dynamic cut on a 180-degree turn, particularly a sudden one, using reverse angles.
theory_units.expected_effect: Seamlessly connects two shots of opposed movement, maintaining clarity of the overall turn because the performer's full movement is clear.
theory_units.caution: Ensure the cuts are precise at the midpoint of the turn for optimal smoothness and to avoid jarring discontinuity.

theory_units.title: Maintaining Screen Sector for Divided Turns
theory_units.summary: When dividing a turning movement into two shots, the performer must be located in the same screen sector in both shots (e.g., center, left third, right third) to maintain continuity.
theory_units.applies_when: Editing any turning movement that is split across two cuts, regardless of camera angle choice.
theory_units.expected_effect: A seamless and non-disorienting transition, as the audience can easily track the performer's consistent position on screen.
theory_units.caution: Failing to maintain the same screen sector can lead to disorienting jump cuts or confusing spatial relationships.

theory_units.title: Framing Rising Movement within Screen Boundaries
theory_units.summary: To keep a rising movement within the boundaries of the screen frame and manage emphasis, cut from a medium shot to a backward full shot (for context) or to a forward close shot (for intensity).
theory_units.applies_when: Covering a character's rising motion while ensuring they remain visibly within the frame and controlling the audience's focus.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains visual continuity of the rising action, either expanding the view to show context or intensifying focus on the character's reaction/effort.

theory_units.title: Rising Movement with Right Angle Camera
theory_units.summary: Cover a rising movement using a right angle camera position to distinctly register the upward motion of the player.
theory_units.applies_when: When desiring a dynamic or alternative perspective on a character's rising action, emphasizing the verticality of the movement.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides a clear visual of the vertical motion from a side perspective, adding dynamic variety and potentially revealing elements within the scene.

theory_units.title: Rising Movement with External/Internal Reverse Angles for Number Contrast
theory_units.summary: Use a combination of an external and an internal reverse angle to cover a rising motion, which provides 'number contrast' in the picture area.
theory_units.applies_when: When covering a rising motion and simultaneously wishing to alter the perceived number of characters or elements in the frame, or to create a dynamic visual shift.
theory_units.expected_effect: Dynamically shifts the composition around the rising performer, potentially altering visual emphasis or context through a perceived change in the number of visible elements.
theory_units.caution: The exact nature of 'number contrast' should be clearly defined by the director's intention for the scene.

theory_units.title: Sitting Movement with Common Visual Axis
theory_units.summary: When covering a sitting motion with camera sites on a common visual axis, keep the player in the same screen sector in both shots. Shot sizes can vary (e.g., full to medium or vice versa) to adjust emphasis.
theory_units.applies_when: Covering a character sitting down in a way that emphasizes smooth, continuous motion and spatial stability, without disorienting the audience.
theory_units.expected_effect: Seamless transition of the sitting action, maintaining character position on screen and avoiding disorientation while allowing for varied shot emphasis.

theory_units.title: Sitting Movement with External Reverse Angles for Opposed Arcs
theory_units.summary: Cover a lone performer sitting down using external reverse angles, which will register as two opposed arc movements on the screen. The opposed directions are obtained due to the player having a profiled body position in both shots.
theory_units.applies_when: Emphasizing the arc-shaped nature and physical effort of a character sitting down, or creating a more dynamic cut while maintaining clarity.
theory_units.expected_effect: Dynamic visual representation of the sitting movement through contrasting screen directions, while remaining clear due to the recognizable body action and profiled position.
theory_units.caution: Ensure the profiled body position is clear in both shots to avoid confusion despite the opposed screen directions.

theory_units.title: Opposed Screen Motion via Internal/External Reverse Angles
theory_units.summary: Cutting between internal and external reverse camera positions for a continuous movement can create a perceived opposition in screen direction and character orientation, even for a single moving player.
theory_units.applies_when: When a single character performs a continuous action (e.g., reclining) and the director wants to visually emphasize the transition, create a dynamic sense of opposed screen direction, or shift the audience's perspective on the character's orientation (e.g., front to back).
theory_units.expected_effect: The audience perceives a visually dynamic continuous movement with a strong sense of directional change and a shift in perspective on the character (e.g., from seeing their front to their back), enhancing engagement with the action.

theory_units.title: Dramatic Angle Shift with Reverse Sequence Opposed Motion
theory_units.summary: Reversing the internal/external sequence (cutting from an external rear view to an internal front view) for a continuous action can achieve contrasting movement directions and allow for the introduction of dramatic camera angles, such as a low angle to emphasize a fall.
theory_units.applies_when: When depicting a continuous action, particularly one with impact like a fall, and wanting to show contrasting movement directions while dramatically shifting the camera's perspective (e.g., to emphasize vulnerability or impact with a low angle).
theory_units.expected_effect: The audience perceives contrasting movement directions within the same screen sector, and the specific change in camera angle (e.g., a low angle) enhances the dramatic impact or highlights a particular detail of the action.

theory_units.title: Fragmenting Unified Two-Player Movement for Opposed Directions
theory_units.summary: When two players move together as a single unit, their continuous movement can be fragmented across two external reverse shots to create an effect of opposed screen directions for both characters, while maintaining their relative screen positions and screen areas.
theory_units.applies_when: When two characters are moving in unison (e.g., reclining simultaneously) and the director wants to dynamically complete their movement with visual directional contrast, without disrupting their unified action or spatial relationship on screen.
theory_units.expected_effect: The audience perceives a continuous, unified movement of both characters, but the transition between shots dynamically reverses their screen direction, adding visual interest while preserving their coherent spatial relationship.
theory_units.caution: Ensure characters maintain constant screen areas from shot to shot to preserve the sense of unity and continuity.

theory_units.title: Opposed Directions & Screen Area Exchange for Single Actor Movement
theory_units.summary: To create opposed senses of movement direction and an exchange of screen areas for a single performer's continuous motion, film the actor moving from side to center in a first shot (e.g., full shot, back to camera) and then from the opposite side to center in a reverse external shot (e.g., close shot, facing camera), ensuring the main actor remains centrally framed.
theory_units.applies_when: When a performer's continuous movement needs to be shown across two shots where perceived screen direction is reversed, and the performer's screen centrality is maintained, causing other background elements or partners to dynamically shift screen areas.
theory_units.expected_effect: The audience experiences a dynamic shift in screen direction and the positioning of background elements/partners, while the main performer remains consistently anchored in the center, making the continuous motion visually engaging and controlled.
theory_units.caution: It is crucial that the primary performer is consistently kept in the center of the screen; supporting elements or partners will naturally shift sides to accommodate the reverse.

theory_units.title: Basic Linear Movement Coverage (Away & Towards Camera)
theory_units.summary: Use external reverse camera coverage to film linear walking or running movement in neutral directions (away from, then towards the camera) to show a player's continuous trajectory. Crucially, all camera positions must be on the same side of the line of movement to ensure background continuity.
theory_units.applies_when: When filming a character walking or running in a generally straight line and needing to show both their departure and subsequent approach to a point, maintaining clear spatial continuity and orientation.
theory_units.expected_effect: A clear, spatially coherent, and continuous portrayal of linear movement, with a strong sense of consistent environment due to stable background elements.
theory_units.caution: Both camera positions must be on the same side of the line of movement. Any identifiable background object seen in the first shot must appear in the same screen sector in the second shot to avoid audience disorientation.

theory_units.title: Reversed Linear Movement Coverage (Towards & Away Camera)
theory_units.summary: A variant of basic linear movement coverage where the player first approaches the camera in a frontal shot and then moves away in a rear shot, without exiting the screen in either shot, maintaining a neutral spatial direction.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character's linear movement needs to be shown from an initial approaching perspective, followed by a receding perspective, with the intent to keep the character within the frame throughout their movement.
theory_units.expected_effect: The audience sees the full range of the character's linear movement, emphasizing both their approach and departure without losing them from the frame, maintaining a neutral and direct spatial journey.
theory_units.caution: Ensure the player does not exit the screen in either shot to maintain continuous presence.

theory_units.title: Two-Shot Discontinuous Walking Movement
theory_units.summary: To cover a walking movement that is intentionally interrupted (where a player approaches, stops, then goes away), use two distinct shots: one capturing the approach and stop, and a reverse shot for the departure towards a new goal.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character's linear movement includes a significant pause, a moment of contemplation, or an interaction before they continue their journey in a new direction or towards a different objective.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clearly communicates the pause in action, highlights the character's immediate focus (e.g., looking off-screen), and defines their subsequent commitment to a new direction, effectively breaking and re-establishing the continuous flow.

theory_units.title: Four-Shot Discontinuous Movement to Goal Strategy
theory_units.summary: To cover an extended, discontinuous movement where a player approaches an identifiable goal (another player), use a four-shot sequence involving alternating external reverse camera positions. This strategy segments the journey and arrival, maintaining actor screen sectors throughout.
theory_units.applies_when: When depicting a significant, extended, and discontinuous movement towards a specific person or object, where the progression of the journey, anticipation, and the final arrival/interaction are important to emphasize.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a detailed and progressive narrative of the character's movement, clearly defining stages of departure, anticipation, and final interaction with the goal, while maintaining strong spatial continuity.
theory_units.caution: Both actors must maintain constant screen sectors across all shots in the sequence to ensure smooth spatial continuity and avoid disorientation.

theory_units.title: High Angle Reverse Shots for Perceived Vertical Movement
theory_units.summary: Filming a neutral horizontal walking or running movement from two high camera positions set on reverse angles will make the player appear to ascend in one shot and descend in the other, while surrounding objects dynamically shift screen sides.
theory_units.applies_when: When a director wants to introduce a dynamic vertical illusion to an otherwise horizontal movement, or to emphasize the shifting environment and changes in perspective around the moving character.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a unique and engaging visual dynamic where horizontal movement gains a perceived vertical dimension (ascending/descending), making the scene more visually interesting and potentially surreal or disorienting, and highlights the changing environment.
theory_units.caution: The pronounced shifting of objects or persons around the performer from one side of the screen to the other might be disorienting or distracting if not intentionally integrated into the scene's narrative or mood.

theory_units.title: Altering Real Movement for Perceived Screen Continuity (Diagonal)
theory_units.summary: To maintain a consistent perceived oblique screen direction (e.g., side to center) across two reverse shots, the actor's actual physical direction of movement in the second shot can be deliberately altered or 'cheated' to match the screen direction established in the first shot.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character's diagonal movement is covered by reverse angles, and the natural physical reversal of the second camera position would cause a confusing or undesired change in perceived screen direction, thus requiring a subtle 'cheat' to maintain visual flow.
theory_units.expected_effect: The audience perceives a smooth, continuous diagonal movement across the cut, avoiding disorientation or jarring transitions despite a subtle alteration in the actor's physical path, thereby maintaining narrative immersion.
theory_units.caution: This technique involves deliberately changing the actor's real movement path in the second shot to maintain screen continuity. It requires careful blocking and clear communication with the performer to achieve the desired visual effect without looking unnatural.

theory_units.title: Common Visual Axis: Forward Cut for Approaching Movement
theory_units.summary: To cover a player moving away from the foreground towards a distant position, place two cameras on the same visual axis. Cut on action from a wider shot (covering most of the path) to a closer shot (forward on the same axis) to show the completion of the movement, maintaining the player's screen sector.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character is moving away from the camera, and the director wants to maintain a strong sense of direct visual continuity while also advancing the viewer closer to the subject's destination or final position without changing their apparent screen direction.
theory_units.expected_effect: A seamless, continuous movement that draws the audience further into the scene along the character's path, emphasizing the distance covered and the destination, creating a sense of progression and intimacy.
theory_units.caution: Careful execution is needed for the cut on action to be smooth and invisible. The player must move in the same screen sector in both shots (e.g., always from right to center) to maintain visual consistency.

theory_units.title: Common Visual Axis: Two Players Moving Away & Converging
theory_units.summary: Apply the common visual axis technique to two players moving away together by cutting from a wider shot (establishing the initial group or context) to a closer shot on the same axis.
