theory_units.summary: Rotating the camera 180 degrees on its vertical axis creates a startling effect and can make a subject appear to reverse direction on screen.
theory_units.applies_when: When desiring a startling or disorienting effect, or to visually reverse a subject's apparent direction within a continuous shot.
theory_units.expected_effect: A startling or disorienting visual effect; an illusion of the subject reversing its direction.
theory_units.caution: Ensure the rotation is precisely a 180-degree arc for the intended effect.

theory_units.title: Movement Quantity and Scene Mood
theory_units.summary: The quantity of movement within a scene can evoke specific emotional responses or suggest a particular mood in the audience.
theory_units.applies_when: When establishing or emphasizing the mood, energy, or tension of a scene.
theory_units.expected_effect: Large numbers of movements create feelings of energy, hurry, excitement, or violence; little to no movement suggests dullness, quietness, depression, solemnity, or extreme emotional tension depending on context.
theory_units.caution: The psychological effect of 'little or no movement' is highly dependent on the scene's context.

theory_units.title: Movement Timing and Dialogue Emphasis
theory_units.summary: The timing of a subject's movement relative to their dialogue determines whether the line spoken or the action performed is emphasized.
theory_units.applies_when: When a specific piece of dialogue or a particular action needs to be highlighted for the audience.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience attention is directed to either the spoken word or the physical action based on the timing.

theory_units.title: Smooth, Constant Speed Tracking
theory_units.summary: Aesthetically pleasing moving shots are achieved with smooth, bump-free camera tracking at a constant speed, with any speed changes being gradual.
theory_units.applies_when: Always, when aiming for high-quality, professional, and visually pleasing camera movement.
theory_units.expected_effect: A visually seamless and professional camera movement that avoids distracting the audience.
theory_units.caution: Avoid any sudden changes in camera speed.

theory_units.title: Enhancing Tracking with Foreground Objects
theory_units.summary: Placing static objects between the camera and subjects in long or full tracking shots enhances pictorial composition by providing planal contrasts and avoiding a flat appearance.
theory_units.applies_when: When tracking subjects framed in long shot or full shot, and seeking to improve pictorial composition and create a sense of depth.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhanced pictorial composition, increased sense of depth, and avoidance of a flat, two-dimensional appearance.

theory_units.title: Tracking Shots with Pauses
theory_units.summary: Incorporating momentary stops for both the camera and subjects during a tracking shot can add variety or break the monotony of continuous, repetitive movement.
theory_units.applies_when: When a continuous tracking shot might become monotonous, or to introduce visual interest and emphasize specific moments.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increased visual variety, broken monotony, and the potential to emphasize paused moments or subjects.

theory_units.title: Avoiding Obstacles During Tracking Pauses
theory_units.summary: During pauses in tracking shots, avoid stopping where obstructive foreground objects exist, as they will be strongly emphasized unless they carry special story significance.
theory_units.applies_when: When planning pauses within a tracking shot, especially where foreground elements are present.
theory_units.expected_effect: Prevents unintended emphasis on irrelevant or obstructive foreground objects, maintaining a clear visual focus on the subjects.
theory_units.caution: Obstructive foreground objects will be strongly emphasized if present during a pause, potentially distracting from the main subject.

theory_units.title: Continuous Tracking of a Diminishing Group
theory_units.summary: A continuous tracking shot can follow a group as individuals or sub-groups halt and progressively leave the frame, maintaining a constant camera direction.
theory_units.applies_when: When depicting a group that gradually diminishes as its members stop or peel off from the main movement or journey.
theory_units.expected_effect: Visually represents the gradual reduction of a group while maintaining a sense of continuous forward momentum and the progression of the journey.

theory_units.title: Guiding Interest with Complex Overlapping Action Tracking
theory_units.summary: Continuous tracking shots can integrate multiple overlapping character movements, often changing focus between individuals, to seamlessly lead the audience's interest towards the shot's culmination.
theory_units.applies_when: When presenting complex character interactions and movements within a single continuous shot, aiming to smoothly guide audience attention through the narrative.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains continuous audience engagement, clearly directs attention through a complex sequence, and creates a fluid visual narrative flow.
theory_units.caution: Requires careful integration and extensive rehearsal, akin to a ballet, for seamless and effective execution.

theory_units.title: Transitioning from Tracking to Static on a Stop
theory_units.summary: Cutting to a static camera position is an easier and often more effective way to transition from a tracking shot of moving subjects to a moment where they stop, compared to trying to slow down the tracking camera.
theory_units.applies_when: When subjects stop moving at the end of a tracking shot and a clean, easy transition is desired without complex camera deceleration.
theory_units.expected_effect: A smoother, more precise transition; avoids the synchronization challenges and potential jerkiness of slowing down a tracking camera.
theory_units.caution: If attempting to slow the tracking camera, framing at the end is critical and requires thorough rehearsals and a skilled camera crew for synchronization.

theory_units.title: Track Back to Static Full Shot Transition
theory_units.summary: When a performer walks towards the camera which tracks back, transition by cutting to a fixed full shot on the same visual axis with the performer centrally placed.
theory_units.applies_when: A performer stops after walking towards a back-tracking camera, and a continuous visual axis is desired for the transition.
theory_units.expected_effect: A seamless transition that maintains visual continuity and keeps the subject as a clear central focus.

theory_units.title: Fast Tracking to Static with Subject Exiting Frame
theory_units.summary: For fast-moving subjects (e.g., running towards a back-tracking camera), it is easier to cut to a static shot if the subject moves out of frame at the end of the tracking shot, then re-enters/halts in the static shot.
theory_units.applies_when: Transitioning from a fast-tracking shot of a subject to a static shot where the subject comes to a halt.
theory_units.expected_effect: A smoother and less abrupt transition for fast movements, avoiding awkward in-frame stops or deceleration.

theory_units.title: Showing Subject Direction Change in Static Shot
theory_units.summary: If a player, tracked by the camera, is to change direction, it is generally better to show this change of direction in the second, static shot after a cut.
theory_units.applies_when: A subject changes direction after being tracked, and a clean, impactful transition is needed.
theory_units.expected_effect: A clearer, more impactful representation of the direction change, contributing to smoother visual flow and narrative understanding.

theory_units.title: Parallel Tracking to Static Full Shot Transition
theory_units.summary: From a parallel tracking shot of a player, cut to a static full shot where the player enters from the side opposite their previous direction of movement and stops centrally.
theory_units.applies_when: Transitioning from a parallel tracking shot (e.g., profile or three-quarters view) to a static shot where the subject halts.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a clean and clear transition, establishing a new, central focus for the audience.

theory_units.title: Panning Shot to Slow Down with Performer
theory_units.summary: A panning shot can be effectively used as the second shot in a transition to slow down with a performer as they stop walking or running, particularly if the initial movement was too rapid for an abrupt static cut.
theory_units.applies_when: A performer stops after being tracked, and a static cut would be too abrupt given their prior speed.
theory_units.expected_effect: A smoother and more natural deceleration and transition as the action comes to a halt.
theory_units.caution: The figure size in both shots and consistent position on the screen area are critical for the success of this transition.

theory_units.title: Static Right-Angle Shot for Running Subject
theory_units.summary: For a running person, use a static right-angle camera position as the second shot: track with them, slightly pan to create space, then cut to the static shot where they run away from the camera to the picture center, maintaining screen position.
theory_units.applies_when: Covering a running person with a transition to a static shot, while aiming to maintain their screen-side position and change camera perspective.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains visual continuity of the subject's screen position while providing a different camera angle and perspective.

theory_units.title: Reverse Angle for Group Halting
theory_units.summary: For a group halting after being tracked, cut to a reverse medium shot (static camera) where the players enter moving in the opposite direction and then stop, creating a dynamic visual conclusion.
theory_units.applies_when: A group of subjects comes to a halt after being tracked, and a dynamic and impactful visual conclusion is desired for their movement.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a very dynamic and impactful conclusion to the group's walking or running movement.
theory_units.caution: The fixed camera position is placed on the other side of the line of action to achieve this effect.

theory_units.title: Flexible Intermittent Tracking
theory_units.summary: During tracking shots, the camera can travel continuously, intermittently, or reverse its direction of movement at any point to precisely accommodate subject action.
theory_units.applies_when: When subject movement involves stops, starts, or changes in direction that the camera needs to follow dynamically and precisely.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows camera movement to accurately match and emphasize complex, non-linear subject action or journey.

theory_units.title: Tracking with Multiple Stops, Starts, and Reversals
theory_units.summary: A camera can track sideways, stop when subjects halt, resume tracking, reverse direction when subjects reverse, and stop again, accommodating various intermittent actions and obstacles.
theory_units.applies_when: Following subjects through complex scenarios with intermittent movement, stops, starts, and changes in direction, potentially navigating obstacles.
theory_units.expected_effect: A realistic and continuous portrayal of arduous journeys or complex character movements, maintaining the viewer's perspective on the subjects.

theory_units.title: Intermittent Camera and Player Movement
theory_units.summary: A complex shot can combine static framing, tracking, and stopping camera movements to follow intermittent player actions and shifts in focus among multiple characters.
theory_units.applies_when: Covering a sequence with multiple character movements, stops, and shifts of focus, requiring a flexible camera to follow the evolving narrative.
theory_units.expected_effect: Dynamic visual storytelling, smoothly shifting audience attention between characters and actions within a fluid sequence.

theory_units.title: Apparent Direction Reversal via Half-Circle Pan
theory_units.summary: The camera can reverse its apparent direction of travel on screen by panning through a half circle to the other side of the track, even if the dolly itself continues moving in one physical direction.
theory_units.applies_when: When needing to reverse the apparent direction of movement within a continuous tracking shot without physically reversing the dolly's direction.
theory_units.expected_effect: A seamless and easily accepted reversal of apparent direction by the audience, who can accommodate the contrasting directions without difficulty.

theory_units.title: Continuous Tracking with Multiple Direction Reversals
theory_units.summary: A continuous tracking shot can periodically reverse its sense of direction by using half-circle pans at the ends of the track, incorporating static obstacles for visual variety.
theory_units.applies_when: Covering complex, reversing subject movement over an extended track, requiring continuous camera follow and sustained visual interest.
theory_units.expected_effect: A dynamic and engaging continuous shot; audience interest is maintained through varied perspective and composition elements.

theory_units.title: Winding Paths for Tracked Actors
theory_units.summary: An actor in a tracking shot does not need to be confined to a straight line; they can follow winding paths, dynamically approaching or moving away from the camera.
theory_units.applies_when: Designing actor movement within a tracking shot to add dynamism, emphasize their journey, or create a more naturalistic feel.
theory_units.expected_effect: More dynamic and natural-looking actor movement, adding visual complexity and depth to the shot.

theory_units.title: Sinuous Actor Path with Straight Camera
theory_units.summary: To convey an actor's struggle or the difficulty of their path when the camera tracks in a straight line, utilize static foreground elements and have the actor interact with their environment.
theory_units.applies_when: When an actor needs to appear to struggle through a difficult medium (e.g., crowd, forest) while the camera maintains a straight track.
theory_units.expected_effect: Illusion of depth, planal contrast, heightened realism of the actor's struggle, and a sense of being 'engulfed' by the environment.

theory_units.title: Straight Track-In with Pan to Central Figure
theory_units.summary: Advance the camera on a straight line into a static group arranged in a semi-circle, using pans to survey the group before settling on a central figure.
theory_units.applies_when: To dramatically emphasize or introduce a central character within a static group, requiring strong dramatic motivation.
theory_units.expected_effect: Draws audience attention to the central figure, building dramatic tension or revealing importance.
theory_units.caution: Requires strong dramatic motivation; overuse without purpose can feel artificial.

theory_units.title: Intermittent Tracking for Variety
theory_units.summary: Cover a character's intermittent, winding path by tracking with them from zone to zone, varying shot sizes, and introducing foreground action to break monotony.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character moves intermittently between distinct zones within a scene, and continuous tracking might become repetitive.
theory_units.expected_effect: Breaks the back-and-forth motion, adding visual variety and dynamism to the screen presentation.

theory_units.title: Alternating Focus with Crossing Winding Paths
theory_units.summary: Utilize a continuously moving camera to cover the crossing, winding paths of two actors, alternating which actor is framed to create contrast.
theory_units.applies_when: When two actors are moving in winding paths and the director wants to dynamically shift focus between them.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates contrast in the number of figures on screen, dynamically shifts audience attention, and can reveal character relationships through proximity and exclusion.

theory_units.title: Mid-Track Pan for Viewpoint Change
theory_units.summary: Introduce a half-circle pan in the middle of a straight tracking shot to change the camera's relationship to the subject, such as from front to rear view or vice versa.
theory_units.applies_when: To subtly or dramatically shift the audience's perspective on a moving character or reveal their reaction/the environment behind them.
theory_units.expected_effect: Changes the framing of the subject from a front to a rear view (or vice versa), adding visual information or dramatic emphasis.
theory_units.caution: If changing from rear to front view, the camera must move faster than the characters during the pan; if changing from front to rear, the camera slows down.

theory_units.title: Camera Repeating Actor's Right Angle Turn
theory_units.summary: To cover an actor's abrupt right-angle turn, the camera tracks and replicates the actor's movement, maintaining a consistent relationship.
theory_units.applies_when: When an actor makes a sharp turn and the director wishes to maintain a continuous, following perspective.
theory_units.expected_effect: Seamlessly covers the actor's change in direction, keeps the actor framed consistently, and maintains audience immersion.

theory_units.title: Suggesting Doom with Camera Motion and Actor Stillness
theory_units.summary: When actors pause their movement but the camera continues to track, a suggestion of doom or unease can be introduced.
theory_units.applies_when: When characters are in a menacing context (e.g., deserted street, war sounds) and temporarily halt their movement while the camera persists.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a strong suggestion of impending doom or heightened tension through the contrast of motion and quietness.
theory_units.caution: Effect relies heavily on the overall context and other elements of the scene.

theory_units.title: Static Player as Pan Pivot
theory_units.summary: Utilize a stationary player as a pivot point for a panning motion during a tracking shot to reframe other subjects.
theory_units.applies_when: When reframing a scene with stationary subjects, and one subject can serve as a natural anchor for the camera's pivot.
theory_units.expected_effect: Dynamically shifts focus and framing within a static group, using one character as a visual anchor.

theory_units.title: Opposing Camera and Player Movements for Emphasis
theory_units.summary: Arrange shots where the camera and performers move in opposite directions (converging or diverging) to stress a performer/situation or underline a mood break.
theory_units.applies_when: To visually stress a character, a situation, or to mark a significant shift in the scene's mood or narrative.
theory_units.expected_effect: Emphatically highlights a performer or situation, underlines a break in the mood of the play through visual means, and can create visual stress with multiple converging/diverging movements.
theory_units.caution: Requires at least two or three players for optimal visual stress when using multiple movements.

theory_units.title: Three-Quarter Angle for Approaching Groups
theory_units.summary: When a camera moves in the opposite direction to an on-coming group and does not pan, angle the camera forward in a three-quarter position.
theory_units.applies_when: To comfortably observe a large group of players approaching the camera and moving out of frame, without using a pan.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows comfortable viewing of the approaching players, preventing the perceived motion from becoming too fast or annoying.
theory_units.caution: Placing the camera parallel (profile view) will make the players appear to cross the screen too quickly, leading to uncomfortable and annoying viewing.

theory_units.title: Inverting Player Positions with Obstruction
theory_units.summary: Achieve an inversion of player positions on screen by having a moving actor walk between a static player and the moving camera.
theory_units.applies_when: To visually shift the prominence or order of subjects on screen, or to reveal new relationships.
theory_units.expected_effect: An inversion of the players' screen positions, adding a dynamic shift to the composition.

theory_units.title: Complex Track and Pan for Mirror Reflections
theory_units.summary: Combine track and pan movements to incorporate mirror reflections, creating intricate framings that show multiple perspectives simultaneously.
theory_units.applies_when: To creatively reveal a character's internal state, relationships, or surroundings by using reflections within the shot.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a complex, multi-layered composition, showing the subject, their reflection, and the reflection of others within a single frame.

theory_units.title: Pan-Track-Pan Structure for Introduction & Destination
theory_units.summary: Use an opening pan to introduce players, track with them as they speak, and cap the shot with another pan to reveal their destination. This technique uses tracking only for the most crucial part of the shot.
theory_units.applies_when: When introducing characters, following their journey, and showing their ultimate destination within a single shot.
theory_units.expected_effect: Smoothly introduces subjects, guides the audience through their journey, and reveals their goal, making the tracking movement impactful.

theory_units.title: Quarter Circle Pan for Group Meeting
theory_units.summary: Employ a quarter circle pan to cover the approach of main players and frame the entire group when they meet.
theory_units.applies_when: When characters are approaching and about to converge with an existing group.
theory_units.expected_effect: Smoothly transitions from an individual or small group approach to a wider shot encompassing the full gathering.

theory_units.title: Faster Tracking for Sequential Revelation in a Line
theory_units.summary: When tracking a single file of players, move the camera faster than they do to reveal each actor one by one and swiftly leave them behind.
theory_units.applies_when: When you want to emphasize individual subjects in a moving line, quickly moving past each one to highlight them sequentially.
theory_units.expected_effect: Highlights individuals in a rapid sequence, conveying a sense of progression or passing time over the line.

theory_units.title: Constant Speed Tracking for Dynamic Single File Presentation
theory_units.summary: Maintain a constant camera tracking speed with a single file line of actors, allowing them to enter range, slow down to pace with the camera, then increase speed and exit as the next person takes their place.
theory_units.applies_when: When presenting a series of individuals in a moving line dynamically and continuously, often to create a rhythmic flow.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a continuous, dynamic presentation of individuals in a line, emphasizing the ongoing nature of the procession.

theory_units.title: Camera-Paced Actor Overtaking Line
theory_units.summary: Move the camera faster than a group of actors in a line, in sync with one particular actor, so that this actor gradually passes each other player.
theory_units.applies_when: When highlighting one individual's progression relative to a group, or to convey a sense of 'passing by' others in a dynamic way.
theory_units.expected_effect: Draws focus to the individual actor's movement and journey through or past the group.

theory_units.title: Counter-Directional Movement for Dynamic Shot
theory_units.summary: Have a line of people move in the opposite direction to the main actor and the camera, keeping the main actor centered in view (foreground or background).
theory_units.applies_when: When creating a highly dynamic shot that emphasizes a central figure against a moving, contrasting background or foreground.
theory_units.expected_effect: Produces a very dynamic shot, highlighting the central actor's presence amidst a moving environment.

theory_units.title: Three-Quarter Angle for Moving Groups
theory_units.summary: When covering a moving group from a tracking camera, angle the camera three-quarters towards the line, rather than parallel to it.
theory_units.applies_when: When filming any moving group or line of people with a tracking camera.
theory_units.expected_effect: Shows the action in a much clearer and more engaging way, providing better depth and perspective.
theory_units.caution: Never position the camera parallel to the moving line, as this offers a less clear view.

theory_units.title: Tracking Speed as Commentary
theory_units.summary: The speed at which the camera moves towards or away from a static subject or group inherently comments upon the scene, influencing the audience's perception.
theory_units.applies_when: Whenever moving the camera towards or away from a static subject or group.
theory_units.expected_effect: Conveys mood, emotion, and narrative emphasis through the pace of the camera's approach or retreat.

theory_units.title: Tracking to Close-Up for Emphasis
theory_units.summary: Use a tracking motion to transition from a full shot to a close shot of a player, specifically to stress a facial expression or body movement at the end of the track.
theory_units.applies_when: When you need to highlight a specific emotional reaction or physical detail of a character with impact.
theory_units.expected_effect: Draws immediate audience attention to the character's nuanced expression or gesture, enhancing dramatic effect.

theory_units.title: Swift Departure Track to Reveal Foreground Information
theory_units.summary: Employ a swift backward tracking movement (departure) to reveal new information in the foreground that has prompted a reaction from a player seen in a close shot.
theory_units.applies_when: When you want to quickly unveil a new plot element or environmental detail in the foreground, directly linking it to a character's recent reaction.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates surprise or clarification by showing the cause of a character's reaction, building tension or understanding.

theory_units.title: Slow Tracking for Intimate Mood
theory_units.summary: Utilize slow tracking movement, quietly creeping in towards a player, to establish an intimate mood.
theory_units.applies_when: When desiring to create a sense of closeness, quiet observation, or personal connection with a character.
theory_units.expected_effect: Cultivates an intimate, quiet, and personal atmosphere around the character.

theory_units.title: Slow Tracking for Audience Identification and Sympathy
theory_units.summary: Slow and steady tracking movements towards a speaking or silent player encourage the audience to identify with them more fully, fostering greater sympathy.
theory_units.applies_when: When aiming for deep audience connection with a character's internal state, thoughts, or problems.
theory_units.expected_effect: Strengthens audience identification with the character, making their problems feel shared and increasing sympathy.

theory_units.title: Slow Backward Tracking for Sadness or Loneliness
theory_units.summary: Employ slow, backward tracking to emphasize feelings of sadness or loneliness, effectively isolating a stationary player from the audience.
theory_units.applies_when: When visually conveying a character's isolation, sorrow, or a growing sense of detachment from their surroundings or others.
theory_units.expected_effect: Stresses sadness and loneliness, visually isolating the player and creating emotional distance.

theory_units.title: Consistent Tracking Speed for Repetitive Movements
theory_units.summary: When utilizing repetitive tracking movements—whether sideways across locations or accompanying different subjects across multiple shots—ensure the tracking speed remains consistent.
theory_units.applies_when: When intercutting or sequencing shots that feature similar tracking movements but cover different subjects or locations.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains visual coherence and rhythmic flow across multiple shots, preventing noticeable and potentially jarring speed changes.
theory_units.caution: Varying speeds from shot to shot will draw attention to the change and mark the effect, potentially breaking consistency.

theory_units.title: Delayed Camera Movement for Motivated Track
theory_units.summary: Begin a shot with a stationary camera as the subject approaches, initiating camera movement (e.g., tracking back) only when the subject is nearby.
theory_units.applies_when: When aiming to introduce camera movement naturally and smoothly, making it feel less arbitrary.
theory_units.expected_effect: Naturalizes the camera movement, preventing it from drawing attention to itself and allowing the audience to unconsciously move with the scene.

theory_units.title: Gradual Camera Movement Start
theory_units.summary: When initiating camera movement, start slowly and gradually gain speed to prevent the camera from drawing attention to itself.
theory_units.applies_when: At the beginning of any camera movement, especially tracking or dolly shots.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures a smooth, unobtrusive start to camera movement, making it feel organic to the scene.

theory_units.title: Player's Action Motivates Camera Movement
theory_units.summary: It is advisable to have a player pause in front of the camera and then, as they move on, start the camera moving with them, so the player's action motivates the camera's movement.
theory_units.applies_when: When initiating camera movement, especially tracking shots, to make the movement feel natural and justified.
theory_units.expected_effect: Camera movement is accepted naturally by the audience because it is motivated by character action, fulfilling their subconscious desire to move with the scene.

theory_units.title: Reverse Tracking for Subjective View (Intercut)
theory_units.summary: Intercut a long tracking shot of a player with reverse tracking shots of what the performer is looking at. This reversed movement creates the player's subjective point of view.
theory_units.applies_when: When you want to visually stress the viewpoint of a moving player and have the audience experience the scene through their eyes.
theory_units.expected_effect: Visually stresses the player's viewpoint, making the audience alternately become the player advancing to a target or observing what they see.

theory_units.title: Intercutting Static Cut-Aways into Tracking Master Shot
theory_units.summary: Intercut static cut-away shots into a continuous frontal tracking master shot, ensuring constant camera and player movement in the master shot. These cut-aways comment on or stress story points.
theory_units.applies_when: When you have a moving character (master shot) and need to insert static shots to show reactions, introduce details, or provide context without interrupting the master shot's flow.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhances story points, provides context or reactions, and maintains visual coherence even if subjects in cut-aways are not directly related visually to the master shot's subject.

theory_units.title: Sound Coherence for Intercut Master/Static Shots
theory_units.summary: When intercutting a master tracking shot with stationary shots, use a common and pervasive noise on the soundtrack to provide coherence, especially when visual connections are indirect.
theory_units.applies_when: When intercutting a tracking master shot with static shots where the visual relationship between subjects is not immediately clear or strong.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhances coherence across disparate shots, immerses the audience, and maintains the overall mood or tension of the scene.

theory_units.title: Restrained Use of Circular Tracking
theory_units.summary: Use continuous circular camera movement with restraint, reserving it only for moments when strong dramatic reasons explicitly demand it.
theory_units.applies_when: Considering any continuous circular tracking shot.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures the camera movement serves the story rather than distracting from it.
theory_units.caution: A continuous tracking circular shot tends to eclipse the story point by calling undue attention to the camera acrobatics.

theory_units.title: Circular Tracking for Overwhelming Emotional Experience (Two People)
theory_units.summary: Use circular tracking around two people to convey an overwhelming emotional experience that becomes a key turning point in their relationship.
theory_units.applies_when: When dramatizing a profound, shared emotional moment between two characters, such as a significant reconciliation or declaration.
theory_units.expected_effect: Magnifies emotional intensity, emphasizes the bond between the characters, and makes the moment feel pivotal and significant.

theory_units.title: Circular Tracking with One Moving Player
theory_units.summary: Achieve variation in circular tracking by having the camera move with one player in a circle around a stationary central performer, keeping the moving player facing the camera while the other is seen from constantly changing viewpoints.
theory_units.applies_when: When exploring the dynamic between a moving and a stationary character within a circular motion, or to highlight one character's perspective while revealing another from multiple angles.
theory_units.expected_effect: Highlights the moving player's perspective, shows the stationary player's reaction from multiple angles, and adds dynamic visual interest.

theory_units.title: Half-Circle Tracking for Mood or Dependence
theory_units.summary: A half-circle camera movement can effectively convey a specific mood, such as moving behind a group of people to keep a central leader framed in the background, stressing a feeling of dependence.
theory_units.applies_when: When establishing a particular mood, showing a group's collective reaction, or emphasizing the influence of a central figure over a group.
theory_units.expected_effect: Conveys a specific mood and stresses dependence on a central figure or force by maintaining focus on them as a pivot point.

theory_units.title: Choreographed Camera Movement for Character Revelation
theory_units.summary: Employ complex half-circle pan/track movements in long takes to reveal frontal views of central characters at key moments, allowing the audience to witness their reactions to continuous background action.
theory_units.applies_when: When a director wants to maintain continuous action in a scene while selectively revealing character reactions to specific, significant moments within that action, especially from different perspectives or with different groups scrutinizing each other.
theory_units.expected_effect: Engages audience by showing continuous action, highlights specific character reactions, creates a sense of scrutiny, and allows for dynamic shifts in perspective within a single take.
theory_units.caution: Activity in the center of the stage should be glimpsed at intervals and only at peak moments of action significant for character reactions, not continuously.

theory_units.title: Crane for Vertical Actor Movement
theory_units.summary: Use a camera crane to follow actors moving vertically (e.g., up/down stairs) to maintain consistent framing (e.g., medium shot) throughout their ascent/descent.
theory_units.applies_when: An actor is moving significantly up or down between different levels in a scene.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains continuity and focus on the actor, providing a smooth visual flow for vertical action.

theory_units.title: Crane for Scene Punctuation and Group Transitions
theory_units.summary: Utilize crane movements to create visual 'punctuation' or to smoothly transition between a tight foreground group and a larger background group.
theory_units.applies_when: When needing to emphasize a moment, or to transition between different group compositions (e.g., moving from individual focus to wider context).
theory_units.expected_effect: Adds emphasis, creates dynamic shifts in perspective and scale, guides audience attention.

theory_units.title: Slow Vertical Crane for Emotional Mood
theory_units.summary: Employ slow vertical crane movements to subtly comment emotionally on the mood of a scene.
theory_units.applies_when: A director wants to convey or emphasize a specific emotional tone or mood in a scene without overt action.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a contemplative, reflective, or weighted emotional atmosphere.

theory_units.title: Aerial View for Detached Perspective
theory_units.summary: Utilize unexpected aerial views, possibly combined with tracking, to provide the audience with a detached and impartial viewpoint.
theory_units.applies_when: A director wants to create a sense of objectivity, detachment, or to show the insignificance of individual characters within a larger context.
theory_units.expected_effect: Fosters a sense of impartiality, detachment, or a God's-eye view, making the audience feel like an observer rather than directly involved.

theory_units.title: Vertical Foreground Prop for Enhanced Height
theory_units.summary: When performing an upward or downward crane movement, include a vertical object in the foreground to create an illusion of depth and enhance the sensation of height for the audience.
theory_units.applies_when: Executing an upward or downward crane movement, and the goal is to emphasize or increase the perceived height/depth of the scene.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a stronger sense of vertical scale and depth, making the ascent or descent feel more dramatic or expansive.

theory_units.title: Crane for Visualizing Complex Sets and Story Points
theory_units.summary: Use crane movements to visually describe complex sets or scenarios, transitioning from a general wide view (e.g., of a crowd/ceremony) to a particular point of interest, or vice versa.
theory_units.applies_when: Introducing a complex setting or scene with multiple elements, and the director wants to guide the audience's attention from the overall context to specific details or characters.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides narrative clarity, creates a sense of scale, and guides the audience's eye through the scene.

theory_units.title: Camera Movement Serves Action
theory_units.summary: Camera movements, especially crane shots, must be designed to adapt to and enhance the dramatic purposes of the scene's action, not the other way around. Action is primary, camera movement secondary.
theory_units.applies_when: Planning any camera movement, particularly complex ones like crane shots.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures camera movement is motivated and contributes meaningfully to the storytelling, avoiding gratuitous or distracting motion.
theory_units.caution: Misuse of crane motion is easy—in particular there is a temptation to swing the camera. This can ruin a film. Crane movements should be used sparsely and only when they contribute something of value to the scene.

theory_units.title: Dynamic Camera for Static Subjects
theory_units.summary: Combine crane and tracking shots to visually describe and inject movement into scenes featuring static groups or situations, highlighting mood and details without character movement.
theory_units.applies_when: Presenting a group of characters or a situation that is inherently static, but the director wants to maintain visual interest and convey mood/details without character movement.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates visual dynamism in a static scene, highlights individual details within a group, and enhances the mood or psychological state of the subjects (e.g., stress, discipline).
theory_units.caution: If static subjects are photographed from static camera positions, a series of jump cuts would result, leading to a visually weaker outcome.

theory_units.title: Antithesis of Static Subjects and Dynamic Camera
theory_units.summary: When subjects are static (e.g., rows of players), employing a dynamic camera (movement) creates a visually stronger and more engaging result than a static camera.
theory_units.applies_when: Photographing static subjects or groups.
theory_units.expected_effect: Avoids visual monotony, creates dynamism, maintains audience engagement, and prevents jump cuts.
theory_units.caution: Static rows of players and static camera set-ups hardly go together. The antithesis is visually stronger.

theory_units.title: Crane Movement for Highlighting Story Points
theory_units.summary: Utilize a complex crane movement (e.g., descending then rising, or an arc) to transition from a wide, general view to a particular story point (often featuring characters making a point) and then back to a broader perspective. Can be adapted for slow or fast action.
theory_units.applies_when: A director wants to emphasize a specific narrative beat or dialogue point made by characters within a larger, ongoing scene, while maintaining a sense of scale and continuous movement.
theory_units.expected_effect: Draws attention to the crucial story point, creates a sense of journey or progression, and can evoke a majestic or expansive feeling.
theory_units.caution: If the camera remains level on the crane platform, it would only show distant views at the beginning and end, and actors would be revealed halfway through the vertical movement, losing early/late emphasis.

theory_units.title: Crane for Coherent Cuts in Disorganized Crowds
theory_units.summary: When filming a disorganized crowd from a height where clear 'cut on action' points are lacking, introduce a camera crane movement to provide the necessary visual coherence for cutting to a reverse or contrasting shot.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming a chaotic or disorganized crowd where clean cuts are difficult due to a lack of clear subject movement for action-based edits.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enables smoother and more motivated cuts between shots, maintaining visual flow despite the disorganized action within the frame.
theory_units.caution: Cutting to a reverse shot is difficult if strong movement is lacking in a disorganized crowd scene.

theory_units.title: Opposing Camera Tracks for Disorganized Action Cohesion
theory_units.summary: When filming disorganized motion (e.g., a crowd), employing two tracking shots that move in opposite directions can provide visual cohesion and allow for smoother cuts, even if the subjects' movements are chaotic.
theory_units.applies_when: Trying to achieve visual cohesion and facilitate cutting in scenes with disorganized or conflicting subject movements.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a dynamic visual flow that makes cuts smoother and the overall scene more coherent, even with chaotic internal action.

theory_units.title: Tracking vs. Zooming: Perspective vs. Magnification
theory_units.summary: Tracking shots alter the scene's perspective (foreground features grow faster than background), while zoom shots magnify all parts of the scene equally without changing perspective, often flattening depth.
theory_units.applies_when: Deciding between physically moving the camera (tracking) or changing the lens's focal length (zooming) to achieve a desired visual effect.
theory_units.expected_effect: Choosing tracking creates a dynamic perspective shift and immersion; choosing zoom creates a flattening effect and direct magnification without spatial distortion.
theory_units.caution: Misunderstanding this fundamental difference can lead to unintended visual effects on perspective and depth.

theory_units.title: Fast Zoom for Shock and Punctuation
theory_units.summary: Use a fast zoom to create a shock effect, provide visual punctuation, and sharply pinpoint a chosen subject, excluding surroundings.
theory_units.applies_when: A director wants to suddenly draw the audience's attention to a specific detail or reaction, or to create a jarring, impactful visual.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates an abrupt, shocking, or emphatic revelation, isolating the subject and intensifying its presence (e.g., stressing a reaction, revealing a hidden object, highlighting a silent witness).

theory_units.title: Ideal Zoom Pacing: Slow-Fast-Slow
theory_units.summary: For zooms utilizing the full focal range, an ideal pacing involves starting slow, gradually increasing speed, and then slowing down for the conclusion (slow-fast-slow).
theory_units.applies_when: Performing a zoom that covers a significant portion or the full range of the lens's focal length, and a pleasing, controlled visual flow is desired.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a smoother, more aesthetically pleasing transition, guiding the audience's eye without jarring movements.
theory_units.caution: A fast start and slow conclusion to a zoom will be quite sharp and disturbing to the eye.

theory_units.title: Short Zoom Sections for Effectiveness
theory_units.summary: Instead of using the full range of a zoom lens in a single movement, employing shorter, more selective zoom sections is generally more effective.
theory_units.applies_when: Deciding how much of the zoom lens's range to use for a particular shot.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates more precise and impactful zooms, avoiding gratuitous or over-extended movements.

theory_units.title: Avoiding Unmotivated Zooms
theory_units.summary: Zooming towards a static subject without clear motivation tends to draw attention to the camera movement itself, potentially distracting the audience.
theory_units.applies_when: Considering zooming on a subject that is not moving or providing other strong visual/narrative motivation.
theory_units.expected_effect: If unmotivated, can break immersion and make the audience aware of the camera; if motivated, maintains immersion and serves narrative.
theory_units.caution: Zooming towards a static subject draws attention to the zoom itself, which can feel artificial.

theory_units.title: Slow Zoom for Intimacy and Participation
theory_units.summary: A slow, creeping zoom towards a subject (e.g., tear-filled eyes) can create an intimate mood, suggesting audience participation in the character's emotion.
theory_units.applies_when: A director wants to draw the audience into a character's emotional state, fostering empathy and a sense of close observation.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhances intimacy, promotes audience identification with the character, creates emotional intensity.

theory_units.title: Player Movement as Zoom Motivation
theory_units.summary: Player movement, especially moving with or against the optical change of the zoom, provides strong motivation and better integrates the zoom into the shot.
theory_units.applies_when: Considering using a zoom, especially to avoid it feeling unmotivated or artificial, by linking it to character action.
theory_units.expected_effect: Makes the zoom feel natural and purposeful, maintaining audience immersion and focus on the action or a key revelation.

theory_units.title: Pan-Zoom for Evolving Interactions
theory_units.summary: Combine a pan with a zoom (e.g., a short pan accompanying a player, concluding on a zoom close-up of both) to dynamically reveal or emphasize character interactions as they unfold.
theory_units.applies_when: A director wants to show a character approaching another, culminating in an interaction, and wants to dynamically shift focus and shot size.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a smooth visual transition, highlights the evolving relationship or confrontation between characters, and brings the audience closer to the interaction.

theory_units.title: Head Turn Motivates Pan-Zoom Exploration
theory_units.summary: A character's head turn, especially in a close shot reacting to off-screen sound, can motivate an exploratory pan combined with a slow zoom to reveal a new point of interest.
theory_units.applies_when: A character reacts to something off-screen, and the director wants to follow their gaze/attention to reveal the source or a new story point dynamically and organically.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a sense of discovery, guides audience attention naturally, and makes the camera movement feel motivated by character action, creating an illusion of smooth travel.

theory_units.title: Half-Circle Pan-Zoom for Sweeping Exploration
theory_units.summary: Combine a half-circle pan with a forward or backward zoom to create a sweeping, arc-like exploratory movement that scans large areas like landscapes, buildings, or interiors, or follows a lone player moving between zones.
theory_units.applies_when: A director wants to convey a sense of vastness, explore an environment dynamically, or follow a character's journey through multiple spaces with a single, fluid shot.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a grand, expansive, or intimate sense of discovery, guiding the audience through the space or following a journey.

theory_units.title: Alternating Pan-Zoom for Comparative Scrutiny
theory_units.summary: Employ alternating pans and zooms between two or more subjects to draw detailed comparative attention to each, often progressively increasing magnification to extreme close-ups.
theory_units.applies_when: A director wants to intensely compare or scrutinize multiple specific items (e.g., photographs, reflections), often from a character's subjective viewpoint.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a sense of intense examination, highlights subtle differences or connections between subjects, and draws the audience into a detailed analytical process.

theory_units.title: Tilt-Zoom Out for Establishing Shots
theory_units.summary: Combine an upward tilt with a backward zoom out to a wide angle to smoothly transition from a close detail to an establishing full shot of a larger scene.
theory_units.applies_when: A director wants to introduce a new location or scene by first showing an intriguing detail and then revealing its broader context.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a smooth, revealing transition that contextualizes a specific detail within its larger environment, establishing the scene effectively.

theory_units.title: Combined Track-Zoom for Narrative Emphasis
theory_units.summary: Combine a continuous camera track with an undulating zoom pattern (e.g., zooming in and out on a specific character) to create multiple layers of movement, emphasizing narrative points within an ongoing scene.
theory_units.applies_when: A director wants to maintain a continuous, overall movement (e.g., tracking through a battle) while simultaneously drawing attention to individual characters or details at specific moments.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains scene flow while allowing for selective emphasis, creating a dynamic and immersive experience that highlights both the broad action and key individual elements.

theory_units.title: Masking Zooms with Track and Pan
theory_units.summary: Combining tracking and panning with a zoom can mask the zoom motion, creating an illusion of unhampered camera movement and rendering the zoom almost imperceptible if executed slowly.
theory_units.applies_when: A director wants to incorporate a zoom effect without it being overtly noticeable or artificial, aiming for a fluid and natural camera flow.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a seamless and organic camera movement, allowing the zoom to serve its purpose (e.g., re-framing, emphasizing) without drawing attention to itself.
theory_units.caution: The zoom must be slow enough to be rendered almost imperceptible when combined with tracking and panning.

theory_units.title: Opposed Track and Zoom Distortion
theory_units.summary: Combining a camera tracking backward with a simultaneous lens zoom forward creates a peculiar optical distortion of distances and object sizes.
theory_units.applies_when: To achieve a startling visual effect, especially in enclosed spaces like corridors, conveying disorientation or a strange perception of depth and size.
theory_units.expected_effect: Peculiar distortion of distances and object sizes, a 'startling visual effect', sense of disorientation.

theory_units.title: Three-Quarter Angle Track Back & Oblique Zoom
theory_units.summary: A camera angled three-quarters to a group, moving backward at full speed, then zooming in obliquely towards the subjects, creates a subtle visual distortion and dynamic movement.
theory_units.applies_when: To create a dynamic and subtly distorting shot when moving in front of a group, such as a cavalry charge, without being as 'blunt' as a full opposed track/zoom.
theory_units.expected_effect: Subtle visual distortion, dynamic movement, immersive feeling with the group.

theory_units.title: Zooming Through Foreground Obstacles
theory_units.summary: Start a zoom shot on wide angle with foreground and background in focus; as the lens moves to telephoto, foreground objects blur into color, revealing the sharply focused main action.
theory_units.applies_when: To dramatically reveal main action or a character by initially obscuring them behind foreground obstacles, creating a sense of discovery.
theory_units.expected_effect: Dramatic revelation of main action, increased visual interest, selective focus, sense of looking through something.

theory_units.title: Animated Foreground Obstacles for Zoom
theory_units.summary: Enhances the effect of zooming through foreground obstacles if the irregular foreground objects themselves have movement, preferably a repetitive motion.
theory_units.applies_when: When utilizing foreground obstacles in a zoom shot, to add an extra layer of dynamism and visual texture to the revelation.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increased visual interest and dynamism, more complex visual texture, heightened sense of movement in the scene.

theory_units.title: Vehicle Overturn Camera Trick
theory_units.summary: Simulate a vehicle overturning by filming it speeding diagonally towards the camera, panning to follow until it fills the frame, then suddenly rotating the camera on its side.
theory_units.applies_when: To create the visual effect of a vehicle overturning spectacularly without actual destruction, often for high-speed crash sequences.
theory_units.expected_effect: Illusion of a vehicle overturning, heightened drama, intense action.
theory_units.caution: The horizon line must not be visible on screen, and the camera must be tilted in a direction contrary to the moving vehicle.

theory_units.title: Show, Don't Tell in Action Scenes
theory_units.summary: Prioritize visual storytelling over dialogue in action scenes to maintain momentum and clarify events, with dialogue reduced to brief commands or used as strategic pauses.
theory_units.applies_when: During action sequences to maximize visual impact, maintain audience engagement, and ensure the narrative is conveyed through direct observation.
theory_units.expected_effect: Heightened action, clearer visual narrative, sustained tension and pace.
theory_units.caution: Continuous action can saturate emotion; dialogue can be used in pauses to clarify story points or give audience rest.

theory_units.title: Pacing Action with Pauses
theory_units.summary: Introduce strategic pauses within continuous action sequences to prevent audience emotional saturation, allowing for renewed interest and clarity, potentially using verbal explanations during these breaks.
theory_units.applies_when: During extended action sequences to manage audience emotion, prevent fatigue, and provide narrative clarification or character respite.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintained audience engagement, prevention of emotional fatigue, clearer understanding of story points, renewed tension after the pause.
theory_units.caution: Pauses should be purposeful and contribute to the rhythm of the action scene.

theory_units.title: Combat Sequence Pacing: Slow Build, Quick Resolve
theory_units.summary: Effectively structure combat by building tension slowly, often including a physical pause for combatants to recuperate, then resolving the fight quickly with a brief, decisive exchange of blows.
theory_units.applies_when: When designing a physical combat sequence to control tension, build anticipation, and deliver a satisfying, impactful resolution.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increased tension, dramatic climax, audience anticipation and emotional investment.

theory_units.title: Visual Introduction of Tools (Mechanism Defiance)
theory_units.summary: When depicting characters overcoming a mechanism, visually present the tools they will use, but provide no or only partial explanations of their intended employment to build suspense.
theory_units.applies_when: In sequences where characters confront and attempt to conquer a dangerous mechanism, to create anticipation and demonstrate ingenuity.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increased suspense, audience engagement through implied ingenuity, anticipation of how tools will be used.
theory_units.caution: Avoid full explanations to maintain mystery and allow for visual discovery during the action.

theory_units.title: Unpredictable Chase Outcome through Obstacles
theory_units.summary: Maintain audience unpredictability in chase outcomes by visually presenting a diverse range of obstacles for both pursuers and hunted, keeping the resolution uncertain.
theory_units.applies_when: When staging a chase sequence to maximize audience engagement and prevent the outcome from being easily foreseen.
theory_units.expected_effect: Sustained audience suspense, dynamic visual variety, unpredictable narrative progression.

theory_units.title: Location Design for Complex Chases
theory_units.summary: Choose intricate buildings and environments for complex chase variations (e.g., double chase) as they offer visual obstacles and possibilities, while open ground nullifies their effect.
theory_units.applies_when: When scouting or designing locations for chase sequences that involve multiple parties, varied paths, or intricate maneuvering.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhanced complexity and visual interest in chase scenes, increased tension through environmental obstacles.
theory_units.caution: Open ground diminishes the effectiveness of complex chase variations like the double chase.

theory_units.title: Pacing Action Resolution
theory_units.summary: Action sequences should conclude promptly after their narrative resolution; a humorous scene can then be used to effectively release built-up tension.
theory_units.applies_when: After the climax or resolution of an action sequence, to ensure efficient storytelling and manage the audience's emotional state.
theory_units.expected_effect: Satisfying and concise conclusion to action, effective emotional release for the audience, smooth transition to subsequent scenes.
theory_units.caution: Do not extend the action beyond its resolution point for too long, as this can diminish impact.

theory_units.title: Impersonal Point of View
theory_units.summary: The camera observes events externally, examining all players and situations without adopting any single character's perspective, thus positioning the audience as a detached spectator.
theory_units.applies_when: When the director wants the audience to observe action objectively, without strong emotional identification with a specific character, for a broader understanding of events.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience detachment, objective observation of events, broad understanding of the scene without deep emotional immersion.
theory_units.caution: This approach deliberately limits emotional participation from the audience towards individual characters.

theory_units.title: Subjective Point of View (Passive Observer)
theory_units.summary: To present action from a central player's passive viewpoint, use frontal close-up reaction shots of the character, intercut with long shots showing the action they are watching from their exact position.
theory_units.applies_when: When a central character is passively witnessing an event, to immerse the audience emotionally through their perspective and reactions.
theory_units.expected_effect: Strong audience identification with the character, emotional participation, heightened empathy and suspense through their gaze.

theory_units.title: Subjective Point of View (Active Participant - Setup)
theory_units.summary: When a player is actively engaged in action, establish the scene by emphasizing the central player with frontal close shots and close-ups, while showing distant views of their opponent.
theory_units.applies_when: During the setup phase of active combat or confrontation, to maintain emphasis on the protagonist's perspective and emotional involvement.
theory_units.expected_effect: Strong audience identification with the central character, heightened sense of their immediate involvement and the challenge they face.
theory_units.caution: This phase focuses on the protagonist's view, keeping the opponent somewhat distant.

theory_units.title: Combat POV Transition: Impersonal to Subjective
theory_units.summary: During physical combat, use full shots (impersonal POV) to clearly cover both combatants, then revert to the central character's subjective close-up POV as they separate, re-emphasizing the main player.
theory_units.applies_when: During direct physical engagement in action scenes, to balance clarity of the fight with emotional emphasis on the protagonist.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clear presentation of combat, re-establishment of emotional connection and visual emphasis with the protagonist after the direct confrontation.

theory_units.title: Exclusions in Subjective Reaction Shots
theory_units.summary: In subjective point-of-view reaction shots, the central character should not be seen in the foreground, nor from their opponent’s point of view, to maintain the immersive illusion of their perspective.
theory_units.applies_when: When maintaining a consistent subjective point of view for a central character, especially in reaction or observation shots.
theory_units.expected_effect: Sustained audience immersion and identification with the subjective character, preventing a break in the illusion.
theory_units.caution: Violating these exclusions shifts the POV to objective and breaks audience immersion.

theory_units.title: Maintaining Subjective POV During Character Movement
theory_units.summary: If the main player (whose POV the audience shares) moves, preserve the subjective perspective by panning or tracking the camera with them within the same static shot, avoiding cuts to wider, objective shots.
theory_units.applies_when: When the subjective character needs to move within the scene, to preserve emotional immersion and consistency of perspective.
theory_units.expected_effect: Preservation of audience emotion and immersion, continuous subjective experience without breaking the 'fourth wall' of the character's gaze.
theory_units.caution: Cutting to a full or wider shot will break the subjective POV and shift the perspective to objective.

theory_units.title: Alternating Subjective POVs for a Single Event
theory_units.summary: To present a central action from multiple perspectives, show each observer in a close shot, then cut to a long shot depicting the main event from their specific point of view, repeating this pattern for all observers.
theory_units.applies_when: When a significant central action is being observed by multiple characters from different vantage points, to build suspense and provide varied perspectives.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhanced suspense, comprehensive visual coverage of the event from different angles, audience engagement through multiple character perspectives.

theory_units.title: Dominant Central Action Payoff (from Multiple POVs)
theory_units.summary: After establishing a central action through multiple subjective points of view, shift emphasis by moving closer to the main action itself, making it dominant and relating it to its immediate climax or center of interest.
theory_units.applies_when: Following a sequence that uses multiple subjective POVs to observe a central action, to deliver the climax, immediate consequence, or direct engagement of that action.
theory_units.expected_effect: Climactic payoff, heightened intensity, a decisive shift from observation to direct involvement with the central event.

theory_units.title: Emotion-Driven Shifting Subjective POVs
theory_units.summary: Instead of a fixed pattern, subjective points of view shift dynamically, guided by the emotional flow of the event, engaging the audience through varying character perspectives as emotional intensity changes.
theory_units.applies_when: When covering an event with multiple key characters, where the director wants to emphasize the emotional impact on different individuals and guide the audience's emotional journey through shifting perspectives.
theory_units.expected_effect: Stronger emotional engagement, dynamic and fluid storytelling, emphasis on character reactions and internal states.
theory_units.caution: Requires careful management to ensure clarity and avoid audience confusion despite the 'random' shifting.

theory_units.title: Strategic POV Selection for Emotional Arc
theory_units.summary: Within sequences utilizing shifting subjective POVs, strategically choose which character's perspective to use at different moments to achieve specific emotional and narrative effects (e.g., initial observation, wider perspective, intimate involvement).
theory_units.applies_when: When designing a scene with multiple key characters where dynamic emotional engagement and varied perspectives are crucial for the narrative's emotional arc.
theory_units.expected_effect: Guided emotional journey for the audience, enhanced narrative complexity, deeper character insight and empathy.

theory_units.title: Dynamic Camera Mix for Chases (Static & Moving)
theory_units.summary: Enhance chase scenes by alternating static long shots with moving (tracking, hand-held) closer views of subjects, repeating this pattern, with short, sometimes jerky moving shots to add excitement.
theory_units.applies_when: To create visual impact, excitement, and a sense of urgency in chase scenes or sequences of running people.
theory_units.expected_effect: Heightened excitement, visual dynamism, increased audience engagement and immersion in the chase.
theory_units.caution: Moving camera shots should be of short duration (e.g., no more than 5 seconds) to avoid annoying the audience.

theory_units.title: Cumulative Action within a Static Deep-Focus Shot
theory_units.summary: Create excitement by staging multiple, overlapping actions within the various planes of depth of a single static shot, either progressively or simultaneously, from background to foreground.
theory_units.applies_when: To create a complex and exciting action sequence within a single shot, leveraging deep staging and intricate blocking.
theory_units.expected_effect: High visual excitement, a sense of continuous, unfolding action, rich visual information, audience immersion.
theory_units.caution: Actions must overlap swiftly and maintain rhythm to prevent the scene from slackening.

theory_units.title: Two-Shot Split for Emphasizing Blows (or Impacts)
theory_units.summary: To stress the violence of a physical blow or vehicle impact, divide it into two shots: the initial motion in a medium shot, and the concluding impact/swing in a close shot on the same visual axis.
theory_units.applies_when: To heighten the perceived violence, force, and impact of physical blows or collisions in action scenes.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increased visual impact and perceived violence, visceral audience reaction, dramatic emphasis.
theory_units.caution: Requires shooting two complete takes for editing; maintain a consistent visual axis between the shots.

theory_units.title: Foreground Obstruction for Action Scenes
theory_units.summary: Introduce moving foreground elements (combatants, animals, machines, or static objects filmed with camera movement) between the camera and the main action to create intermittent glimpses, heightening audience interest.
theory_units.applies_when: To add dynamism, suspense, and visual complexity to fighting or action scenes by partially obscuring and revealing the main event.
theory_units.expected_effect: Heightened audience interest and engagement, a sense of chaos or crowdedness, dynamic visual flow, increased intensity.
theory_units.caution: Foreground elements must not linger too long and should exit to be replaced; a long focal lens can be used to throw foreground combatants out of focus.

theory_units.title: Expanding-Contracting Pattern for Battle Coverage
theory_units.summary: In large-scale battles, alternate between wide crowd shots of general action and close-up scenes of hero(es) in personal combat, creating an expanding-contracting pattern that shifts audience focus from general to particular.
theory_units.applies_when: When directing large-scale battle scenes to manage audience perspective, maintain identification with main characters, and convey both spectacle and personal stakes.
theory_units.expected_effect: Stronger audience identification with characters within a larger spectacle, dynamic coverage of the battle, varied emotional engagement, a clearer narrative amidst chaos.
theory_units.caution: Both crowd scenes and protagonist scenes must have a central purpose and not be 'loose' or aimless.

theory_units.title: Climax Pacing: Random Shot Shortening
theory_units.summary: To build tension towards an imminent violent conclusion, use a succession of short shots leading to the payoff, with shot durations randomly decreasing to accelerate the pace.
theory_units.applies_when: When an imminent violent conclusion is anticipated by the audience, to build suspense and accelerate the narrative towards the payoff through abrupt cuts.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increased urgency, heightened tension, swift and jarring acceleration towards the climax.
theory_units.caution: While 'random', shot lengths should be purposefully shortened to achieve the desired effect.

theory_units.title: Climax Pacing: Progressive Shot Shortening
theory_units.summary: To build tension towards an imminent violent conclusion, use a succession of shots with progressively decreasing durations, culminating rapidly in the climax itself.
theory_units.applies_when: When an imminent violent conclusion is anticipated by the audience, to build suspense and smoothly yet rapidly accelerate the narrative towards the payoff.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increased urgency, heightened tension, swift, linear acceleration towards the climax.

theory_units.title: Parallel Editing for Pre-Climax Reactions
theory_units.summary: When building to a disaster or violent conclusion, use parallel editing across multiple narrative lines to showcase various characters' reactions preceding the event, enriching the build-up.
theory_units.applies_when: Leading up to a disaster or violent conclusion, to build suspense and provide a broader emotional context and stakes for the impending event.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increased suspense, multi-faceted emotional build-up, broader narrative engagement and understanding of the stakes.

theory_units.title: Progressively Diminishing Shot Length for Climax
theory_units.summary: Reduce the length of individual shots progressively as an event builds towards a visual climax to accelerate tempo and build tension.
theory_units.applies_when: Prior to a visual climax in a sequence, especially when building tension.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a mounting crescendo, quickens the film's tempo, builds brief tension in the audience, which finds relief in the outburst itself.

theory_units.title: Fragmenting Climactic Action with Intercut Reactions
theory_units.summary: Divide expected climactic, exciting, or violent actions into multiple shots and intercut them with character reactions to extend the event and maintain dramatic impact.
theory_units.applies_when: When the audience is expecting a climatic action, especially if the destruction is slow and massive.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides a detailed account of the catastrophe, stretches the event in time, doubles the visual pleasure for the audience, maintains dramatic impact, and enriches the version of the event.
theory_units.caution: Presenting the event in its entirety without interruptions lessens its dramatic impact and limits audience pleasure.

theory_units.title: Covering Climaxes with Multiple Points of View
theory_units.summary: Film a single climactic event from several distinct points of view, using each perspective judiciously within the sequence, to provide comprehensive coverage and emotional depth.
theory_units.applies_when: When covering a major catastrophic event or complex climax where multiple facets and emotional impacts are important.
theory_units.expected_effect: Obtains a richer version of the event, extends its on-screen duration by including varied perspectives (e.g., reaction shots), and provides a comprehensive understanding of the catastrophe.
theory_units.caution: Observe that the blowing up of the train was filmed from three points of view. Each of these shots was used only twice in the whole sequence to cover the catastrophe from beginning to conclusion. (Implies judicious use rather than overuse).

theory_units.title: Accelerated Motion (Undercranking)
theory_units.summary: Film at a slower frame rate than normal (e.g., 16 fps or 8 fps) and project at the standard rate (24 fps) to increase the apparent velocity of subjects.
theory_units.applies_when: For chase or action sequences to impart a dynamic effect, or when aiming for a comedic, jerky movement.
theory_units.expected_effect: Imparts a dynamic effect, increases the apparent velocity of the subject, makes movement appear more dramatic. At very low frame rates (e.g., 8 fps), it can produce laughter.
theory_units.caution: Care must be taken not to overdo this effect, or the movement will become so jerky that it will produce laughter (unless laughter is the desired effect).

theory_units.title: Slow Motion (Overcranking)
theory_units.summary: Film at a higher frame rate than normal (e.g., slightly higher than 24 fps) and project at the standard rate (24 fps) to slow down movement on screen.
theory_units.applies_when: To impart majesty to a movement, enhance climactic moments (jumps, plunges, explosions), or for dramatic death scenes.
theory_units.expected_effect: Acquires grace of movement, appears imposing, enhances the scene, adds dramatic weight to climaxes or death scenes.

theory_units.title: Maintaining Sharp Focus (Follow Focus)
theory_units.summary: Continuously adjust the lens focus to keep a subject sharply defined as the camera or subjects move, or as points of interest shift within the frame.
theory_units.applies_when: The camera tracks, pans, or tilts; actors move towards/away from the camera or pass by at different ranges; the camera remains stationary but shifts focus between subjects at different distances.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures the subject remains sharply defined and clear, guiding audience attention effectively.

theory_units.title: Deliberate Selective Focus for Dramatic Effect
theory_units.summary: Intentionally shift focus from one plane of depth (e.g., foreground) to another (e.g., background) within a single shot to create specific dramatic emphasis.
theory_units.applies_when: When a director wants to draw the audience's attention to a different part of the scene, reveal information, or create a specific dramatic effect by changing visual emphasis.
theory_units.expected_effect: Obtains many dramatic effects by selectively highlighting different subjects or areas within the frame.

theory_units.title: Editing in the Camera (Master Shot Choreography)
theory_units.summary: Achieve narrative and dramatic effects within a single, continuous film frame by meticulously choreographing camera and subject movement, eliminating the need for traditional visual cuts.
theory_units.applies_when: When desiring a smoothly flowing scene where the audience is not distracted by cuts, and actors can deliver continuous, uninterrupted performances, similar to theatre.
theory_units.expected_effect: Scene flows smoothly, audience is unaware of the technique, actors have a better chance to drop into their characters, dynamic results, faster shooting speed (if well-executed).
theory_units.caution: Requires careful pre-planning and precise execution; mistakes can be quite expensive, especially for limited budget productions, due to the amount of film expended in retakes. Thorough rehearsals are vital.

theory_units.title: Integrating Physical and In-Camera Editing
theory_units.summary: Combine traditional physical editing (fragmentation) with 'editing within the film frame' techniques to leverage the strengths of both approaches for maximum expressive potential.
theory_units.applies_when: When a filmmaker seeks to overcome the individual limitations of either traditional editing or in-camera editing, and to enrich their expressive screen language.
theory_units.expected_effect: Benefits from the best of both systems, surmounting their individual limitations, resulting in a richer and more versatile expressive screen language.

theory_units.title: Pause Between Movements (In-Camera Editing)
theory_units.summary: Within a continuous 'editing in the camera' shot, introduce deliberate pauses after a player or camera moves to a new zone, holding the position before proceeding to the next.
theory_units.applies_when: When executing a continuous shot where the camera or subjects move through multiple pictorial variations or zones.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows the audience sufficient time to appreciate and establish each new player or camera position and its pictorial variations.
theory_units.caution: If the movement is continuous and unbroken by pauses, it will become just a following shot, and the audience would not have time to appreciate the pictorial variations.

theory_units.title: Varying Action Zones (In-Camera Editing)
theory_units.summary: Manipulate the arrangement and relationship of action zones within the frame (using stationary, panning, or tracking cameras) to create an impression of space and prevent a static background in continuous shots.
theory_units.applies_when: When using 'editing in the camera' techniques to maintain visual interest and spatial impression in a continuous shot.
theory_units.expected_effect: Gives the impression of space wherein the actors move, prevents the background from becoming annoying or monotonous, and enhances visual dynamism.
theory_units.caution: If the camera remains stationary with a constant background, it will constitute a limitation and become annoying in a very short time.

theory_units.title: Approaching or Receding from Camera (Motion in Depth)
theory_units.summary: Utilize motion in depth (moving from foreground to background or vice versa) by subjects within a continuous shot, recorded by a stationary, panning, or tracking camera, to create visual variations and shift attention.
theory_units.applies_when: Desiring dynamic visual changes and clear shifts of action zones within a continuous shot, especially with multiple players.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures clear changes of action zones, is easy to execute, simple to understand, and unobtrusive for the audience, who will naturally follow the dominant motion.
theory_units.caution: When a group is involved, it is important that only one player at a time moves from zone to zone, with others remaining in their places.

theory_units.title: Panning to Unite Action Zones
